member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.AmbientOcclusionSettings
member.summary: How much of the sky each surface can actually see, and what colour the surfaces around it bounce onto it.

remarks.para: A flat ambient term says every surface receives the same light from every direction. Nothing in a real room does: the inside of a corner sees a sliver of sky, the underside of a crate sees none, and the difference between them is most of what tells the eye that two surfaces are touching. The original bought that with hand-painted lightmaps, which is why its interiors read so well and why nothing it did not bake — a soldier, a door, the player's own weapon — sits in a room rather than floating in it.

Both effects here are screen-space, and that is a real limitation rather than an implementation detail: they can only account for surfaces the camera can see. A wall just outside the frame neither occludes nor bounces, so turning the camera changes the shading slightly. The alternative is the probe volume in the next stage, which knows about geometry off screen and is correspondingly slower to update; the two are complementary and are meant to run together.

member.param: How many directions each pixel searches, or 0 for no occlusion at all. The cost is very nearly linear in this, and the noise it leaves is what the temporal accumulation is for — which is why this can be far lower here than it could be in a renderer resolving one frame at a time.

How far, in metres, a surface is considered able to occlude another. Small values darken only where surfaces touch; large ones shade whole rooms but start to look like a smudge, because a screen-space search cannot tell a distant wall from a near one it happens to line up with.
How strongly the result is applied, where 1 is the physical amount. Above 1 is a deliberate exaggeration, and is the usual setting, because the ambient term it multiplies is itself a simplification.
How many samples are spent gathering colour from neighbouring surfaces, or 0 for none. Reuses the same horizon search as the occlusion, so it is much cheaper than the number suggests.
How strongly the gathered colour is added back.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.BinocularDisplaySettings
member.summary: Turns the resolved frame into the picture seen through the remastered binocular optics: a glass lens display transform plus the fade that raises it.

remarks.para: This is a display transform, not an overlay. The world under it has to stay readable -- the whole point of the optics is to study the ground -- so the tint, the highlight lift and the vignette are derived from the resolved picture and the terrain, the buildings and the enemies all survive it.

It is separate from rather than a generalisation of it. That one is the map computer's tube; this is the first-person binocular's glass. The two are never on together -- the computer replaces the first-person view -- so they can coexist as independent uniforms without either changing what the other puts on screen.
Everything is continuous because the raise is the point: the glass bends into existence as the device comes up rather than snapping on. A boolean cannot express that.

member.param: How much of the glass transform is applied, 0 for the ordinary picture to 1 for full optics. Scales the bezel vignette, the tint and the edge falloff so the lens fades in as the binoculars are raised.
Extra chromatic fringing toward the lens edge, on top of the ordinary post-process value. Reserved for a bespoke edge split; 0 leaves the global chromatic-aberration pass to carry the fringing.
A continuously rising wall-clock time in seconds, for the animated grain and any breathing. Wall clock rather than a frame counter so the glass does not shimmer faster on a faster machine.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode
member.summary: How a draw call's fragments combine with what is already in the render target.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.Opaque
member.summary: Source replaces destination; alpha is ignored.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.AlphaBlend
member.summary: Standard source-alpha blending: src * srcA + dst * (1 - srcA).

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.Additive
member.summary: Additive blending: src * srcA + dst. Used by muzzle flashes, glows and lens effects.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.Modulate2X
member.summary: Doubled modulation: src * dst + dst * src, which is 2 * src * dst.
member.remarks: I.G.I. 2's terrain lightmap pass. TerrainRender_SetBlendMode (igi2ed 0x666B90) case 3 sets SRCBLEND = D3DBLEND_DESTCOLOR with DESTBLEND = D3DBLEND_SRCCOLOR, which the blender evaluates as the sum of the two products — a MODULATE2X. It is why a terrain lightmap's neutral is a half rather than white: the doubling is in the blend, not in the texels.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.SourcePlusAttenuatedDestination
member.summary: The source added in whole over the destination kept at the source's alpha: src + dst * srcA.
member.remarks: I.G.I. 2's water above quality nought. WaterRender_SetBlendState sets SRCBLEND = D3DBLEND_ONE with DESTBLEND = D3DBLEND_SRCALPHA, so a sheet's Alpha is how much of what lies under it shows through and its own colour is laid on top undimmed: a sea of alpha 0.13 is a dark, nearly opaque surface, not a faint one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.Modulate
member.summary: Plain modulation: dst * src, the frame multiplied by what is drawn.
member.remarks: Project I.G.I.'s terrain lightmap pass: sub_5144E0 mode 2 sets SRCBLEND = ZERO and DESTBLEND = SRCCOLOR over a SELECTARG1(TEXTURE) stage, so the page's colour multiplies the ground the material passes left, once -- white leaves it as it was.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.Darken
member.summary: Darkening: dst * (1 - src), the frame dimmed by the brightness of what is drawn.
member.remarks: Project I.G.I.'s sprites flagged 0x10 (D3DQVertex_SetBlendStates, 0x50E000: ZERO, INVSRCCOLOR): an explosion's black smoke, whose faint colour takes a little of the light behind it rather than painting it out.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode.AddColour
member.summary: Additive at full strength: src + dst, whatever the source's alpha.
member.remarks: Project I.G.I.'s additive face groups (0x49EC70's set_alpha_states: ONE, ONE, unlit and unfogged), its explosions' fireballs among them. weighs the source by its alpha, as I.G.I. 2's additive groups (Direct3DRender_SetBlendStateAdditive: SRCALPHA, ONE) and both games' sprites do; a fireball drawn that way burns at a fraction of its brightness.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable
member.summary: An authored colour grade, as a cube of output colours indexed by input colour.

remarks.para: The grading knobs — r_contrast, r_saturation — do this job procedurally, one named operation at a time. A lookup table is the same job with the answer written down instead: whatever the grade does to a colour, it does the same thing to that colour every time, so the whole of it can be sampled onto a grid once and read back with three coordinates. That buys two things the knobs cannot give. Any grade at all fits, including ones with no name and no formula, and the cost is one texture fetch however complicated it was to author.

Why 32 and not 64. The table is trilinearly interpolated, so what it must resolve is not the colour but the curvature of the grade between samples, and a grade is smooth almost everywhere. 32³ is 32,768 entries and the industry's default for exactly this reason; 64³ is eight times the memory to describe the same curve. A grade with a hard break in it — a key, a hue isolation — is the case that wants more, and this reads whatever size the file declares.

The .cube format, because it is text. Every colour tool exports it, and it can be read and corrected in a diff — which the alternative, a PNG strip of the cube's slices, cannot be. That matters more than it sounds: a grade is content, and content that can only be inspected by opening it in an image editor is content nobody reviews. Lines are R G B triples in 0–1, red varying fastest, then green, then blue.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable.MaxSize
member.summary: The largest cube edge that will be read.
member.remarks: 64³ is a quarter of a million entries and already more than a smooth grade needs; past that a file is far likelier to be malformed than to be a grade somebody meant.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable.MinSize
member.summary: The smallest cube edge that describes anything.
member.remarks: Below two there is nothing to interpolate between and the table is a single colour.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable.Name
member.summary: Gets what the table is called — its file name, for logging and for r_lut.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable.Size
member.summary: Gets the cube's edge length in samples.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable.Entries
member.summary: Gets the table as RGB triples, red varying fastest.
member.remarks: Length is cubed times three.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourLookupTable.Identity(System.Int32)
member.summary: Builds the table that changes nothing.
member.param: The cube's edge length.
member.returns: A table whose output colour is its input colour.
member.exception: is outside the supported range.
member.remarks: Worth having as more than a curiosity: sampling it is the test that the sampler's coordinate mapping is right. A LUT read with the naive colour instead of the half-texel inset colour × (N−1)/N + 0.5/N still looks plausible on a real grade and is visibly wrong on this one, because here any error is the whole of the difference.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourTemperature
member.summary: The colour a black body glows at a temperature, as a light's linear colour.

remarks.para: The Planckian locus in CIE 1931 chromaticity by Kim et al.'s cubic spline fit (valid 1667 K to 25000 K), taken to XYZ at unit luminance and then to linear Rec. 709 -- the space the renderer lights in. The result is normalised to a luminance of one, so a temperature changes a light's tint and never its strength.
A white LED torch sits around 5500-6500 K; an old incandescent one near 3000 K, which is the yellow beam of every film before the LEDs arrived.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ColourTemperature.ToLinearRgb(System.Single)
member.summary: Converts a colour temperature to a linear colour of luminance one.
member.param: The temperature, clamped to the fit's range.
member.returns: The colour, every channel non-negative.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.CombatEffectCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for what gunfire draws: the muzzle flame, impacts and the marks rounds leave.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.CombatEffectCVars.MuzzleFlash
member.summary: How bright a gun's muzzle flame draws, as a fraction of the original's.

remarks.para: The flame is an additive glow whose brightness rides its vertex colours, so this scales those at upload. Zero removes the flash entirely; one is the retail fireball, which vanilla pins so the original's picture stays exact.

The remastered presets sit at 0.45, measured against the tactical-ballistics tracers: the retail flame is bright enough to swallow the first metres of a tracer, and a subtler flash is what every modern shooter draws anyway.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.CombatEffectCVars.ImpactEffects
member.summary: Whether the original's own impact effects are drawn.
member.remarks: Retail behaviour, on everywhere including vanilla. The GunShotEffect a struck material names (0x438440) — a puff of concrete1.spr half the time and two to four chips of the material's own model — and the blood a body throws (0x463AD0), which is separately gated by the game's own blood option. This exists to be turned off for diagnosis, not for taste; is the remaster's extra burst on top.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.CombatEffectCVars.ImpactParticles
member.summary: How rich the extra remaster particle burst where a round lands is, or 0 for none.
member.remarks: A remaster addition on top of : sparks and dust composed from the material table's own row for the struck surface — metal showers sparks, dirt breathes a slow brown plume, a body a brief red mist. One is the authored look, two doubles the particle counts, and vanilla pins zero so a vanilla run shows the original's effects and nothing else.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.CombatEffectCVars.BulletMarks
member.summary: Whether the marks rounds leave on the world are drawn.
member.remarks: Presentation only — the marks are still recorded, so turning this back on shows them. Exists as much for diagnosis as for taste: decals are one of a handful of world-space quad renderers, and being able to rule them in or out from the console in seconds is worth a variable.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView
member.summary: What the frame shows instead of the scene, for looking at a pass rather than at the picture.
member.remarks: Every effect from here to the end of the remaster track reads a buffer it does not draw, and a buffer that is subtly wrong produces a picture that is plausibly wrong — a normal encoded in the wrong space still lights, a motion vector with a flipped sign still reprojects. The only cheap way to tell is to look at the buffer itself.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.None
member.summary: The scene, tone mapped as usual.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Albedo
member.summary: Surface colour with no lighting at all.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Normal
member.summary: View-space normals, remapped so that each axis is a colour.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Depth
member.summary: Depth, curved so that the near field is not all one shade.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Material
member.summary: Roughness in red, metallic in green, emissive in blue.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Motion
member.summary: Per-surface screen motion, scaled up hard because a frame's worth of it is a fraction of a pixel. Green is rightwards and red is downwards; a static world should be flat grey, and anywhere it is not is something the temporal resolve believes is moving.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.BakedLight
member.summary: The baked irradiance the original's lightmaps carry.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Ao
member.summary: How much of the sky each surface can see, white for open and black for buried.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Ssgi
member.summary: The colour neighbouring surfaces bounce onto each surface, with nothing else added.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Ssr
member.summary: What each surface reflects, with the scene under it removed.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Probes
member.summary: What the probe field alone says each surface receives, with no sun, no albedo and no occlusion. The one view that shows whether light is leaking through a wall, because leaked light is invisible once it has been multiplied by a dark surface.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Lighting
member.summary: The full lighting on a neutral grey material, a "lighting only" view. Base colour is replaced by a flat mid-grey so what remains is the light itself -- the sun, its shadows, the bounce and the sky fill, shaped by the surfaces' normals -- with the level's own textures taken out of the picture. The view for comparing this renderer's lighting against another's without the materials confusing the two.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.SunShadow
member.summary: How much of the sun reaches each surface after shadowing, white for lit and black for occluded. The view that separates "the sun never arrives" from "the surface faces away", because both look identical once multiplied into the shaded scene.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Wetness
member.summary: The standing water: where it lies, and what shape its surface is. Red is how much of the pixel is under water and green and blue are the water's own normal, so a puddle that is not rippling and a puddle that is not there look nothing alike — which, once they are shaded, they very much do.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.LampLight
member.summary: The lamps' light alone, with the sun, the sky, the bounce and every surface's own colour taken out — only what the level's local lights put on each surface, AFTER their shadowing. The view that settles whether a lamp is lighting through a wall: if a surface the wall should hide is lit here, the occlusion missed it; if it is black, the light on it in the finished picture came from somewhere else.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.UpscaleParallax
member.summary: The temporal pass's parallax verdict: white where the reprojected history held this surface, black where it was hidden behind something nearer and the history restarts.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.UpscaleShading
member.summary: The temporal pass's shading verdict: white where the history's shading still agrees with this frame, black where it has been contradicted and the history is clamped or rebuilt.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.UpscaleHistory
member.summary: How many frames' worth of samples each history texel holds, as a fraction of the ceiling: white is a fully converged history, black a texel that restarted this frame.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Roughness
member.summary: The G-buffer's roughness alone, black for a mirror and white for fully matte. The view that settles whether a derived roughness map is reaching the shader at all, because once it has been through a GGX lobe a twelve-per-cent spread at the matte end is invisible.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Metallic
member.summary: The G-buffer's metallic alone, black for a dielectric and white for bare metal. Expected to be flat black everywhere the level has no authored metal, which is how a channel that is carrying nothing is told apart from one that is carrying zero on purpose.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.MaterialAo
member.summary: The material occlusion the base colour's alpha carries, white for open and black for a crease. Distinct from , which is the screen-space horizon search: this one is baked into the texture and is the same in every frame from every angle.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.Glass
member.summary: What the level's glazing reflects, on its own, with the scene under it removed and BEFORE the Fresnel term is applied.
member.remarks: The one view that tells the three ways glass can come out wrong apart, which nothing in the final picture can: a reflection is a few per cent of a lit pixel head-on, so all three look identical there. Nothing visible anywhere means the panes never reached the layer at all — the raster half is not writing it. Panes visible as flat black shapes means the layer is right and the trace found nothing to resolve. Panes visible carrying the room means both halves work and the only thing left between here and the picture is the Fresnel weight.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.GlassRoute
member.summary: Which ROUTE each pane pixel's reflection came from, as a flat colour per route rather than as light.

remarks.para: says whether a reflection arrived; this says where it came from, and the two answer different questions. A pane can be carrying the room convincingly and still be resolving almost every pixel out of the surface cache, because a card of a wall looks like that wall — just flatter, coarser and lit by a bake rather than by this frame. That is invisible in the finished picture and invisible in the raw view, and it is the whole difference between a window that can show a person standing at it and one that never can.

Blue is a surface-cache CARD: static geometry, lit by the cache's own lighting. Yellow is the hit's own MATERIAL -- a body, or something the cache is too coarse to hold -- under the light the cards around it receive. White is a LIGHT: a lamp showing its own glow. Red is a ray that struck something solid nobody could name a material for, shaded as a neutral surface. Grey is the SKY on a clean miss.

Green, the LIT FRAME, should never appear. The frame is no longer a route: whether a reflected place is on screen depends on where the camera looks, so reading it made a pane change colour, gain and lose whole regions as the mouse moved. Green here means that route has come back.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.GlassAlbedo
member.summary: The TEXTURE a reflected ray found at the point it struck, with no lighting applied to it at all.

remarks.para: A reflected body that comes out flat and colourless has two causes that are indistinguishable in the finished picture, and this is what separates them. If the body appears here carrying its own colours and markings, the texture reached the shader and the LIGHTING crushed it. If it appears as a uniform mid-grey, that grey is the albedo array's own clear value, and the layer the hit named was never written — a registration problem, not a lighting one.
Only the material route writes anything here; a pixel resolved from the lit frame or from a card is black, because neither of those ever reads a texture.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.GlassRay
member.summary: The DIRECTION each pane pixel reflects in, as a colour.
member.remarks: Red is east, green is north, blue is UP, and each is centred on mid-grey so a negative component reads dark — so a pane reflecting the ground is dark blue and one reflecting the sky is bright. The question it answers is the one no other view can: whether a reflection that shows the wrong part of the world is aiming somewhere wrong, or aiming correctly and failing to find what is there. Those have nothing in common and look identical in every other view.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.GlassNormal
member.summary: The pane's own world normal, already turned to face the camera.
member.remarks: One step behind : the aim is twice the normal's error, so a reflection that points somewhere impossible is nearly always this. Blue is the UP component, and a vertical pane should have almost none of it — a window whose normal tilts is a window reflecting the sky where it should reflect the ground.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.LampShadow
member.summary: How much of each surface's lamp light gets past what stands in its way, after the denoisers: white where all of it arrives, black where none does, red where no lamp reaches the surface at all.
member.remarks: The traced ratio itself, before any lamp's colour, distance or facing multiplies it -- the one view that separates a lamp that is shadowed from a lamp that is simply far away or pointed elsewhere, which look the same once shaded.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.FlashlightLight
member.summary: The player's flashlight alone: what its beam puts on each surface, shadowed, and nothing else.
member.remarks: The beam's shape on the world -- its hot core, its rim and its spill -- with the rest of the frame's light taken away, for tuning the cookie without the room's own light in the way.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.FlashlightShadow
member.summary: How much of the flashlight reaches each surface: white where it all arrives, black in shadow.
member.remarks: The mask the shading multiplies the beam by, after its filter; white everywhere without one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.LampMarch
member.summary: What the software lamp march decided, where lamp shadows are marched through the distance field: red for the share of rays it stopped, green for the share it let through past a surface it was touching -- a receiver's own plane, a fitting, a slab the plane tests took for one of those.
member.remarks: The view that tells a leak through a thin canopy (green over the leak: the field held the slab and a test waved it through) from a slab the field never held at all (black: nothing near the ray). Black everywhere with ray tracing on, which does not march.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DebugView.LampMaps
member.summary: Which answer each software lamp-shadow ray got: red where a lamp's own cube of shadow maps held it shadowed, green where its map held it lit, blue where the lamp had no map covering the point and the distance field was marched instead.
member.remarks: The view that tells a lamp whose map is wrong (red over a wall it plainly lights) from one that has no map at all (blue: the coarse field decided), and both from a lamp whose map is right. Black everywhere with ray tracing on, which reads no maps.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.DeferredLocalLight
member.summary: One real-time local light handed to the deferred lighting for a single frame — a lamp fixture a level's emissive geometry implies, treated as a punctual source.

remarks.para: I.G.I. declares no point lights at all; these are inferred from where a level's emissive textures are drawn (see the game layer's light-fixture proposer). This struct is the renderer-facing form of one: the position is already in view space, the frame the lighting pass shades in, so the game layer does the world-to-view transform in double precision — the level sits at large world coordinates and subtracting the camera in float first would cost most of the mantissa.
The set is uploaded whole each frame and cleared after the pass, so a frame that submits none lights from none. is the shader's array size; a longer list is truncated.

member.param: The light's position in view space, in metres.
How far the light reaches before its windowed falloff takes it to zero, in metres.
The light's linear colour, its brightest channel around one.
The light's relative strength, already scaled by whatever global knob the caller applies.

The way the fixture faces, in view space, or zero for a light that shines every way.
A lamp is a housing with an opening: it throws light out of the opening and nothing out of the slab it is bolted to. Lit as a bare point instead, every ceiling fixture in the game puts a bright disc on the ceiling ABOVE it — light on the one surface that is physically behind the emitter — and there is nowhere in a room to stand where that is not visible.
Zero is a real answer and not a failure. A fixture whose geometry does not agree on a facing — a lamp modelled as a closed box, whose faces cancel — is better lit as a point than as a spot aimed at a guess, and the shader reads a zero vector as exactly that.

How big the fixture itself is, in metres — not how far it reaches, which is .
This is what makes a shadow a shadow rather than a stencil. Traced as a point, a lamp gives one binary answer per pixel: a hard edge, aliased along it, and identical whether the thing casting it is touching the wall or a room away. A real fitting is tens of centimetres across, so its shadow has a penumbra that widens with the gap between occluder and receiver — sharp under a crate, soft on the wall behind it. Only the source's size can say how wide.
The fixture's own extent, so it costs nothing to know: the extractor already measures how far the emitting geometry reaches from its centroid, because it needs that for the light's reach.
The long axis of the fixture's emitting rectangle in view space, scaled to HALF its length, or zero for a fixture lit as a point. Its shadow rays are aimed at points on this rectangle.

member.summary: One real-time local light handed to the deferred lighting for a single frame — a lamp fixture a level's emissive geometry implies, treated as a punctual source.

remarks.para: I.G.I. declares no point lights at all; these are inferred from where a level's emissive textures are drawn (see the game layer's light-fixture proposer). This struct is the renderer-facing form of one: the position is already in view space, the frame the lighting pass shades in, so the game layer does the world-to-view transform in double precision — the level sits at large world coordinates and subtracting the camera in float first would cost most of the mantissa.
The set is uploaded whole each frame and cleared after the pass, so a frame that submits none lights from none. is the shader's array size; a longer list is truncated.

member.param: The light's position in view space, in metres.
How far the light reaches before its windowed falloff takes it to zero, in metres.
The light's linear colour, its brightest channel around one.
The light's relative strength, already scaled by whatever global knob the caller applies.

The way the fixture faces, in view space, or zero for a light that shines every way.
A lamp is a housing with an opening: it throws light out of the opening and nothing out of the slab it is bolted to. Lit as a bare point instead, every ceiling fixture in the game puts a bright disc on the ceiling ABOVE it — light on the one surface that is physically behind the emitter — and there is nowhere in a room to stand where that is not visible.
Zero is a real answer and not a failure. A fixture whose geometry does not agree on a facing — a lamp modelled as a closed box, whose faces cancel — is better lit as a point than as a spot aimed at a guess, and the shader reads a zero vector as exactly that.

How big the fixture itself is, in metres — not how far it reaches, which is .
This is what makes a shadow a shadow rather than a stencil. Traced as a point, a lamp gives one binary answer per pixel: a hard edge, aliased along it, and identical whether the thing casting it is touching the wall or a room away. A real fitting is tens of centimetres across, so its shadow has a penumbra that widens with the gap between occluder and receiver — sharp under a crate, soft on the wall behind it. Only the source's size can say how wide.
The fixture's own extent, so it costs nothing to know: the extractor already measures how far the emitting geometry reaches from its centroid, because it needs that for the light's reach.
The long axis of the fixture's emitting rectangle in view space, scaled to HALF its length, or zero for a fixture lit as a point. Its shadow rays are aimed at points on this rectangle.
Half the emitting rectangle's width, across , in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.DeferredLocalLight.Maximum
member.summary: The most local lights a single frame can carry, matching the lighting shader's array size.

remarks.para: Sixty-four rather than thirty-two, because a level has more lamps than this and the ones that do not fit are SWITCHED OFF: with a smaller budget the far end of a corridor stayed dark and lit itself a few at a time as the player walked towards it, which reads as the lighting failing rather than as a budget being spent. Doubling it is most of the fix, and it is nearly free — the shader culls a light against its own reach before doing any work for it, so a lamp the pixel is nowhere near costs one distance test.

A hundred and sixty, which the OpenGL backend cannot hold. Sixty-four was its ceiling — default-block array uniforms, three vec4 arrays deep, 768 components of a guaranteed 1024 — and holding the Vulkan path to it meant lamps still went out as the player crossed a compound with more fittings than slots. That backend is on its way out and Vulkan carries these in a uniform block with room to spare, so the ceiling now follows the backend that is staying. If OpenGL is ever revived it needs its own, smaller, budget rather than this one lowered.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.DepthUnprojection
member.summary: What a full-screen pass needs to rebuild a view-space position from the depth buffer.

remarks.para: Every effect the remaster track adds after the G-buffer — shadows, ambient occlusion, reflections, volumetric fog — starts by asking "where in the world is this pixel". The projection's last row is (0, 0, 1, 0), so w is the view depth and the inverse has a closed form; passing these four numbers is cheaper and steadier than inverting a matrix per frame and uploading it.
Build it from the same projection the scene was drawn with. Taking the scales from anywhere else — a remembered field of view, a window size — is how a reconstruction ends up subtly stretched.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Diagnostics.StageTimingLedger
member.summary: The rolling statistics behind the stage timings: what each stage costs, what the worst frame cost, and how much of the GPU frame no stage claims.

remarks.para: Separated from the measuring because none of it is a graphics question. Where the numbers come from differs by backend — timestamp queries written around a pass, read back once the frame has drained — but what is done with them is arithmetic, and arithmetic that is worth checking: a rolling window, a percentile, a peak that must survive the window scrolling past it, and a warm-up that must be discarded or the first frames' compile stalls are reported as the steady state.

Smoothed rather than instantaneous because a single frame's query is far noisier than the thing being judged: the driver batches, the clock boosts, and a stage costing a steady 0.8 ms reports anywhere from 0.4 to 2 ms frame to frame. A budget is a claim about the steady state, so the steady state is what is shown.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.DistanceFieldBinding
member.summary: The level's global distance field, handed across the renderer seam so a pass can march it without knowing what built it.

remarks.para: What this is for. A reflection needs to know what a ray hits. Where the adapter can trace, an acceleration structure answers that; where it cannot, the only description of the world a shader can walk is the distance field — and until this existed it lived entirely on the game's side of the seam, so the backend's own reflection passes could not reach it. Glass on a machine without ray tracing therefore reflected the sky and nothing else.

Software tracing marches a global distance field and resolves what it hits against the same surface cache the hardware path uses. Nothing here is a lesser approximation of the traced answer — it is a different way of finding the hit, feeding the identical resolve.

Four levels, by value. The shader declares four and the settings clamp to four, so this carries them as fields rather than an array: a record struct with a list would allocate on a handover that happens every frame, and the fixed shape is the shader's own.

member.param: The volume texture holding every level, stacked as the build wrote them.
How many levels are real; zero means there is no field to march.
How many voxels square one level is.

The third level.
The coarsest level, whose box is as far as the march can see.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureAdaptation
member.summary: The eye adaptation's host half: a metered histogram turned into the exposure the resolve applies, eased over time.
member.remarks: The GPU half counts the lit frame into buckets spanning a fixed log2 luminance range. Here the darkest and brightest tenths of that count are trimmed away, the rest is averaged in log space, the average is clamped to a plausible band and expressed relative to middle grey, and the result is eased toward over time in stops: at a constant rate while far away, proportionally once near, so a large change sweeps steadily and a small one settles without a visible tail.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.WhitePoint
member.summary: The linear value that maps to display white.
member.remarks:
How much headroom above white the tone map reserves. It must match what the scene produces: this world is LDR textures multiplied by LDR lightmaps, so almost nothing exceeds one, and the old fixed value of 4 spent the curve's whole range compressing a span that was not there. One disables the roll-off completely.
It is a Reinhard parameter, and only the Reinhard operator has one. A white point is the single number that curve is shaped by; the film curve the higher presets run is shaped by its own slope, toe, shoulder and black/white levels instead, and has no scalar for this to be. So at any preset above r_tonemap 1 this setting is inert — not ignored by the backend, which would be a bug, but meaningless to the curve in use. It was found by the cvar sweep reporting it as reaching nothing with nothing saying why, which is exactly what that sweep is for.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.Exposure
member.summary: A linear multiplier applied to the scene before tone mapping.

remarks.para: With on this becomes a bias on the adapted exposure rather than the whole of it: the eye adapts to the scene's own brightness and this nudges the result up or down.

This is the player's knob and nothing else writes it. The day/night cycle's own dimming is a SEPARATE term -- see and -- so that a night which darkens the picture never rewrites, and never has to restore, the brightness the player chose. Read , not this, wherever the frame is exposed.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.MinimumExposure
member.summary: The least exposure the frame may be shown at, which is the floor on .
member.remarks: Named because subtracts from the player's value and has to land somewhere: a night deep enough to take the whole of a low brightness setting must still leave a picture, not a black screen.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.NightBrightnessDrop
member.summary: How much brightness a full night takes off .
member.remarks: Subtractive, in the slider's own units, so a default brightness of one is shown at 0.7 under a midnight sky. It is deliberately small: the lighting model already darkens a night scene on its own, and this exists because the eye adaptation then spends most of that darkness lifting the picture back towards day. Taking a little off the compensation is what lets a night read as one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.Nightfall
member.summary: How far into night the day/night cycle has taken the scene: 0 in daylight, 1 at full night.

remarks.para: Written by the day/night cycle once per frame from the swept sun's own elevation, and read only through . It is the hidden half of the brightness: the player owns , the sky owns this, and the two are combined at the point of use rather than the sky editing the player's setting behind their back.

Published rather than kept as a private field so the console can be asked what the night is currently doing to the picture; read-only there, because the next frame's sweep would overwrite anything typed at it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.DayNightCycle
member.summary: Whether the time of day runs on its own while a mission is played.

remarks.para: Off, a mission stays at the hour its authors lit it at, which is what every mission in the original does and what its lighting was designed around. On, that authored hour is merely where the mission opens: the sun then sweeps on from there at whatever is set to, which is quick enough by default that a mission of ordinary length ends under a different sky than it began under.
Default off, because it changes the look of every level away from the one its artists chose, and because a mission whose sun set halfway through is a different mission to play.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.DayLength
member.summary: How long a whole day of the cycle takes, in real minutes.

remarks.para: Forty minutes by default: long enough that the light is a setting rather than a strobe, short enough that a mission of ordinary length visibly ends under a different sky than it opened on. An hour was the first figure tried and it was too slow to be worth having -- most missions finished under the sun they started with, so the setting did nothing anybody could see.

Free to set to anything, including a minute, which is the honest way to LOOK at the sweep: a whole sunrise-to-night pass in the time it takes to walk across a level. The cycle steps the clock a fixed slice of the arc at a time rather than a fixed number of seconds, so the sweep is equally smooth at a minute a day and at half a day a day; what changes is how often it steps.
Does nothing at all unless is on. It is not the scrub keys' rate -- those sweep a day in thirty seconds and are meant to be held and watched.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.LampDaylight
member.summary: Which of the level's lamps go off by day and come on at dusk.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original's lamps are painted into its lightmaps and burn at noon as at midnight. Here each one follows the sun through a photocell of its own -- see LampPhotocells -- so as the sky darkens the yard's lamps strike one by one, raggedly and audibly, and at dawn go out again.

Outdoors by default: a lamp with a roof over it is lit by day as by night in any real building, and a windowless room whose lamps had gone out at noon would be a room the player cannot see in. Everywhere puts every lamp on the daylight. Off is the original's lamps, always lit.

Follows the sun whether or not the clock is running: the scrub keys move it either way. Nothing happens under the vanilla preset, which draws the original's lamps, or with a pinned -sundir, which is a comparison capture and keeps every lamp as the level ships it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.EffectiveExposure
member.summary: The brightness the frame is actually exposed at: the player's, less the night's.
member.remarks: Every consumer of the exposure reads THIS, including the two that only want to divide a display-referred colour by whatever the resolve is about to multiply it by -- the first-person rig's lighting and the selection glow. Reading there instead would leave them compensating for an exposure the frame is no longer using, so the arms and the marker would drift brighter as the night came in.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.AuthoredNightDrop
member.summary: How much darker a title's OWN night makes the picture, in stops, at full night.

remarks.para: Far more than , and for a different reason. That one trims the eye's compensation as a sun sets, over a scene the adaptation is otherwise handling. This one answers a scene the adaptation cannot handle at all: I.G.I. 2 authors night by leaving the sun UP and painting it nearly black, so every luminance in the frame is low together and the adaptation reads it as a correctly-exposed dark subject and lifts the whole thing back to mid grey. The sky blows out, the sun-facing hillsides go white, and the mission reads as an overcast noon.

Fitted against vanilla's GROUND, which is the one surface both paths composite from the same product -- texture times detail times the tile's bake -- so a difference there is the exposure and nothing else. Frame means are no use for this: the sky is most of the frame and the two paths draw different skies, so fitting on the frame fits on the sky.

Mission 1, mean ground luminance over the lower half of the frame against vanilla's 15.22, swept on r_exposure (which enters this the same way, one for one): 0.909 at 1.55, 1.101 at 1.62. The crossing is 1.585, which is an EffectiveExposure of 0.482 at full night.

Stated per unit of the SWEEP's nightfall, because that is what now drives it: a night-bound level sits at midnight where the sweep reads a full one, so 1.414 - (0.3 + this) x 1 = 0.482. It used to be stated against the level's own authored figure of 0.85, which is where the 0.8 came from -- the same exposure, said against a number that no longer reaches it.

The previous value was 1.0, and it was fitted against a broken picture. The ground's bake was being written into its albedo then, so every lit pixel of it was about thirty-five times too dark and the adaptation was opening against that; the drop was compensating for a bug. Refitting had to wait for the ground to be right AND for its false specular to go, because that lobe was carrying about a third of the ground's brightness on the dynamic model alone.

It is a bias on the adapted value, not a fixed exposure, so a dark interior in the same mission still opens up. And it is multiplied by what the LEVEL says about its own darkness, so a title that says nothing -- Project I.G.I. -- pays none of it whatever this is set to.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.AuthoredNightDropFor
member.summary: How many units of exposure the current level's own night takes off, at full night.
member.remarks: unless the title says otherwise. It was fitted against I.G.I. 2's night missions, which leave the sun up and paint it nearly black. Project I.G.I.'s night missions are bound through the cycle's own moon instead, whose darkness the lighting already computes, so they carry a drop of their own. Set by the shell as a level loads; read only through .

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.AuthoredNightfall
member.summary: How dark a title says its own level is, 0 to 1; 0 for a title that does not say.
member.remarks: Separate from so the two cannot be confused: that one is the day/night sweep's reading of its own swept sun, this one is what the level itself declares. Project I.G.I. declares nothing and leaves this at nought, which is what keeps its exposure exactly as it was.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.TimeOfDay
member.summary: The hour a level's sun starts at, or -1 for the hour the level's authors gave it.

remarks.para: The day-night cycle reproduces a level's authored sun EXACTLY only at the level's own authored hour -- its elevation and bearing are fitted through that hour -- so a fixed start hour is the authored sun for the levels authored at that hour and a different sky for every other. Negative means "the level's own", which is what every mission should open on.

Not archived, deliberately. It used to be, and one scrub written to the settings file made every mission afterwards open at night -- a preference nobody remembers making, and one whose effect reads as the game being broken. A start hour set at the console or in the menu now lasts the session and no longer.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ExposureCVars.AutoExposure
member.summary: Whether the exposure adapts to the scene's own brightness over time.
member.remarks: Off by default, and only ever engages where a tone map is on -- the vanilla copy path returns before exposure is applied at all, so a traced preset can adapt while vanilla stays byte-identical. A traced scene without eye adaptation reads worse than one lit the original's way, which is why the plan calls it non-optional there; it is opt-in here until a preset turns it on.

member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightBlock
member.summary: The flashlight as the shaders read it: six vectors, the same in every block that carries it.

remarks.para: The deferred shading's GI block and the fog's block both carry the flashlight, and both are written through here, so the lit wall and the lit air cannot disagree about where the beam is. The layout is FlashlightParams in Common/Flashlight.slang:

item.description: view xyz, the cosine of the spill's half-angle -- the hard cull.
linear rgb times the intensity, the near core squared.
tan of the outer half-angle, then the inner's and the spill's tangents over it, and the spill's level.
whether a shadow mask was made, the volumetric scale, the throw, the dust.

remarks.para: A flashlight that is off writes zeros, and a range of nought is what every shader tests.

member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightCVars.Flashlight
member.summary: Whether the player's flashlight can be switched on.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original has no flashlight; this is the remaster's, toggled by the Flashlight action (F by default). Vanilla pins it off, and there the key does nothing at all -- no light and no click -- so a vanilla run is the original and nothing else. The light also needs the deferred path, which vanilla does not draw, so a Custom preset that switches that off switches this off with it.
It works the same with the RT switches on or off: its shadow is traced against the world where the adapter can and marched through the depth buffer where it cannot ().

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightCVars.FlashlightShadows
member.summary: Whether the flashlight casts shadows.
member.remarks: One ray a pixel from each lit surface to a point on the lens, then a small filter sized by the penumbra; traced against the world, cut-out masks and all, where the RT switches allow, and marched through the depth buffer everywhere else. Nothing runs while the light is off.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightCVars.FlashlightFog
member.summary: How strongly the flashlight's beam shows in the air.
member.remarks: Scales what the beam scatters out of the volumetric fog, plus the thin dust only it sees (). Needs the volumetric fog; with none there is no beam in the air.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightCVars.FlashlightIntensity
member.summary: How strong the flashlight is on its axis: its irradiance at a metre, in the lamps' units.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightCVars.FlashlightRange

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightCVars.FlashlightThrow
member.summary: How well the flashlight's beam carries to its range.
member.remarks: Past five metres a surface's falloff is eased by the distance raised to this: 0 keeps the inverse square, 1 leaves one over the distance, 2 holds the beam level out to its range. The inverse square alone leaves a wall at a hundred metres a five-hundredth of the near spot, which one exposure for the whole frame cannot show; an eye adapts to each part of the view and sees it lit. Captured on mission 3 at night from the hill over the base, 1 still left the compound unlit under the beam's own glow in the rain, 1.75 lit it grey, and 2 lit the tower and the walls. Only surfaces are thrown -- the beam in the air keeps the inverse square, or it hangs a column of haze down the whole range.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightLight
member.summary: The player's flashlight for one frame: a spot light hung off the body, in VIEW space like the lamps.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original has no flashlight; this is the remaster's, and every graphics preset but vanilla draws it. It is not a lamp slot: the lamps share one traced occlusion ratio, drawn from reservoirs and averaged over thirty-two frames, and a bright light glued to the camera would take over the reservoirs, ghost through the history and change every other lamp's shadow. It is shaded on its own, with a shadow of its own that keeps no history -- the light moves with the view, so nothing it lit last frame is where it is now.

The beam is a torch's rather than a cone's: a hot core, a body that falls away to the reflector's edge, a faint ring where the reflector ends, and a dim spill beyond it (see Common/Flashlight.slang). The angles are half-angles from the axis.

The way the beam points, in view space; unit length.
The reflector's up, in view space, which turns the lens's small irregularities with it.
The light's linear colour, luminance one.
How strong the beam is on its axis: irradiance at one metre, in the lamps' units.
How far the beam reaches before its windowed falloff takes it to nothing, in metres.
The hot core's half-angle.
The main beam's half-angle, where the reflector's light ends.
How far the dim spill reaches past it.
How bright the spill is, against the core.
How wide the emitter is, in metres, which is what gives a shadow its penumbra.
The distance inside which the falloff stops rising, in metres: a torch pressed to a wall lights a disc, not a point of infinite brightness.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.FlashlightShadowParameters
member.summary: The parameter blocks of the flashlight's two shadow dispatches, the same for every backend.

remarks.para: FlashlightShadow fires one ray per pixel from the surface to a point on the lens -- against the world where the adapter traces, through the depth buffer where it does not -- and stores whether it got there and, if not, how wide a penumbra the occluder implies. FlashlightShadowFilter spreads each answer over that penumbra, weighted by depth so one surface's shadow does not bleed onto the next. The shading reads the result at its own pixel.

There is no temporal half, on purpose. The light hangs off the player, so a shadow it cast last frame moved with the player: reprojecting by the world would drag it, and keeping it at the same pixel would smear it through every turn. A torch's shadow is nearly hard -- the emitter is a couple of centimetres across -- so one ray and a small filter is both the cheap answer and the right one.

member.summary: The anisotropy of the fog's second, backward-scattering lobe.
member.remarks: Haze scatters mostly forward, but not only: with one forward lobe a shaft of light shows only looking into the sun, and vanishes seen from the side. A weak backward lobe keeps it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FogCVars.RetailFog
member.summary: Whether the world wears the original's own per-vertex distance fog.

remarks.para: The retail picture is a fogged one. Every shipping level's FlatSky asks for a fog amount between 0.70 and 0.975, which is half of a surface gone by four hundred metres and nearly all of it by two and a half kilometres, and the same slate blue to fog into. Without it the ground runs to the horizon in full colour and the mountain ranges of missions 5, 9 and 11 stand up sharp behind the level -- which is not what the original draws, whatever the far plane is.

On for vanilla and off above it, because the modern tiers already integrate the same level data through 's froxel volume, which scatters and shadows it rather than lerping towards a constant. Turning both on would fog the frame twice. See for the arithmetic and where it was read from.

member.remarks: The single biggest cost in the pass, and the quality dial.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.FogTarget
member.summary: The colour a run of draws fogs towards: the scene's own, half of it, or white.

remarks.para: I.G.I. 2's ground is three passes multiplied together, and its fog is divided between them so the product still lands on the scene's fog colour at distance. TerrainRender_SetBlendMode (igi2ed 0x666B90) writes D3DRS_FOGCOLOR per mode: the base pass (mode 1, SRCALPHA/ZERO) and the overlay passes (mode 2, SRCALPHA/ONE) fog to the fog colour times 127 out of 255 — half of it — and the lightmap pass (mode 3, DESTCOLOR/SRCCOLOR) fogs to 0xFFFFFFFF, white. The lightmap pass doubles what is under it, so far away the frame holds 2 × (fog / 2) × 1 = fog; nearer in, the bake is fogged away towards white before the texture is fogged away towards the haze, which is why distant rock in the original keeps its texture at full brightness under a thin blue veil instead of sinking into fog squared.
Every other draw fogs to the scene's colour. A title that never sets this leaves it at , which is the fog the forward shader always applied.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ForwardDrawMarker
member.summary: The one number a forward draw carries that says what it is: the world, the first-person rig, or something translucent — and, for the rig, whether there is a light to key it with.

remarks.para: It rides the first component of the mesh push block and does two jobs, which is why it is a number rather than a flag. The fragment stage branches on it to choose the shading, and an opaque draw leaves it in the lit target's alpha so that a later pass reading that colour back can tell world geometry from geometry that only exists in front of the eye — the eye adaptation must not meter the arms, and the indirect gather must not bounce light off them.

is the fourth value and the newest. The studio key light the rig is shaded with is a remaster light: the original draws the first-person layer through the same fixed-function lighting as every other model (sub_49F700 installs the layer's own view block and hands the mesh to sub_49B700, which writes position, normal and UV and no colour at all). Under there is nothing to key with — SceneLighting.Baked is a black sun over a black ambient, on purpose — and the rig came out as a solid black silhouette in the corner of every vanilla frame. It is still the rig, so it still leaves the rig's zero in the alpha; what the extra value buys is the shading branch.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for how a frame is made and shown: presentation, the scene path, what is drawn of the player, and the diagnostics laid over it.

remarks.para: The renderer's variables are declared next to the renderer seam, rather than in a central settings type, and grouped by what they govern: this class, and its siblings , , , and the rest. The console, the settings file and the options menu all reach them through , so there is one value and three views onto it.
Each remaster stage adds its own variables to the container for what they govern and, where the value differs by quality tier, registers them with in the same place.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.VSync
member.summary: Whether presentation waits for the vertical blank.
member.remarks: On under every preset, so choosing one brings back a tear-free picture whatever was saved.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.MenuBackdropLite
member.summary: Whether the level behind the menu is drawn without the expensive parts of the preset.
member.remarks: The backdrop is looked at through a blur, never played, and it is replaced every time the player settles on another mission. Building its real-time lighting -- the surface-cache capture and the distance field -- and tracing its shadows and reflections made every swap a stall the player saw, for detail nobody could. On, the menu draws it on the level's own bakes with no shadows, traces or screen-space gathers; the full preset comes back when Play is pressed, behind the going-in sequence. Imposed through overrides, so the settings screen and the saved file still show the player's choice.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.SmoothPresentation
member.summary: Whether the presentation interpolates between simulation ticks.

remarks.para: The simulation is fixed at 30 Hz and stays there — that is the determinism contract. What this changes is how each frame renders bodies, poses and the player's own eye blended between the last two tick states, so an uncapped frame rate looks uncapped instead of a 30 Hz slideshow with a smooth mouse. AI and ballistics keep reading tick states. IGI2 also uses linear mouse counts for both the frame preview and the next tick's aim, bypassing its retail pitch filters and turn cap. Off retains that title's retail mouse response.

On under vanilla too. The original presents exactly one tick's state per frame and vanilla is otherwise held to what the original did, but a 30 Hz slideshow is not a look anyone chose to preserve -- it is what a 1998 target frame rate left behind, and the tier exists to show the original's picture, not its schedule. Reference captures use -lockstep, which disables interpolation and unfiltered mouse aim ahead of this setting.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.OffscreenScene
member.summary: Whether the scene is rendered offscreen instead of straight to the back buffer.
member.remarks: The switch between the original's path and the modern one. Off, the frame is drawn and presented exactly as the game shipped, and none of the remaster track's effects can run, because every one of them needs the frame and its depth to still exist after being drawn.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.MissionWarmUp
member.summary: How many frames a level is drawn for, unseen, before it is shown to the player.

remarks.para: Most of this renderer's lighting is defined in terms of frames rather than of state: the screen probe gather accumulates per pixel, the radiance cache fills its probes, the temporal resolve needs a history before it can reconstruct anything, and the eye adapts towards a scene instead of snapping to it. A load cannot produce any of that, however long it takes -- there is no history without frames -- so a level that is shown the instant it finishes loading is shown mid-converge, and the player watches it settle over the next second or two.

This draws those frames with the picture withheld. The scene renders exactly as it will in play, so every temporal pass advances normally; what is held back is only the presentation. It is what a loading screen is actually for, and it is why no shipping game shows its world changing after the loading screen has gone.

Forty-five, measured rather than picked: with doing the view-independent half at load, frame twenty is about 7% off the settled image and frame forty-five about 3%, which is past telling apart. Zero shows the level the moment it loads, which is the old behaviour.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.MultiSampling
member.summary: How many samples per pixel the scene is rasterised with.
member.remarks:
Resolved down before anything samples the target, because the effects that follow read depth and a multisampled depth buffer is not something a shader can read usefully.
It applies ONLY on the original's forward path (r_hdr 0): the deferred/HDR path records into a single-sample G-buffer and is anti-aliased by the temporal upscaler instead, so MSAA there would be pure cost for no effect. Every preset from enhanced up is deferred, so they set it to off — a value above one on those presets did nothing but read as if it were working.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.PlayerBody
member.summary: Whether the player's own body is drawn while the camera is in first person.

remarks.para: The body already exists and is already animated — third person draws it, and so does the death camera. Two gates hold it shut in first person: the follow that places it, and the draw latch the third-person camera keeps closed until it has left the head. This opens both.

It does NOT put the player in a window, and it is worth being exact about why. A traced reflection resolves its hit out of the lit frame first and the static surface cache second. Facing a window, the player's own body is BEHIND the camera — so the hit fails the first test at the very first line, on being behind the eye, and the cards never held a moving body to begin with. Drawing it changes nothing about that. What it does reach is the cases where the body is partly in frame anyway: a pane off to one side, or a glancing angle along a glass wall.
What it buys unconditionally is the player's own shadow and its ambient occlusion, which the original never had, and the body being visible on looking down.

Off by default, and that is not timidity. The camera sits at the head, so the head is either clipped by the near plane or seen from the inside — the skull filling the screen that the draw latch exists to prevent. Hiding the head bone is the usual answer and is not done here yet, so switching this on today trades a known artefact for a benefit most players will not see.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.PerformanceLog
member.summary: Whether each stage of the frame is timed on the GPU and shown in an overlay.

remarks.para: The instrument the remaster track's frame budget is checkable with, and it did not exist for the five stages that were written against it: shadows ≤1.0 ms, occlusion ≤1.0, lighting ≤2.0, reflections ≤1.5, fog ≤1.5, post ≤1.5. Every performance claim made before this was an estimate.

Developer rather than archived, and off by default, because it is not free: a timer query is a synchronisation point in the command stream, so measuring the frame does change it a little. It is close enough to judge a budget by and not close enough to leave on.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.FrameCVars.PerformanceLogPasses
member.summary: How many of the most expensive individual passes r_perflog lists under its stages.
member.remarks: A stage is the sum of its passes, and the global illumination alone is a dozen dispatches; a stage over budget says where to look but not at what. Every pass is also written to the log on exit.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for the geometry it draws: terrain detail and caching, culling and visibility queries.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.WorldCull
member.summary: Whether the world pass culls back faces of eligible meshes after repairing triangle winding.
member.remarks: The mesh builder repairs winding using authored vertex normals. Interior sectors and meshes without usable normals remain two-sided even when this setting is enabled: in particular, IGI2 lightmapped geometry carries no normals. Off draws both facings for every world mesh.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.TerrainDetail
member.summary: How far the terrain keeps subdividing before it settles for a coarser mesh.

remarks.para: Not an optimisation that can be switched off. The terrain is an octree, so there is no underlying full-detail mesh to stop simplifying — this is the depth the descent runs to, and removing the limit would mean subdividing a cube 262 km on a side.

Retail runs 96, 129 or 163 for low, medium and high, and 163 is the shipped default (sub_406390). The remaster's tiers go well past it, which is what actually removes the popping as ground resolves ahead of the player.

Zero means "as retail derives it", and is not the same as writing 163: the renderer takes 163 as a base and divides it by the square root of the horizontal half-angle tangent, so at anything but a 4:3 window the two differ. Vanilla therefore asks for zero, not for a number that only looks like the default.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.TerrainCache
member.summary: How many uploaded terrain chunks the renderer keeps before evicting the oldest.

remarks.para: Paired with , because how far the ground resolves is what decides how much of it there is to hold. The number that matters is not what one frustum holds but what a PANORAMA holds: a frustum is a quarter or so of the circle a player turns through, so a cache sized to the view drops the ground behind them and rebuilds it as they turn back. Measured on level 1 at the ultra distance, a frame draws about 2500 chunks and a full turn from one spot touches about 9000; at 4096 that is a hundred chunks rebuilt every frame for as long as the player keeps turning, and at 16384 or more the turn evicts nothing at all and settles at zero.

A whole turn from one spot on level 1 touches 2363 chunks at 220, 4681 at 320 and 8979 at 450, costing 6.5, 12.5 and 23.0 MB of page buffers. Each tier is set to between two and three times its own figure, so that a player who walks while they turn keeps the headroom the fixed-spot measurement does not show. Vanilla keeps retail's own 4096 — it also draws retail's much shorter view, which fits.

The cost of raising it is the geometry held, and that is only affordable because a batch page is now created with room for what a page actually holds rather than for 4096 vertices apiece: the same ultra panorama that would have charged 918 MB of buffers charges 23 MB.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.TerrainCacheDefault
member.summary: Retail's own chunk bound, which is the smallest this cache is allowed to be.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.TerrainOcclusion
member.summary: Whether terrain batch pages use asynchronous visibility queries.
member.remarks: The query result is consumed only after OpenGL reports it ready, so this never stalls the CPU. Keeping this as a CVar also makes the query cost directly A/B testable on a given mission.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.WorldOcclusion
member.summary: Whether placed world objects use asynchronous visibility queries in the geometry pass.
member.remarks: The frustum keeps most of a level's objects while the camera stands indoors — a wall hides them, a frustum does not. On by default because interiors are where the geometry pass was measured most over budget; a CVar so the gain is A/B testable per mission like the terrain's.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.GeometryCVars.Presets
member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.GlobalIlluminationCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for baked indirect light: the probe field and the level's lightmaps.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GlobalIlluminationCVars.GlobalIllumination
member.summary: Whether surfaces take their indirect light from the baked probe field.
member.remarks: Costs a trace of the level at load rather than anything per frame, which is why it is a restart-scope setting in practice even though nothing enforces that: turning it on mid-level finds no field baked and changes nothing until the next load.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.GlobalIlluminationCVars.BakedLightmaps
member.summary: How the level's static object lightmaps are sourced: shipped, augmented, or our bake alone.

remarks.para: 0 uses the shipped .olm object lightmaps, exactly as retail. 1 re-bakes them with the path tracer at load -- per-texel, coloured, multi-bounce, from the level's own sun and sky -- and swaps a baked page in wherever there is one, falling back to the shipped page where the bake produced nothing. 2 discards the shipped lightmaps entirely: a surface the bake did not reach reads black rather than borrowing the artists' light, so what the frame shows is ONLY our own lighting -- the honest state of the system, gaps and all.

A restart-scope setting: the bake runs once at load (on a worker, cached to disk) and only ever reaches the baked and hybrid models, which sample the lightmap; vanilla and the dynamic path are untouched. Interiors a sealed room's sun cannot reach stay dark until the lamp fixtures are baked.

member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether BC1 and BC7 textures can be created and sampled as they are.
member.remarks: Where it is false a block-compressed texture is expanded on the CPU before it is uploaded -- correct, and four to eight times the memory the compressed form would have taken.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.GraphicsCapabilities.SupportsRayQuery
member.summary: Whether a compute shader on this device can trace rays against the world directly.
member.remarks: The difference between marching a distance field towards a surface and asking the hardware where the ray actually lands. Both answer the same question; the ray answers it exactly, and against geometry rather than an approximation of it. A backend that says yes here is expected to accept a compute shader that declares an acceleration structure and to have one bound for it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.GraphicsCapabilities.MaxSampleCount

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.GraphicsCapabilities.MaxComputeGroupsX
member.summary: Gets the most workgroups one compute dispatch may have along x.
member.remarks: What a one-dimensional dispatch over a long list has to be sliced to. Vulkan drivers commonly offer billions along x; WebGPU guarantees 65535 and adapters rarely offer more, and a dispatch past it is refused outright. 65535 unless a backend says otherwise, because every API promises that much.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.GraphicsCapabilities.UnimplementedSettings
member.summary: Gets the names of the settings this backend accepts and records but does not yet act on.

remarks.para: A setting that is stored and then ignored is the worst kind of dead control: the value persists, the options screen shows it, and the picture never changes — so the person changing it concludes the effect is broken rather than absent, and anyone comparing two renders is comparing configurations that were never the same. Naming them here lets the app say so out loud at start-up instead, and the entry disappears from the list on the day the pass lands.
These are console-variable names, so a reader can match them against what the settings file holds.

member.summary: Why the frames before this one should be forgotten.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.InteractionPrompt
member.summary: Whether a usable object is marked in the world rather than captioned across the screen.

remarks.para: The modern presentation of the same offer: a key badge pinned to the door, cabinet or ladder the activation scan resolved, carrying the control the player actually has bound, the action's name, and — for the timed states — the hold as a ring that fills. Off returns the remaster HUD to its single centred line of text.

Presentation only, and only while is on. What can be used, from where, and for how long is decided by the retail activation scan either way; this changes where the player reads it. Off under vanilla with the rest of the remaster, which keeps the original's action sprites.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.TacticalComputer
member.summary: Whether the C-key map computer is the remaster's interface rather than the retail one.

remarks.para: Two entirely separate presentations of the same data. Off is the original's: a low-resolution mapcomputer.mef panel held up in front of the camera, its aperture filled by a 4:3 screen set in the game's own bitmap faces. On is a full-screen interface set in the shell's Barlow, reached through a camera move and a phosphor display transform, with no device model at all.

Off under vanilla for the reason everything else is: -vanilla and -vanillarender exist to put the original's picture on screen, and a redesigned computer is not that. The retail path is kept whole rather than emulated by the new one — it is the regression gate, and a gate that shares an implementation with the thing it is gating is not a gate.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.BinocularLens
member.summary: Whether the remastered binocular applies its glass-lens display transform.
member.remarks: The optics tint, highlight bloom and bezel vignette are a resolve-time display transform over the finished picture, raised as the device comes up. Off under vanilla for the reason the tactical computer is: the retail binocular is the regression gate and must stay untouched.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.BinocularOutline
member.summary: Whether binocular-detected enemies are given a through-wall silhouette glow.
member.remarks: A team-coloured selection glow drawn over each scanned soldier while the remastered optics are up, so a marked contact stays legible through cover. Off under vanilla with the rest of the remaster.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.BinocularSilhouette
member.summary: Whether the binoculars' highlight is drawn in the silhouette style rather than as a glow.
member.remarks: On, a marked contact is filled faintly and outlined softly over the finished picture, by its group, and the highlight fades towards the screen's edges; off, it is the glow of , drawn into the scene. Only while that is on.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.BinocularRange
member.summary: The remastered binocular detector's range at the default zoom, in metres.
member.remarks: A modern optics touch: the detector has a finite range rather than tagging every enemy in the frustum however far off, and that range grows as the operator zooms in -- from this value at the default field of view up to at the tightest zoom. The vanilla optics ignore both and stay retail-uncapped.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.BinocularRangeZoomed
member.summary: The remastered binocular detector's range at the tightest zoom, in metres.
member.remarks: The range scales from at the default field of view to this at the closest magnification, so leaning into the optics sees further, the way a real scope resolves a distant figure the naked view cannot.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.TacticalMessages
member.summary: Whether the mission's status messages are drawn as the remaster's comms cards.

remarks.para: Presentation only. Both paths draw the same messages at the same moments, in the same order, with the same typewriter: when a message arrives is decided by the simulation, and neither renderer can reach that. Off is the original's placement and bitmap face; on is a card set in the shell's Barlow.
This preference only applies while is on. The retail HUD always uses its own bitmap message block and original display timing.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.HudCVars.DamageFlash
member.summary: How strongly the screen washes red when the player is hit.

remarks.para: A multiplier on the alpha of the full-screen quad HumanPlayer_DrawDamageFlash (0x4bb770) paints, where 1 is the original's own strength and 0 removes it. The decay is untouched either way: this changes how red the wash is, not how long it lasts, so the feedback still tells the player which direction the hit came from and for exactly as long.

Below 1 by default outside vanilla. The original's full-strength wash was tuned for a 640x480 display a good distance from the player's face; the same alpha across a modern screen is enough to hide the thing that is shooting at you, which turns a damage cue into a punishment.

remarks.para: The display is drawn into a layer of its own and laid over the picture by one full-screen pass that bends it as a visor would (), splits its colours at the edges as a projection does (), runs scanlines through it and lets them roll (, ), flickers it in band by band as it appears (), shakes it when the player is hit (), tears the picture on the side the hit came from (), and lays its own glow back over it ().

remarks.para: Distinct from , which describes a frame. This describes an atlas that outlives every frame: each model is drawn into it a handful of times at load, through an orthographic camera per card, and read for the rest of the level.

member.summary: Reads one of the card atlas's targets back into memory.
member.param: Which target: 0 albedo, 1 normal, 2 material, 3 depth.
Receives the texels, row-major and top row first.
member.remarks:
For looking at the atlas, and that is not a luxury. A capture is the kind of thing only an eye can judge: wrong winding shows as models captured inside-out, a wrong card rotation as mirrored pages, a missing scissor as pages bleeding into each other — and all three produce a perfectly plausible atlas full of perfectly plausible surfaces.
Synchronising, so it belongs at load or behind a developer switch rather than in a frame.

Which compiled form to load.

remarks.para: A member of this seam that not every backend can honour. Compute needs GL 4.3, which desktop has and macOS -- frozen at 4.1 -- does not, so a caller must check and have a path that does not need it.

The module was compiled by the build rather than at load, so a mistake in it is a failed build instead of a level that does not start. Programs are still created up front rather than lazily: a pipeline that cannot be built is a fault to find at load, not on the frame that first needed the pass.

A buffer holding three consecutive unsigned integers: the group counts.
