member.remarks: What lets a pass size the next one. The culling stage cannot know how many meshes fall inside a clipmap until it has looked, and reading its count back to the CPU to launch the next dispatch would cost a full synchronisation every frame — so it writes the count into a buffer and the GPU reads it without anybody waiting.

member.summary: Makes a previous dispatch's writes visible to what follows.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IDrawStateDevice.SetFirstPersonGeometry(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Marks the draws that follow as geometry that exists only in front of the eye.
member.param: Whether the following draws are the view model rather than the world.

remarks.para: The arms and the held weapon are drawn into the same lit colour as the world, and two passes read that colour back as though everything in it were world: the eye adaptation meters it, and the screen-space indirect gather traces against it. Neither is true of a view model. A white knife held up to the camera raises the metered luminance and darkens the whole frame, and bounces light off itself onto the room -- so pressing the free-camera key, which simply stops drawing it, visibly changes the lighting of a scene that has not moved.
Device state, like : it spans a run of draws and must be cleared after them. A backend that does not separate the two may ignore it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IDrawStateDevice.SetObjectMotion(System.Boolean,System.Int64)
member.summary: Marks the draws that follow as moving under their own power.
member.param: Whether the object being drawn has its own motion this frame.

Which object this is, the same number every frame, or nought to pair by the mesh alone. A renderer that skips some of its objects on some frames -- occlusion, a frustum -- changes which draw of a shared mesh comes n-th, and paired by the mesh alone the n-th draw of a crate is a different crate from one frame to the next.

remarks.para: The velocity the temporal passes read is derived from depth and the two cameras, so it describes only what the camera did. A car, a jet, a train or a swinging door drawn without this is reprojected as if it were the scenery behind it, and its history trails behind it as a ghost. With it set, each geometry draw is paired with its own transform from the frame before and stamps its true motion.
Device state, like : set it around a run of draws and clear it after. A backend without per-object motion may ignore it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IDrawStateDevice.SetPaintedSky(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Says that the title draws a sky of its own, which the frame should keep.
member.param: Whether the sky about to be drawn is the game's own painted one.

remarks.para: A deferred frame has to decide what to put where nothing was drawn, and a remaster's answer is its own atmosphere — which is the right answer for a game whose sky is a flat painted gradient and whose missions are daylight. It is the wrong answer for a game that authors a sky per mission: an atmosphere knows night only as a sun below the horizon, and I.G.I. 2's night missions leave the sun up and paint it black, so its night skies came back as daylight blue.

Setting this says two things at once: keep what the dome drew, and treat it as a picture rather than a radiance — divide it by the exposure the resolve will multiply back, the same compensation already earns for the view model. Defaulted to nothing, so a backend that never exposes anything ignores it and a title that has not asked keeps the picture it had.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IDrawStateDevice.SetAlphaHash(System.Single)
member.summary: Sets the seed for the following draws' hashed alpha test, zero for the hard cut-out.
member.param: Zero draws cut-outs with a hard per-pixel test. A value above zero turns on the hashed test, whose dithered coverage the temporal resolve averages into a smooth edge; vary it each frame so successive frames dither differently and the average converges.
member.remarks: Device state, like : it spans a run of draws.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IDrawStateDevice.SetAlphaReference(System.Byte)
member.summary: Sets how much texture alpha a cut-out draw needs to survive, for the following draws.
member.param: The threshold, out of 255. A fragment whose texture alpha is below it is discarded; is the port's long-standing half and zero turns the test off.

remarks.para: A byte rather than a fraction because that is the original's own type: D3DRS_ALPHAREF takes an integer out of 255, and I.G.I. 2 sets it to exactly two values — 64 for cut-outs generally (Direct3DRender_SetBlendStateAlphaTest, igi2ed 0x56C960) and 32 for foliage, which lowers it so the thin edges of a leaf sprite survive (ForestRender_SetStates_Foliage, 0x57BDF0). The comparison there is D3DCMP_GREATEREQUAL, so the test is "alpha at least the reference" and this discards below it, which is the same rule.

It matters more than a threshold usually does. The port had it hard coded at a half, which is neither of the original's numbers: on I.G.I. 1's foliage, whose texture alpha is strictly nought or 255, any threshold in between gives the same picture and the constant was harmless. I.G.I. 2's is not — a leaf sprite's alpha ramps, and testing at a half erodes it to a fraction of its authored shape.
Device state, like : it spans a run of draws and must be set back after them. A backend may treat it as part of the pipeline, so callers should change it in runs rather than per draw.

member.summary: Turns per-stage GPU timing on or off.

remarks.para: Off by default and worth keeping that way when nobody is reading it. A timer query is a synchronisation point: the driver is free to reorder and batch work between draw calls, and asking when a stage began and ended narrows what it may do. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IGpuTimingDevice.GpuMeasuredTiming
member.summary: Gets the whole GPU frame measured end to end, rather than summed from its stages.

remarks.para: adds up the stages, so it can only report work somebody remembered to bracket. A pass recorded outside every stage scope contributes to nothing and costs real time, and the totals stay quietly wrong -- which is how a millisecond of lamp-shadow tracing read as free here for an entire session. This is a single timestamp pair around the frame's whole command buffer, so the difference between the two is precisely the work no stage claims.

remarks.para: The member names deliberately mirror the original's RenderMode method names so the mapping stays checkable — is DisplaySetMode, is DisplaySwapBuffers, is ClipWindowPrimitive, is BlitPrimitive, and the texture members are the twelve-method texture set.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice.SetVertexSun(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Lights the following draws' vertices with the scene sun, from this direction; zero switches it off.
member.param: The unit vector towards the sun in the MODEL space of the draws that follow, or zero for draws that take no vertex lighting.

remarks.para: What Direct3D's vertex pipeline computed for an I.G.I. 2 object with no baked lightmap (Direct3DRender_SetGenericStateRigid, igi2ed 0x56CA90: D3DRS_LIGHTING = 1 over a white material): each vertex's colour becomes saturate(ambient + colour · max(N · L, 0)) and the texture is modulated by it. In model space so that the vertex stage needs nothing but the normal it already has; the caller knows the placement's orientation and the backend need not.
Device state, like : it spans a run of draws and must be cleared after them.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice.SetLightmapModulates(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Makes the following draws multiply their lightmap texture into the base colour.
member.param: Whether the lightmap slot is a colour to modulate rather than a bake.

remarks.para: Two of I.G.I. 2's surfaces put a colour in that slot rather than a bake to keep apart, and both want it multiplied into what stage 0 laid down — which is what the original's stage 1 does and what the forward path here does already. The FOREST is the other one: its second texture is a single texel holding the tree's own baked colour, because the original's foliage stage 0 is MODULATE2X(TEXTURE, DIFFUSE) with fixed-function lighting off (ForestRender_SetTextureState_AlphaTestFoliage, igi2ed 0x57C4B0, and ForestRender_SetGenericState_AlphaTestFoliage, 0x57C770, writing D3DRS_LIGHTING = 0) and this port has nowhere else to put a per-draw diffuse: the forward push block is full.

For I.G.I. 2's ground, whose second texture is a DETAIL map rather than a lightmap. TerrainRender_SetMaterialTextures (igi2ed 0x667330) binds the material's diffuse to stage 0 at 1 / (TextureScale * 4096) and its detail texture to stage 1 at 1 / (DetailTextureScale * 4096) — the two scales it writes into vertex-shader constants 11 and 12 — and TerrainRender_SetTextureState (0x66B810) gives stage 1 TEXCOORDINDEX = 1 and COLOROP = MODULATE(TEXTURE, CURRENT). The ground's colour is therefore the diffuse times the detail, at two different tiling rates, and it is where the rock and grass grain in the original's hillsides comes from: the diffuse alone repeats every few tens of metres and reads as a smooth wash.

The forward path needs nothing said to it — it already multiplies the lightmap into the colour, which for a bound detail map is exactly the stage-1 modulate. The deferred path routes the lightmap to its own G-buffer attachment instead, which is right for an object's bake and wrong for this, so this is how it is told which of the two it has.
Device state, like : it spans a run of draws.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice.SetTextureDetail(OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle,OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle)
member.summary: Attaches a derived surface-detail map to a diffuse texture.
member.param: The diffuse texture the map belongs to.
The packed map — the tangent-space normal's x and y, a roughness multiplier, and metallic — or to detach whatever was attached.

remarks.para: I.G.I. ships no normal maps and no roughness maps, so a physically-based shading model has three inputs it cannot answer from the data. This is how the answers get in: a map derived from the diffuse texture, or authored, or generated, registered once when the texture is loaded.

A property of the texture rather than of the draw, and that is what makes it cheap to adopt. A detail map belongs to a diffuse texture wherever that texture is used, so registering the pairing here means no renderer has to carry it, no draw call grows an argument, and a renderer that has no detail maps needs no change at all.
Only the deferred path reads it, and only when asks for a non-zero strength. Nothing under the original's path is affected.

member.exception: is not a texture of this device.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice.MarkRecordedWork
member.summary: Marks the work recorded so far, to learn when the GPU has finished it.
member.returns: A marker that completes once the GPU has finished everything recorded before this call.

remarks.para: Including the frame still being recorded. That work has not gone to the GPU yet -- it goes when the frame is presented, or flushed -- so a marker taken inside a frame is held until then and only begins to be answered once it has.

The pacing signal for work spread across frames. The time a frame takes on the host cannot be one: the host records a frame and moves on, and until the frames in flight fill up nothing it times includes the GPU work it has queued. Sizing work by host frame time buried the GPU in the first few frames of a level's lighting convergence, and on a laptop's integrated GPU one frame's command buffer ran long enough for the system to kill it.

member.summary: Begins a frame for latency measurement, pacing its start when low latency is on.
member.returns: when a new frame began; false while the last one is still unpresented.
member.remarks: Called at the top of every pass of the host loop, before input is read; the device begins a frame only once the previous one has reached the screen, so the loop passes that only tick neither pace nor count. member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ILatencyDevice.PresentsOnRecord
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the frame should be presented the moment it is recorded.
member.remarks: The original presents the frame at the head of the NEXT pass of its loop, and the engine keeps that cadence. Latency measurement cannot work that way: the frame would be submitted to the GPU only once the next one had begun, and every marker would describe the wrong frame. Where this is true the host presents at the end of its recording instead, and the scheduled present finds nothing left to do.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IMeshDevice.CreateMesh(System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Vertex3D},System.ReadOnlySpan{System.UInt16})
member.summary: Uploads a mesh and returns a handle to it.
member.param: The vertices.
Indices into , three per triangle.
member.returns: A handle to the new mesh.
member.exception: is not a multiple of three, or an index is out of range.
The mesh could not be created.
member.remarks: Meshes are immutable once uploaded. The original packs many models into a shared vertex buffer and flushes it when the running vertex count would pass 65535 (0x49B430/0x49B4B0) — a constraint of the hardware it targeted, not of the data, so OpenIGI gives each model its own buffer and keeps the 16-bit indices the models already use.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IMeshDevice.CreateAnimatedMesh(System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Vertex3D},System.ReadOnlySpan{System.UInt16})
member.summary: Uploads a mesh whose vertices will be replaced every pose, keeping the pose before.
member.param: The rest pose, replaced by the first .
The triangle list, three indices a triangle. Fixed for the mesh's life.
member.returns: A handle naming the mesh.

remarks.para: For CPU-skinned bodies. An ordinary mesh is immutable; an animated one is double-buffered, and each makes the vertices it replaces the mesh's previous pose — a second vertex stream the shaders can reach. That stream is what makes two things possible for a skinned body that a rigid transform cannot express: exact per-vertex motion for the temporal resolve, and drawing between two simulation poses (see ).
A mesh made by reports its own vertices as its previous pose, so every static mesh has exactly zero pose motion without paying for a second buffer.

member.summary: Allocates an empty mesh with fixed capacity, to be filled by .

member.remarks: For meshes that grow by appending — the terrain's batch pages. A mesh from is immutable, so growing one means destroying it and re-uploading everything it held; done every time a streamed-in chunk joins a page, those re-uploads were the single largest source of frame spikes. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IMeshDrawDevice.DrawOutline(OpenIGI.Rendering.MeshHandle,System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Rendering.MeshDrawRange},OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@,OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32,System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Draws a glowing selection outline around a mesh.
member.param: The mesh to outline.

Every index range making up the model. All of them at once, not one call each: the interior is masked out before the glow is drawn, and a model outlined a piece at a time would show each later piece's glow lying across the pieces before it.
The model-to-view transform the mesh itself would be drawn with.
The glow's colour; its alpha scales the whole effect.
How far the glow reaches past the silhouette, in pixels — not in world units, so a distant object keeps a mark of the same visible size instead of collapsing into a hairline.
Whether the glow ignores the depth buffer. Set, it marks something the reader cannot otherwise see; clear, it is occluded by the world like any other geometry.
member.exception: The handle is unknown, or a range lies outside the mesh.

remarks.para: An inverted hull expanded in screen space, drawn as a stack of shells that fade outwards, with the model's own silhouette masked out so only the rim survives. It costs a handful of extra draws of geometry the caller already has, and generates nothing.

Colour is never written where the model is, and depth is never written except by the mask, so the effect cannot occlude what is drawn after it. The mask does leave the near plane written across the model's silhouette, which is why this belongs late in a frame rather than in the middle of the world pass.
A posed mesh is outlined in the pose currently set through , so an animating character's glow tracks its limbs.

member.summary: The passes mods run over the picture, and the values their settings give them.

remarks.para: Part of . Every pass is one compute dispatch written against the contract in Shaders/Source/Mod/PostPass.slang: the picture and the scene's depth in, the picture out, sixteen values. The passes of each stage run in the order given.

A pass runs after the shutter and before the bloom and the tone map, so the game's exposure and grade see what it leaves. A pass runs after the tone map and the grade, over the picture as it is shown and before the interface is drawn over it. A device that runs no such passes ignores both members.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.IrradianceVolumeSettings
member.summary: How the baked probe field is applied to the frame.
member.remarks: The volume itself is handed over separately and only when it changes, because it is megabytes of baked transfer and does not vary per frame. What varies is here: the colours the sun and sky are this frame, and how strongly the result is applied.
member.param: Whether surfaces take their indirect light from the volume.
How strongly the volume's light is applied. One is the amount the bake computed; the useful range is around it, since the bake carries a single bounce and a real room has several.
What the open sky is worth this frame. The bake stored how much sky reaches each probe, not what colour it was, so a mission's own sky decides that here without rebaking anything.

How much of the volume's answer has replaced the flat ambient it stands in for, from 0 to 1.
The field is traced on a worker and arrives several seconds into a level, and until it does every surface is lit by one constant colour. Switching between the two in a single frame relights the whole world at once — which reads as a fault rather than as a load finishing, and is worse the more the field differs from the ambient it replaces.
A blend rather than a fade to black and back: both terms are meaningful at every point in between, so the intermediate frames are a lighting solution rather than a transition artefact.

member.remarks: Told once a frame, or once a mission, and read by the passes that shade it. Part of .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneEnvironmentDevice.SetVolumetricFog(OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogSettings@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalFogVolume})
member.summary: Sets the participating medium the scene is seen through.
member.param: The medium, or for none.

The camera's world position in metres. The march works in camera-relative world space, so the medium's base height and every volume's centre are rebased against this; passing it explicitly is clearer than having the shell pre-subtract it and hand over coordinates that are no longer world coordinates.
Regions where the medium differs from the level's base fog — rooms, basements, smoke. Retail has no such entities, so these are authored for the port.
member.remarks: Applied after lighting and before the forward pass, so translucent surfaces and the view model sit in front of the fog rather than being fogged twice.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneEnvironmentDevice.SetWetness(OpenIGI.Rendering.WetnessSettings@)
member.summary: Sets how wet the world is, which the lighting pass applies to every surface it shades.
member.param: The state of the ground, or for none.

remarks.para: Applied inside the deferred lighting pass, between unpacking the G-buffer and shading it: the albedo is darkened, the roughness collapsed and the normal replaced by the water's, so the sun, the lamps, the sky and the bounce all light the wet surface rather than the dry one underneath. See for why it cannot be done in the G-buffer instead.

A backend that has not implemented it does nothing, which is why this has a body: adding standing water to one renderer should not stop the other one compiling, and a device that ignores it says so through where the shell can report it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneEnvironmentDevice.SetShelterMap(OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle,OpenIGI.Rendering.ShelterMapTransform@)
member.summary: Sets the top-down map of the level's roofs, which decides what the rain reaches.
member.param: The raster, packed as describes, or for a level with no map.
How to read it, or when nothing is sheltered. Set once when a mission loads: the map is a property of the level rather than of the frame.
member.remarks: Ground under a roof stays dry however hard it is raining outside — without this the floor of every building in the level pools with water while its own roof keeps the rain off it. Both the shading and the reflection march read it, and they must read the same one: a reflection that disagreed with the shading about where the water is would land beside it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneEnvironmentDevice.SetReflections(OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionSettings@)
member.summary: Sets what surfaces reflect and how far the frame is searched to find it.
member.param: The search, or for none.
member.remarks: Applied after the lighting and before the fog: a reflection is of the lit world, and it belongs behind the air rather than in front of it.

member.param: The table, or to forget the one held.
member.remarks: Separate from , and called only when the grade changes — which in practice is when the mission does. The table is a volume texture upload; how much of it to apply is a number per frame.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneEnvironmentDevice.SetEnvironmentCube(OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle)
member.summary: Hands over the cube map reflective draws sample, or clears it.
member.param: The cube, or for none.

remarks.para: Device state rather than a texture unit, and that is a fact about this seam rather than about cube maps: a 3D draw here takes its diffuse and its lightmap as arguments, and the unit array writes is read by the compute path alone. A reflection belongs with and — something the frame is told once and a run of draws then uses.
A device with no cube reflects nothing; so does a draw made while none is set. That is the state every non-reflective draw is in, which is nearly all of them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneLightingDevice
member.summary: What the deferred lighting lights the scene with: the sun, the lamps, the flashlight, and the indirect light the surface cache and the probe fields carry.
member.remarks: Part of .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneLightingDevice.SetSurfaceCache(OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheBinding@)
member.summary: Hands the backend the surface cache, so a traced ray can be turned into light.
member.param: The cards, the grid and the lighting atlas, or while the level has no cache — during loading, or on a mission whose cards failed to build.
member.remarks: Called every frame rather than once per mission, because the camera offset in it moves. Everything else is a property of the level and is simply repeated; the backend stores the struct and resolves nothing until a pass that traces actually runs.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneLightingDevice.SetDistanceField(OpenIGI.Rendering.DistanceFieldBinding@)
member.summary: Hands over the level's distance field, for the passes that march it.
member.param: The clipmaps and their boxes, or .

remarks.para: The counterpart to , and handed over the same way and at the same point: every frame, because the boxes are camera-relative and move with the camera, with the backend storing the struct and resolving nothing until a pass that marches actually runs.

This exists so a reflection can find a hit on an adapter that cannot trace. The field is the only description of the world a shader can walk without an acceleration structure, and it lived entirely on the game's side until now — which is why glass without ray tracing reflected the sky and nothing else. A no-op by default: a backend that marches nothing has nowhere to put it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneLightingDevice.TryGetSkyIrradiance(System.Span{System.Single})
member.summary: Copies the sky's irradiance harmonics into .
member.param: Room for 28 floats: seven vectors of four.
member.returns: when the backend has an atmosphere to report.
member.remarks: The seven coefficient vectors of the deferred sky term — third-order harmonics of the sky's light, cosine-convolved with the Lambert one-over-pi folded in, exactly as the lighting pass consumes them. A game-layer pass that traces its own rays evaluates these along each escaping ray so its sky matches the sky the lighting shows, one frame behind (the values are read back from the device). A backend with no atmosphere tables returns and the caller keeps whatever flat approximation it has.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneLightingDevice.SetScreenIndirect(OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle,System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Feeds a screen probe gather's indirect light into the deferred lighting.
member.param: The probe atlas of indirect irradiance, covering the frame.
How strongly to apply it. Zero, or an invalid handle, is a no-op.
When set, the handle is a full-resolution atlas the temporal resolve already upsampled, read straight per pixel; when clear it is the sparse probe atlas the deferred fill upsamples itself.
member.remarks: Set while the G-buffer is live, before the geometry pass closes: the deferred lighting reads it as its diffuse fill in place of the flat ambient, where the surface's own albedo and the light scale are already applied -- so this is not a post-pass over the lit frame but part of the shade itself, in the renderer's albedo * E convention with metals excluded. A no-op when the target is not deferred or the strength is zero, so a preset that leaves it off pays nothing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISceneLightingDevice.SetLocalLights(System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Rendering.DeferredLocalLight})
member.summary: Sets the level's real-time local lights for the next deferred lighting pass.
member.param: The lights, in VIEW space; a set longer than is truncated. View space because the level sits tens of kilometres from the world origin, where a float has metres of resolution left: the camera-relative subtract has to happen in double precision on the game's side, and by the time it arrives here it has already happened.

remarks.para: Held rather than acted on, like : this records what the next lighting pass folds in, and the pass clears it after, so a frame that sets none lights from none. Called each frame while the G-buffer is live, before the geometry pass closes.

These are the lamps a level implies and never declares — see the game layer's lamp detection. They are what lights a windowless interior: there is no daylight to gather in a sealed room, so no amount of exposure or bounce can find light that has no source, and this is the source.

member.summary: Starts rendering the scene into an offscreen target instead of the back buffer.

remarks.para: This is the one addition the whole remaster track rests on. The original throws each frame away as it presents it; shadows, ambient occlusion, reflections, volumetric fog and temporal anti-aliasing all need the frame and its depth to still be there afterwards.

member.summary: Gets the current scene target's lit colour, or .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.IScenePassDevice.SceneExposure
member.summary: What the resolve is about to multiply the lit buffer by — the exposure a display-referred colour must be divided by to survive it.

remarks.para: A forward draw that declares itself emissive writes straight into the SCENE-REFERRED lit buffer, which the resolve then exposes and tone maps. A colour authored in display terms and written raw is at the mercy of the eye adaptation: in a dark scene the exposure is high, and a saturated red sprite comes back pink because the red channel clips long before the other two stop rising. Dividing by this lands it at the colour it was asked for whatever the scene is doing — the same correction the first-person rig's lighting and the selection glow already take.
One on a backend or a path that draws straight to a display-encoded target, where a colour already means what it says. Never zero.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.IScenePassDevice.BeginPass(OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass)
member.summary: Declares which part of the frame the following draws belong to.
member.param: The part of the frame.

remarks.para: The renderers themselves never call this; the shell does, around the groups of draws it already makes. That is what lets the backend shade an opaque surface into a G-buffer and a translucent one directly, without any renderer in the game learning that there are two ways to be drawn.

The glazing's front layer is the one pass that may begin while another is open: it begins with the geometry pass still open and closes it, without the shading that ending the geometry pass would run -- the front layer has to be drawn between the two.

member.exception: No capture is in progress, or a pass is already open other than the geometry pass the front layer closes.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ISdfTextDevice
member.summary: An optional device capability: drawing signed-distance-field text with the distance-field shader.

remarks.para: Kept off the main because it is a specialised path, not something every backend must offer and not something the 2D pipeline needs in general. A caller checks device is ISdfTextDevice; when the capability is absent — as it is for the recording device used in tests — the sprite batch falls back to drawing the atlas as ordinary coverage, which the coverage atlas is built to render correctly.

The geometry is the same two buffers a textured draw uses; the difference is the program, which reads the atlas as a distance field and thresholds it into a crisp, optionally outlined and glowing, edge.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ITemporalDevice
member.summary: How a frame accumulates into the ones before it, and what reconstructs it to the output size.
member.remarks: Part of .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ITemporalDevice.SetTemporalAntiAliasing(OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalAaSettings@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f)
member.summary: Sets how this frame accumulates into the ones before it.
member.param: The accumulation, or for none. Its jitter is the offset the caller has already applied to the projection it draws with; it is reported here so the backend can account for it, not so the backend can apply it.

The scene's projection without the jitter. Reprojection has to compare two frames in one frame of reference, and the jitter is precisely what differs between them; the unjittered matrix is that shared reference. This is passed rather than read from because the view model draws with a projection of its own, and by the time the frame resolves that is the one the device last saw.

The camera's world position in metres, used to work out how far it has travelled since the previous frame. Supplied in double precision: this world's coordinates run to tens of thousands of units, and the per-frame travel is often a fraction of one, so the backend must difference two positions of that magnitude to recover it. Doing that in single precision loses the travel to cancellation and smears the reprojection under translation; passing it double lets the backend keep the subtraction exact and narrow only the small result to float.
The rotation taking a view-space direction back into camera-relative world space.
member.remarks: The backend keeps the previous frame's values itself, so a caller supplies only what is true now. A frame in which this is not called is a frame with no history, which is the correct behaviour on a camera cut.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ITemporalDevice.ResetHistory(OpenIGI.Rendering.HistoryResetReason)
member.summary: Forgets every temporal history at the start of the next scene capture.
member.param: Why, for the log.
member.remarks: The upscaler's history, the traced shadows' and the fog's accumulation, the occlusion's, and an NVIDIA reconstruction's own (its reset flag) all start over, and the frame's motion is measured as none. Reasons accumulate until the capture that consumes them; calling it twice costs nothing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ITracedWorldDevice.ReleaseWorld
member.summary: Drops everything a backend has accumulated about the level being left.

remarks.para: Some of what a backend builds is discovered from the frames it draws rather than handed to it: the traceable copy of the world is assembled from geometry-pass draws over a level's first seconds, and it has no other way of learning that the level has gone. Destroying the meshes tells it that each one has gone, which is not the same thing -- the material records a structure's hits are looked up in are append-only by design, so a session that entered six missions carried six missions' worth of them and the seventh would have overflowed the buffer they live in.

Called when a mission is released, before its meshes and textures are destroyed. It is not a device reset: nothing the front end is still drawing with is touched, and a backend with nothing accumulated does nothing.

The player's own body in first person is the case this exists for: it has to be in the acceleration structure or no reflected ray can strike it and no window can show the player standing at it, and it must not be in the G-buffer or the camera is inside its head.

remarks.para: For geometry whose traceable shape is not what the rasteriser is handed: the terrain. Its pages hold every chunk ever streamed into them at every level of detail, at positions the vertex stage then slides towards the next level as the camera moves — so a structure built over a page casts from a surface that is not the one on screen, and the ground shadows itself in patches. The terrain instead writes the chunks it drew, at the positions it drew them, into a mesh of its own and offers that here each frame; the placement lasts one frame, and the structure is rebuilt whenever the mesh's contents change.
A backend without a traced world ignores the call, which is the default implementation.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.LampFill
member.summary: How much light the level's lamps put on the first-person rig.

remarks.para: The lamps reach the renderers in VIEW space -- that is how the deferred shading wants them -- and the rig sits at the eye, so the sample point is very nearly the view-space origin. A hand's length in front of it, because the arms are, and because a fitting directly overhead otherwise reads as being exactly at the sample point.

The falloff is the same windowed inverse square the shading applies, deliberately: the arms and the wall behind them should agree about how bright the room is. What it does NOT do is trace -- the rig is lit by a two-light studio setup that has never cast a shadow, and a shadow ray per lamp per frame to shade two hands would cost more than the whole rest of the rig. Shared so both renderers light the rig alike.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.LampShadowParameters
member.summary: The parameter blocks of the traced lamp visibility's three dispatches, the same for every backend.

remarks.para: The trace fires one ray per half-resolution pixel at the lamp its reservoir picks (the LampShadow module); the temporal half accumulates that onto a reprojected, neighbourhood-clamped history (LampDenoiseTemporal); the spatial half filters what is left where its variance says there is still noise (LampDenoiseSpatial). The shading reads the result. Written once so the renderers cannot drift apart: the blocks are the shaders' own layouts, and the trace's carries the shading's lamp block byte for byte, so the two cannot disagree about which lamp is which.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LampShadowParameters.ResolutionDivisor
member.summary: How many frame pixels each side of one lamp-visibility texel covers.
member.remarks: One: the visibility is traced and denoised at the frame's own resolution. It was two, and at half resolution one sample stood for four pixels -- which is harmless on an open wall and wrong wherever a thin occluder crosses the view. Seen through a chain-link fence, nearly every two-by-two block held a wire and the building behind it, the building's pixels inherited the wire's clear line to the lamps, and the building glowed through the fence in the fence's own diamond pattern. Every pixel asking its own question is the only answer that does not depend on what stands in front of it.

member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingCVars.Deferred
member.summary: Whether surfaces are recorded into a G-buffer and lit afterwards.
member.remarks: Required by everything from stage R3 on. Kept separate from so the offscreen pipeline can be exercised on its own — which is what the round-trip check in docs/remaster/reference/README.md does.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingCVars.Lighting
member.summary: Where surfaces take their light from.
member.remarks: This waited on baked for every preset until the sun of stage R3 and the probe irradiance of R7 existed, because promoting it before then would have traded hand-authored lighting for a flat ambient term. Both exist now, and every preset above vanilla has been promoted — see the note on the rows below for what carries the surfaces the screen gather cannot resolve. Vanilla stays baked for the same reason it stays on the forward path: it is the regression gate, and it has to keep reproducing the picture the game shipped with.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingCVars.LightScale
member.summary: Scales the whole dynamically-computed irradiance.
member.remarks: Not a taste control, a calibration. I.G.I.'s diffuse textures are not albedo: they were painted to be multiplied by a lightmap averaging well below one, so they already carry lighting. Lighting them at unit irradiance counts that painted-in brightness twice, and it lands hardest on the brightest textures -- which is why the sand and the snow blew out while the concrete looked right. The default is measured against the artists' own bakes rather than chosen.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingCVars.AmbientScale
member.summary: Scales the flat ambient stand-in the dynamic model fills unlit surfaces with.
member.remarks: TEMPORARY. Until the probe volume of stage R7 gives ambient a sense of place, the dynamic model lights every surface with one flat ambient colour from the level's Dirlight -- so a sealed, windowless room reads as bright as open ground. This scales that stand-in so the effect can be dialled down to see enclosed spaces go dark, or to nothing (0) to prove it is what lights them. Not archived and not part of any preset: it exists to diagnose, not to ship. Only the dynamic model reads it -- the baked model lights from the lightmaps and has no ambient term of its own.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingCVars.SunScale
member.summary: Calibrates the real-time sun against the sky fill.
member.remarks: Only the dynamic model reads this; the baked model lights from its lightmaps and never adds a live sun. The atmospheric source has its own independently normalised control so changing this value does not move the sky with it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingCVars.Presets
member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingModel
member.summary: Where a surface's light comes from.

remarks.para: The original lights its world entirely with baked lightmaps — one texture per surface, multiplied into the diffuse. That is beautiful, hand-authored and completely static: nothing casts a shadow, nothing responds to a muzzle flash, and the sun cannot move. Replacing it is the largest single change in the remaster track and the one most able to make the game look worse, so it is a setting with a way back rather than a decision taken once.

The G-buffer keeps albedo and baked irradiance in separate targets precisely so these three can be chosen at run time. Storing the product, as the original's shader does, would make and impossible without re-rendering.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LightingModel.Baked

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalFogVolume
member.summary: A region of the world where the medium is thicker than the level's base fog.

remarks.para: A single height-exponential medium describes outdoor air well and describes nothing else at all: it cannot put mist in a basement that sits above the fog line, or smoke in one room and not the next. These are the exceptions, authored per mission.
The retail data has no such entities — there is no fog-volume task in objects.qvm — so these are a deliberate addition of the port's, and only the modern path reads them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for the level's lamps: how they are detected, how far and how brightly they light, and their shadows.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.LocalLightScale
member.summary: How strongly the level's detected lamp fixtures light the scene as real lights.

remarks.para: The screen gather only carries light that already exists in the frame -- daylight through a window, a sunlit wall -- so a windowless interior it cannot help: there is no source to gather. This turns the fixtures the lamp detection proposes into direct lights, which is the honest way to light such a room -- a real source with a real falloff, not exposure lifting a black frame into grey.

Each is punctual with a windowed inverse square, and DIRECTIONAL where the fixture's own geometry says which way it faces: the light falls off as the cosine of the angle off that axis, so a ceiling tube lights the floor and leaves the slab it is bolted to dark, which is what a real fitting does and what an omnidirectional point emphatically does not. Scales the whole set; the fixtures' relative intensities are the detection's, and this is the one number tuned by eye.

Off at vanilla, where the shipped bakes still carry the interiors and adding a second set of lights on top of light that is already painted in would count the same lamp twice. Every preset above it lights dynamically and so discards those bakes, which is exactly why they need this: without it a windowless room has no source at all and reads black.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.LocalLightShadows
member.summary: Whether the level's lamps cast shadows, traced against the world like the sun.

remarks.para: A punctual light with no shadow term passes through whatever stands between it and the surface. So a corridor fitting lights the room on the other side of the partition, a floodlight lights the inside of the building it is bolted to, and the more reach a lamp is given the further that wrongness spreads -- which is what makes a knob with a ceiling rather than a number to turn up. This removes that ceiling.

One ray per lamp per pixel, and only for the lamps that survive the reach and facing culls, so indoors it is a handful and outdoors usually none. Traced inside the shading pass rather than in a pass of its own, which is what keeps it to that: there is no screen-sized buffer to allocate, no ordering to agree with a second pass, and nothing is spent on a pixel no lamp reaches.

Needs an adapter that can trace, and does nothing without one -- the shading pass compiled for such a device has no trace in it at all. Unlike the sun's shadow this one is OPAQUE: a wire fence in front of a lamp casts a solid shadow rather than a patterned one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.LampDenoise
member.summary: Whether the lamp shadow is denoised before the shading reads it.

remarks.para: On, which is the only setting anybody should play with: one traced ray per pixel is a coin toss, and drawing it straight is grain rather than a shadow. This exists so the denoiser can be measured against its own absence in a single build — the pass still runs and still carries the depth the shading's upsample needs, it simply stops filtering — which is the only honest way to say what it is worth.
Not archived. A debug lever that persisted itself into settings.cfg would be a shipped regression waiting for somebody to trip over, and this renderer has already been bitten once by exactly that.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.LocalLightSource
member.summary: The largest a fixture may be treated as when its shadow ray samples it, in metres.

remarks.para: A shadow's penumbra widens with the size of the source casting it, and the size this starts from is the fixture's extent — a bound on the whole clustered housing, which for a merged fitting can measure most of two metres. That is not the width of the thing actually emitting, and treating it as though it were is where the grain came from: the wider the penumbra, the more of it each of the two taps a pixel can afford has to stand for.

A quarter of a metre is about the glass of a real fitting. The softness the eye expects survives and the variance does not. Raise it for a deliberately diffuse look and expect noise; lower it towards nought for hard, cheap, obviously-computed edges.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.LocalLightRange
member.summary: How far a detected lamp reaches, against the reach its own size and colour imply.

remarks.para: The extractor derives a reach from the fixture's size and brightness, and that derivation is conservative: it comes from cutting an inverse square at a fixed threshold, so it stops where the light becomes arithmetically negligible rather than where it stops being visible. On a dark interior wall the difference is the whole tail of the falloff, and the symptom is a corridor whose far end is black until the player walks into each lamp's reach in turn — the light appearing to switch on rather than to fall off.

Two doubles every fixture's reach. The near field barely moves — the windowed inverse square is still an inverse square, and a wider window only lifts what was being cut off at the edge — so this extends the pool of light rather than brightening the middle of it.

It is a knob rather than a bigger constant because there IS an upper bound, and it is not about taste: these lights cast no shadows. Nothing stops a lamp reaching through the wall it is mounted on, so a reach much past the room the fixture stands in lights the rooms either side of it too, and a level lit that way glows from the inside out. Raise it for a big hall; lower it if light is appearing where a wall should have stopped it.

Doubled to four, and the selection no longer scales with it. Raising this used to do two unrelated things at once: it widened the reach the shader culls and falls off against — which is what anyone raising it wants — and it also scaled the term LevelLamps.SelectNearest ranks by, distance - radius * range. The second is why raising it once made lamps go out EARLIER than before: scaling the radius term scales how much a fixture's own size counts in the comparison, so big distant battens crowded the small near fittings out of a budget only sixty-four deep. The ranking now uses the unscaled radius, so this widens the light and nothing else, and a lamp keeps its slot on where it is rather than on how big it is.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.GlobalIlluminationLamps
member.summary: Whether the level's lamps are detected at all: as emission, as lights and in the bounce.

remarks.para: The level declares no point lights. Its lamps are worked out from what the artists baked around each texture and from the SHAPE of the geometry that draws it -- small, above head height, flat, facing down and painted near-white is a light fixture and very little else -- and the conclusion then does three things at once: the fixture geometry is made emissive so a lamp looks like the thing doing the lighting, a punctual light is placed at every one so a windowless room has a source, and the same fixtures feed the surface cache so that room bounces. All three or none: a lamp that lights a floor without glowing reads as a room lit by nothing, and a lamp that glows without lighting reads as a decal.

Off is the honest reading of a level with no lamps at all -- a sealed interior goes dark, which is what it would be. Turn it off to see what the level looks like on daylight alone, or when a detection has gone wrong in a level whose fixtures file has not been corrected yet.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.LocalLightCVars.LampEmissiveScale
member.summary: How brightly the detected lamp geometry itself glows, against what the detector proposed.

remarks.para: This is the FIXTURE, not the light it casts -- is that. A lamp has to be brighter in the frame than any surface it lights or it does not read as the source: at its own albedo a fluorescent panel is a pale grey rectangle with a mysterious pool of light beneath it, and what makes it a lamp is being written above what a lit surface can reach, where the bloom finds it.

One means the strength the detection proposed, which is a lamp at six times its albedo and a merely-bright surface -- an advert panel, a lit sign -- proportionally less. The two knobs are separate because they answer different complaints: a room that is too bright wants the light turned down, and a fixture that looks like a sticker wants this turned up.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for surfaces: the derived material maps, overrides, cut-outs and texture filtering.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.MaterialDetail
member.summary: How strongly the derived surface-detail maps are applied, or 0 to ignore them.

remarks.para: I.G.I. ships a diffuse texture per surface and nothing else — no normal map, no roughness map. A physically-based shading model has four inputs and the data answers one, so the rest are derived from the diffuse itself and registered per texture. This is how far to trust that.

Invented data, and a deliberate divergence. It is off under vanilla and enhanced, because those presets exist to reproduce and to gently improve what shipped rather than to add detail nobody painted. It is what makes brick read as brick when the sun crosses it, which is a larger visible gap between this renderer and a modern one than any amount of indirect lighting.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.FloorGloss
member.summary: How an up-facing surface's (a floor's, a desk top's) roughness differs from a wall's.

remarks.para: A multiplier on an up-facing surface's roughness, keyed off how far the surface faces the world up. One is off, every surface as its material said. Below one smooths floors towards a sheen so they take a reflection while the walls stay matte; above one ROUGHENS them, so they shine less than the walls. Only the dynamic model reads it.

The game ships one roughness for every surface, and a building's floor at the default 0.6 read as the shiniest thing in the room even with this off: a floor is the one surface nearly always seen at a grazing angle, where a dielectric's Fresnel term climbs towards all of the light, so the same lamp and ambient highlight a wall shows faintly lies across a floor as a polished sheen. It also sits exactly on the traced reflection's roughness ceiling (r_rt_reflection_roughness 0.6), so anything that took a texel a little smoother handed it a reflection at the 1.7 intensity.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.OverridesEnabled
member.summary: Whether the overrides folder is drawn, for comparing against the game's own assets.

remarks.para: The successor to r_hd, which switched an upscaled-texture pack in and out of the frame. That pack no longer exists: replacement art goes in the installation's overrides folder and arrives through the ordinary resource path, which is how every other asset arrives and is why it needs no setting of its own to point at it.

The comparison it made is worth keeping, though, and it is worth more now — the folder can replace anything, not only a texture. Off bypasses every override without deleting a file, so the two pictures are one keypress apart. Not saved: it is a switch for looking at something, and a player who put files in the folder meant them to be used.
Toggling costs a reload of the level's textures, because what is already uploaded was decoded from the bytes this changes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.MaterialDetailEnabled
member.summary: Whether the derived surface maps are applied, for comparing against flat shading.

remarks.para: The F9 half of the same pair, and not archived for the same reason. is the authored strength and is a quality level the presets own; this multiplies it by one or zero so the normal, the roughness and the metal can be taken out of the frame and put back without disturbing what the player chose or what the preset set.
Toggling r_material_detail directly would do the same thing visually and would write the player's setting to zero on the way past, which is exactly the fault this arrangement exists to avoid.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.HashedAlpha
member.summary: Whether cut-outs use a temporally-resolved hashed alpha test rather than a hard one.
member.remarks: A hard cut-out keeps or drops whole pixels, so a chain-link fence or a wire thinner than a pixel aliases into a shimmer. The hashed test recovers the edge's coverage from the alpha gradient and dithers it, which the temporal resolve then averages into a smooth edge. It therefore only helps where the temporal filter runs, so it follows the same presets: off where is one, on above it.
member.para: Off at every preset now, on two independent grounds. The target look has no dithered opacity mask, so the look says off. And measured here it costs more than it buys: still-camera stability goes from 0.390% to 0.483% consecutive-frame RMSE and detail from 45.9 to 44.5, because the dither is noise until a temporal filter resolves it and ours does not fully resolve it even with the camera stopped. It buys a slightly better yard whole-frame figure (12.76% to 12.48%) and that is not worth a quarter more shimmer on the exact geometry the shimmer was complained about.

It is implemented rather than removed: the value used to be one here and the Vulkan backend silently ignored it, which is the failure mode the settings sweep exists to catch. It now does what it says, and says off.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.Anisotropy
member.summary: The anisotropic filtering ratio, 1 for none.
member.remarks: The single cheapest visible win in this renderer. A ground plane at a grazing angle is the worst case trilinear filtering has: a pixel's footprint is a long thin sliver, the mip level has to be chosen for its widest axis, and all the detail along the other axis is discarded. That is why terrain smears towards the horizon without it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.PointMips
member.summary: Whether a texture picks its nearest mip level rather than blending between two.
member.remarks: Both games filter linearly within a level and take the nearest level (D3DTSS_MIPFILTER point: Project I.G.I.'s stage setup at 0x49D730, and its terrain at 0x512C30), which is the original's look.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialCVars.Presets
member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack
member.summary: A directory of derived surface-detail maps, attached to textures as they are loaded.

remarks.para: I.G.I. ships a diffuse texture per surface and nothing else. The maps a physically-based shading model needs — the normal, the roughness, whether it is metal — are derived from those textures by and written out as PNGs named after them. This finds them and registers each one against the texture it belongs to.

Absent is a supported state, not an error. An installation with no derived maps renders exactly as it did before any of this existed, which is why every failure below is a warning and a null handle rather than an exception.

Maps built by a tool do not come through here. Those travel inside the asset they describe, as a second layer of a replacement in the overrides folder, and reach the device with the texture. This is the fallback for everything else: given a cache directory and , a texture with no map derives its own on first sight and the result is written out, so the second run reads a PNG where the first computed one. That is what lets the maps be a per-user cache built from the player's own installation rather than an asset this repository carries — the game's art with a filter over it is not ours to redistribute.
One instance per device. It owns the textures it uploads, so disposing it releases them; the diffuse textures it attaches them to belong to whoever loaded those.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.#ctor(OpenIGI.Rendering.IGraphicsDevice,OpenIGI.Core.Threading.IWorkScheduler,OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.IOpenIgiLogger,System.String)
member.summary: Initialises a new instance of the class.
member.param: The device the maps are uploaded to.
Where maps are read and derived off the frame, where the platform has anywhere.
Where to report what was found and what would not load.
Where maps derived on demand are written, or empty for none. Read from as well as written to, and created on first write, so an installation with no replacement art still fills it in.
member.exception: is .
member.remarks: There is no authored-pack directory any more. A map built by a tool travels inside the asset it belongs to, as a second layer of the replacement in the overrides folder, and reaches the device through the ordinary texture path — so there is nothing left for a separate directory of PNGs to be the source of, and nothing to keep in step with the textures it describes. What remains here is the derivation this process does for itself, for the surfaces nothing has built a map for.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.KeyFor(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Builds the name a texture's map is kept under, cached on disk and in memory.
member.param: The texture's name.
The stamp of the content-pack file standing in for the texture, or when the texture is the game's own.
member.returns: The bare name for a shipped texture, or the name and the stamp for a replaced one.
member.remarks: A map is derived from the picture, and the name alone is shared by the shipped picture and every pack's replacement of it: keyed by the name, whichever was derived first was handed to all of them, across runs. The shipped key is unchanged, so caches filled before content packs keep working.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.IsAvailable
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether maps can be derived and cached at all.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.DeriveMissing
member.summary: Gets or sets a value indicating whether a texture with no map derives one and caches it.

remarks.para: Off by default, and pointless without a cache directory. The caller owns this because the answer is a rendering policy rather than a property of the pack: r_material_detail is zero under the vanilla and enhanced presets, and deriving a level's worth of maps that the shader is about to multiply by nothing is pure waste.
Read on every miss rather than captured once, so raising the setting mid-session starts deriving for whatever loads next.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.Enabled
member.summary: Gets or sets a value indicating whether detail maps are used at all.
member.remarks: Off where the shader multiplies them by nothing (r_material_detail 0). Nothing is then read, loaded or derived -- a cache an earlier session filled was otherwise decoded and uploaded on every load at presets that never sample it -- and nothing is remembered as missing, so turning detail on later finds every map.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.Count
member.summary: Gets how many maps have been uploaded.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.Unclaimed

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.Prewarm(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.String})
member.summary: Reads and decodes the maps for a set of textures on the thread pool.
member.param: The texture names, as the pack records them.

remarks.para: A detail map is a PNG on disk, and finding and inflating one is file I/O and CPU with no graphics in it at all -- yet it happened inside Attach, on the thread that was uploading the texture it belongs to. Measured over one level's surface-cache capture: 219 ms of the render thread, most of it inside the inflater.

So the reading is done here instead, wherever the caller has a worker to spare, and Attach finds the pixels already in hand and does nothing but upload. Optional in exactly the way the pack itself is: a name that was never prewarmed, or one prewarmed after the frame asked for it, is read inline as it always was.

member.returns: The reads, finished when every map has been read; already finished where none are run.
member.exception: is .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.Attach(System.String,OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle)
member.summary: Attaches this texture's detail map, if the pack has one.
member.param: The texture's name, as the pack records it and as the file is named.
The loaded diffuse texture to attach it to.
member.remarks: Safe to call for every texture as it loads. A texture with no map in the pack is remembered as having none, so a level full of them costs one failed lookup each rather than one per frame.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialDetailPack.Attach(System.String,OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureHandle,System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32},System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Attaches this texture's detail map, deriving and caching one if there is none.
member.param: The texture's name, as the pack records it and as the file is named.
The loaded diffuse texture to attach it to.
That texture's top-level pixels, for deriving a map from on a miss.
The texture's width in pixels.
The texture's height in pixels.

remarks.para: The lookup runs pack, then cache, then derivation. A miss with set hands the pixels to a worker and returns immediately: the derivation measured at tens of milliseconds for a single texture, and a level loads a thousand of them, so doing this inline would put most of a minute on the first load of every level. The texture keeps its flat normals until installs the result, which is the same state an installation with no pack renders in permanently — a supported one, and invisible at the strengths these maps are applied at.

Several textures may ask for the same name before any answer arrives, which is ordinary across two renderers loading the same wall; they queue against the one derivation rather than starting their own.

The texture's height in pixels.

remarks.para: For the textures the pack cannot be asked about, because they have no name to ask with. The terrain's ground tiles are the case that matters: they arrive as an indexed atlas rather than as named resources, and they are also the single largest surface on screen, so leaving them flat while every wall gained detail would be the most visible half of the job left undone.

Runs the derivation in process rather than reading a file. That is affordable here precisely because it is the exception — a level has a handful of ground tiles and a thousand other textures, and the thousand come from the pack.

is still the policy gate. Ground tiles have no authored name to look up, but deriving maps for them while material detail is disabled is wasted CPU and can turn a mission load into a multi-minute stall on some systems.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.MaterialLibrary
member.summary: What each of a level's textures is made of, as far as the renderer is concerned.

remarks.para: The obvious design does not work here, and it is worth saying why. The usual way to give an old game surface materials is to match on texture names — snow* is a rough dielectric, metal* is a conductor, and so on. I.G.I.'s textures are not named that way: they are numbered. Level 1 alone draws 203_04_1, 216_01_1_argb8888, 219_02_1 and a hundred more like them, and no rule over those strings can know which is glass.

So there are two things to match on instead. The first is the one piece of meaning the names do carry: the _argb8888 suffix marks the textures the packs store with an alpha channel, which in this game is the glass, the wire fences and the foliage — everything cut out or seen through. The second is the texture's own number, listed explicitly. That is laborious, and it is also the only honest way: deciding that 216_03_1 is polished metal means looking at it.
Data rather than code, and loaded the same way the fog presets are, so a surface can be re-judged by editing a file rather than by rebuilding.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.MemoryBarrierScope
member.summary: What a compute pass wrote, so the next reader can be made to see it.

remarks.para: Compute dispatches are not ordered against each other by default — the driver is free to overlap them, which is most of why compute is fast. A barrier is how a pass that depends on a previous one's output says so, and naming what kind of access has to be visible is what keeps the barrier from being a full pipeline flush.
Flags rather than one value: a pass that wrote both a buffer and an image needs both, and issuing two barriers where one would do is a stall the driver cannot optimise away.

Reading a texture back with the API after a shader wrote it through an image binding needs THIS one, and the difference is not academic: without it the readback returns the texture's allocated contents rather than what the pass computed, which reads as a pass that never ran.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.CardPushBlock
member.summary: The 128 bytes a card capture pushes: where the model is, and what it is made of.

remarks.para: A card is a flat window onto part of a model, drawn through an orthographic camera sitting on the card's own plane, so the only transform there is is the one that puts the model in that window.

The three normal rows go unused — a page stores the model's own normal, which needs no transform — but the block is shared in size and shape with the mesh paths, so they are written as nought rather than left holding whatever the last draw pushed. A push block is not cleared between draws, and a shader that reads a slot nobody wrote reads the previous draw's value.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardPushBlock
member.summary: The 128 bytes a forward mesh draw pushes, filled from the scene rather than from a device.

remarks.para: Lifted out because it is the part of the 3D path most easily got wrong and least visible when it is: every float of the block is spoken for, several slots carry different things depending on what the draw is, and a slot written with the wrong one shades plausibly and incorrectly. As a function of a state and a draw it can simply be checked.

The layout, slot by slot: the model-view-projection in the first sixteen; the marker and the lightmap scale or inverse exposure; the pose blend; and the rig's ambient level. The last three rows are read three different ways — as the terrain's fade ramp and camera offset, as the model-to-view rotation with the key colour in the w's for the lit rig, or as a single model-space sun plus the flat model light for an ordinary world draw — and the frame's fog rides in the final row of the two that do not need it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardPushBlock.WriteTerrain(System.Span{System.Single},OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardDrawState@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@,OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode)
member.summary: The terrain's rows: the fade ramp, and where the chunk's origin sits from the eye.
member.remarks: Terrain slides each vertex between levels of detail, and the slide is measured along the world axes from the eye, so the vertex stage needs the ramp and the offset. A chunk is drawn unrotated, so the model-view's rotation is the view's own and its transpose undoes it: the offset is that transpose applied to the model-view's translation. The rows this takes carry the rotation and the key colour for the lit rig, and a chunk is never the rig — the first row's w, zero for every other draw, is what says so.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardPushBlock.WriteRotation(System.Span{System.Single},OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardDrawState@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@,OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode,System.Boolean,System.Boolean)
member.summary: The rotation rows, each w carrying a channel of the key colour or something else.
member.remarks: The key is read by the lit rig alone, so every other draw leaves the first w at zero: that is the terrain flag the vertex stage reads, and a sun tint there would morph the world. A negative value marks material-weighted fog instead; it does not activate that morph. The other two w's are a world draw's remaining components of the direction towards the fixed-function sun.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardPushBlock.WriteFog(System.Span{System.Single},OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardDrawState@,OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode)
member.summary: Writes the frame's fog into the last row of the block.
member.remarks: The colour follows the blend the way sub_5144E0 sets FOGCOLOR per blend mode: an additive pass fogs to black, so that a surface drawn as several passes is fogged once and not once per pass. The density is per metre of view depth, and zero means the vertex stage leaves the draw alone.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardPushBlock.WriteObjectFog(System.Span{System.Single},OpenIGI.Rendering.Mesh3D.ForwardDrawState@)
member.summary: Turns the frame's exponential fog into the straight line an object is fogged along, where the draw names one.
member.remarks: Fog_SetRange (0x49B2D0) and I.G.I. 2's Direct3DRender_SetFogParameters set linear fog from the object's sphere: the line through the exponential's values at its near and far depths. The value at the eye goes in the second row's w, which an ordinary world draw leaves at nought, and the fall per metre in the density's place.

member.summary: The 128 bytes a geometry draw pushes: where it is, which way it faces, and what it is made of.

remarks.para: The layout: the model-view-projection in the first sixteen, then three rows that are read two different ways, then the material. The rows are normally the object-to-world rotation the G-buffer's world-space normals need — the model-view's own rotation followed by the view-to-world one, composed here so the shader needs one matrix rather than two.

A terrain page puts something else there. It slides each vertex along the offset in its normal channel as the ground changes level of detail, and that needs three numbers for the ramp and three for where the page sits relative to the camera — and the block is full. It has room all the same, because a page is drawn with no rotation of its own: its normal matrix is the identity, and nine floats of identity carry nothing. The fourth component of the first row, nought for everything else, is what says which reading applies. The identity is CHECKED rather than assumed, so a page that ever came in rotated keeps its matrix and simply does not morph.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.MissionConditions
member.summary: The conditions the campaign is being played under: what hour missions open at, and what falls out of the sky while they are played.

remarks.para: They belong to the campaign, not to a mission. Chosen beside the difficulty on the campaign screen and carried from there into every mission that follows, so picking night for mission one means the whole run after it is at night as well — the same way the difficulty already behaves. A player who wants one mission in the dark and the next in daylight says so on the campaign screen again; nothing resets the choice behind their back.

Session-scoped on purpose. Nothing here is written to the settings file. An hour that outlives the session is how every mission afterwards silently opens at night with nobody remembering asking for it, which reads as the game being broken rather than as a preference — see the remarks on r_time_of_day, which was made non-archived for exactly that reason.

member.param: The hour missions open at.
The weather missions are played in.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MissionConditions.SunriseHour
member.summary: The hour the sun comes up: the arc's own sunrise.
member.remarks: Elevation crosses zero here — ((hour - 6) / 12) * pi is the phase the sun's height is a sine of — so this is the boundary between a level lit by the moon and a level lit by the sun.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MissionConditions.SunsetHour
member.summary: The hour the sun goes down.
member.remarks: Twelve hours on from , which is the same arc read the other way.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.MissionConditions.HorizonOffsetHours
member.summary: How far past its horizon crossing each choice actually opens, in hours.

remarks.para: Neither choice is any good at the crossing itself. At the exact hour the sun touches the horizon it is half a sun: the sky is part lit, the moon has not risen, and the level reads as the same ambiguous half-light whichever side of the day it is on — a "night" mission that looks like a late afternoon and a "day" mission that is a wall of orange.

An hour either way is enough to be unambiguous, and it is a narrow window: the sun's warmth is faded across the first 0.3 of its height, which an hour of arc very nearly clears, so 7 is ordinary morning light where 6 is the reddest moment of the whole day. Past the crossing the other way, the sun is properly under the world, the moon has taken the directional slot and the sky fill has reached its night blue.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.MotionBlurParameters
member.summary: The motion blur's four parameter blocks and its shutter, the same for every backend.
member.remarks: The blur is a tile-based reconstruction filter in the manner of McGuire et al. 2012: the screen is cut into tiles, each tile records the slowest and fastest motion inside it, the fastest is spread to the neighbours it could smear into, and every pixel then gathers along its tile's dominant motion.

member.summary: The longest smear, end to end, as a percentage of the screen's width.
member.remarks: Half of it goes either side of a pixel. Past this a fast turn would read as a wash rather than as motion, and the gather's sample count could no longer cover the distance without gaps.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.NightSky
member.summary: What a night sky holds that the atmosphere's scattering does not.

remarks.para: A clear moonless sky is not black. Most of its light is airglow, the upper atmosphere's own faint emission, which is brightest a little above the horizon, where the eye looks through the most of that layer. Starlight adds a little and the moon a great deal more (Jensen et al., "A Physically-Based Night Sky Model", SIGGRAPH 2001). The atmosphere march only knows about a single source it scatters, so it supplies the moonlit blue and none of the rest. This record carries the rest.

All radiances are in the atmosphere's own units: the scale its source illuminance is written in, before the frame's light scale. That keeps them in proportion to the moonlit sky they are drawn over, whatever the exposure does to both.

member.param: The zenith radiance of the airglow floor; nought by day.

How bright the moon's disc is drawn; nought hides it and its halo.
The game's running clock, which the stars twinkle on.
