member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.NightShift
member.summary: How far dim parts of a night picture shift towards night vision, 0 to 1.
member.remarks: The Purkinje shift: see PostProcessSettings.NightShift. Scaled by how far into night the sky is, so a day is untouched whatever this is set to.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.MotionBlur
member.summary: How much of a frame's movement is smeared.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.SpatialAa
member.summary: How strongly edges in the finished frame are smoothed, or 0 for no anti-aliasing.
member.remarks: Spatial, and therefore free of ghosting: it reads the displayed picture and nothing else. With the temporal path repaired it is a choice rather than the only option — the ghost-free alternative for anyone who dislikes accumulation — and the presets that run TAA leave it off, because smoothing an already-converged frame only softens it a second time.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.SpatialAaThreshold
member.summary: The contrast below which a pixel is left untouched.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Bloom
member.summary: How much of the blurred bright pass is mixed back in, or 0 for no bloom.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.BloomThreshold
member.summary: The luminance above which a pixel starts to bloom, or negative to bloom everything.

remarks.para: Ultra does not threshold at all: every pixel spills in proportion to its brightness rather than only those above a cut. That is what makes the bloom read as lens scatter instead of as a glow that switches on -- a hard cut shows as a contour where a surface crosses it.

Zero is that "do not threshold" case rather than a negative sentinel such as minus one, because a console value beginning with a minus cannot be typed: the argument parser reads it as the next option, so `+r_bloom_threshold -1` exits rather than setting anything. A value nobody can type is not a control. Zero is unambiguous because a threshold of zero and no threshold at all differ -- the first still scales dim pixels down towards nothing, the second passes them through.
The lower bound had to open to admit it: the range was 0.1 to 8, which cannot express the case at all, so ultra carried 2.47 -- a number the backend ignored, because the bloom chain was written unthresholded directly. The value now says what the picture actually does. Vanilla keeps a real threshold, having no tone curve for this to be calibrated against.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Contrast
member.summary: How far colour is pushed away from mid-grey.
member.remarks: Ultra sits at 1, which is neutral, because its target look grades to identity — contrast, gamma and gain all 1, offset 0, and no lookup table. It had been carrying a value that came in with a preset seeded from a saved config, and tinting a picture that is meant to be untinted only ever moves it away. Enhanced and high keep a gentle grade of their own; it is taste rather than fidelity, and the settings menu offers all four as one Image Style choice.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Saturation
member.summary: How far colour is pushed away from its own luminance.
member.remarks: Ultra sits at 1, which is neutral, because its target look grades to identity — saturation, gamma and gain all 1, offset 0, and no lookup table. It had been carrying a value that came in with a preset seeded from a saved config, and tinting a picture that is meant to be untinted only ever moves it away. Enhanced and high keep a gentle grade of their own; it is taste rather than fidelity, and the settings menu offers all four as one Image Style choice.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Vignette
member.summary: How much the corners of the frame are darkened.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Grain
member.summary: How much film grain is added.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.ChromaticAberration
member.summary: How far the red and blue channels separate towards the corners.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.ColourLookup
member.summary: How much of the level's authored colour table is applied.

remarks.para: Per mission and per preset. A mission's grade is loaded from Assets/luts/<name>.cube when one exists, and this is how much of it to use — the same relationship the fog presets have with r_fog_density. Zero at vanilla, because vanilla is the game as it shipped and it shipped ungraded.

Below one on purpose at the middle presets. A grade authored against a clean daylight frame is usually too strong once the same frame is also carrying volumetric fog and bloom, and the levels this game ships are already strongly coloured by their own lightmaps.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.ColourLookupTable
member.summary: The colour table to use instead of the mission's own, or empty for the mission's own.
member.remarks: An override for authoring, not a setting: naming a table here loads Assets/luts/<name>.cube whatever the mission is, which is how a grade is compared against another one without restarting into a different level. identity is always available and is the table that changes nothing — the one that shows whether the sampler's coordinates are right, since with it any visible change at all is a bug.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Sharpen
member.summary: How much local contrast is restored after the temporal accumulation softens the frame.
member.remarks:
Ultra takes 0. That is not declining a free improvement: sharpening is a correction for a soft resolve, and ultra runs its temporal reconstruction at native resolution, where there is no upsampling softness to correct.
Enhanced and high keep theirs, and the reason is now rather than a cruder resolve — they run the identical reconstruction, but from 70% and 85% of the output pixels, and upsampling is exactly the soft resolve this corrects. The ladder follows the deficit: the further below native a tier renders, the more of this it wants.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.SunShafts
member.summary: How strongly light shafts radiate from the sun when it is on screen.
member.remarks: The sky round the sun blurred outward in screen space, so a lattice, a fence or a roof edge between the eye and the sun cuts rays into its glow. The volume's own shafts need air thick enough to show them; a clear morning has none, and still shows these.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostCVars.Presets
member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostProcessSettings
member.summary: What happens to the scene between it being drawn and it reaching the screen.

remarks.para: Passed to once per frame. Everything here is a property of the frame rather than of any one draw, which is why it travels as a single value rather than as device state that could be left set.

is the settings under which the offscreen path must produce exactly what the original's direct-to-backbuffer path produces. It is the regression gate for the whole remaster track, so it is named here rather than assembled by a caller who might get one field wrong.

member.param: How out-of-range light is brought back into what a display can show.
A linear multiplier applied before tone mapping. One leaves the scene's own brightness alone.
How much of the bloom is mixed back in, or zero to skip the pass. Bloom is what makes a bright fog bank or a muzzle flash read as light rather than as a pale patch.
The luminance above which a pixel contributes to the bloom.

The linear value that maps to display white. This is the amount of headroom the tone map reserves above white, and it has to match what the scene actually produces: reserving four stops for content that never exceeds one spends all of it compressing a range that was not there, which shows up as a washed-out picture rather than as a setting being wrong. One disables the roll-off entirely.
Whether the captured scene holds display-encoded colour rather than linear light.

How far colour is pushed away from mid-grey, where 1 leaves it alone. Applied in the display space after the tone map, because contrast is a statement about the picture rather than about the light, and doing it in linear light crushes the shadows before the curve has had a chance to shape them.
How far colour is pushed away from its own luminance, where 1 leaves it alone. Zero is greyscale.
How much the corners are darkened, from 0 to 1. Every lens does this and every photograph has it; its absence is one of the quiet reasons rendered images read as rendered.

How much film grain is added. Subtle by default and animated per frame, because static grain is dirt on the lens rather than grain — and because a little of it hides the banding that an 8-bit display gives a smooth gradient.

How far the red and blue channels are separated towards the edges of the frame, in pixels at the corner. A real lens cannot focus every wavelength to the same point, and the error grows with distance from the axis — which is why this is zero in the middle however high it is set.

How strongly edges in the finished frame are smoothed, from 0 to 1, or 0 for none. Spatial rather than temporal: it works from the displayed picture alone, so it cannot ghost — which is why it is here at all, the temporal path being unusable on this game's skinned soldiers.
The luminance contrast below which a pixel is left untouched. Most of a frame is below it, which is what makes the pass nearly free and what stops it softening texture detail that is not an edge.

How long the frame being resolved took. Motion blur needs it because the velocity buffer holds one frame's travel: without rescaling to a fixed shutter, the same movement would smear half as far at double the frame rate and the look would be a readout of the hardware rather than of the scene.
How much of a frame's movement is smeared, where 1 is the whole of it. A real shutter is open for part of a frame rather than all of it, so values below 1 are the physical range.

How much local contrast is restored after the temporal accumulation and any upsampling have softened the frame. Distinct from the sharpening inside the temporal resolve: that one fights the history's own resampling blur, and this one is a look.

How much of the authored to apply, where 1 is the whole grade and 0 leaves the picture as the procedural knobs left it. A fraction is a genuine control rather than a convenience: a grade authored for a mission's daylight is usually too strong once the level is also carrying fog and bloom, and dialling it back is easier than re-authoring it. Has no effect unless a table has been handed to the device.

Whether the exposure adapts to the scene's own average brightness over time, with becoming a bias on the result. Has no effect under the identity tone map: the vanilla path resolves as a straight copy and never applies exposure at all.

Converts the resolved picture to the high-contrast green emission of the SIMOTECH map-computer CRT. This is a display transform, not a translucent overlay: the world must remain readable underneath it.

The remaster's own map-computer display: the same idea as carried on continuous parameters, so the tube can be brought up and taken down as part of a camera move rather than switched. The two are never on together — see .

The remastered first-person binocular's glass lens transform, carried on continuous parameters so the optics fade in as the device is raised. Mutually exclusive with — the map computer replaces the first-person view — see .

How fast the adapted exposure eases towards the scene's brightness each frame, from 0 to 1, when is on. The small default is a slow eye-adaptation. The game raises it for the moment after a level loads: the real-time GI takes many frames to converge from dark to its full bounce, and a slow exposure would over-lift the dim early frames and then walk visibly back down as the light fills in -- a scene that loads bright and dims. A fast rate during that window lets the exposure track the convergence instead, holding the displayed brightness steady while the light settles.

How far the dim parts of the picture shift towards the eye's night vision, 0 to 1: the Purkinje shift. Under moonlight the rods take over from the cones, so dim surfaces lose their colour and read as a cool blue-grey while anything lamp-lit stays in colour. That shift is what makes a night read as night, and what lets it be shown bright enough to play without looking like a dim day. Nought by day.

member.summary: What happens to the scene between it being drawn and it reaching the screen.

remarks.para: Passed to once per frame. Everything here is a property of the frame rather than of any one draw, which is why it travels as a single value rather than as device state that could be left set.

is the settings under which the offscreen path must produce exactly what the original's direct-to-backbuffer path produces. It is the regression gate for the whole remaster track, so it is named here rather than assembled by a caller who might get one field wrong.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostProcessSettings.SteadyExposureRate

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PostProcessSettings.ExposureDeltaSeconds
member.summary: How much time this frame advances the eye adaptation by.

Scaled by against the steady rate, which is how the game's faster adaptation while the GI converges after a load reaches the easing -- the rate was set and never read. Capped, so a hitch does not snap the exposure.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings
member.summary: Everything the remastered storm is tuned by: how much falls, how it moves, and how it reads.

remarks.para: The vanilla path draws rain the way the original does — a fixed band of thin streaks around the camera, alpha from the level's RainEffect task, and nothing else (see RainRenderer). This is the model behind the remastered one, which is a different thing entirely: drops that are spawned into a volume that travels with the eye, blown by a wind that gusts, stretched along the direction they are actually moving, faded where they would otherwise clip through a wall, and answered on the ground by splashes.

Metres, seconds, degrees. Every distance here is metres and every duration seconds, matching the weather renderers rather than the 4096-units-per-metre world space — a storm is authored by eye at human scale, and converting once at the point of use is cheaper to reason about than carrying engine units through thirty fields.

Why a record, and why defaults that already look right. These are read every frame and written rarely — from a preset, a console variable, or a level's own weather task — so the type is an immutable record with init setters and a that is not a neutral zero but a working drizzle. A field left alone must produce something plausible; a settings object where half the defaults render nothing is a trap that costs an afternoon before anyone suspects the defaults rather than the renderer.

The spawn volume is the thing that gets sized wrong. A volume tuned for a courtyard — ten metres across, a metre thick, a second of life — produces almost nothing over open ground, because the drops die before they cross the eye and the column is narrower than the view. The defaults below are sized for an outdoor level; see .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Default
member.summary: A working outdoor storm: the defaults every other field is measured against.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Intensity
member.summary: How much of the authored fall rate is used, from 0 (dry) to 1 (the full rate).
member.remarks: Separate from so a level, a script or the console can dial the storm up and down over time without losing the tuned density it is dialling away from.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.DropsPerSecond
member.summary: Drops spawned per second at full .

remarks.para: This is the number that decides whether the storm reads as rain or as a few streaks drifting past, and it was set far too low. Eight hundred a second over a forty-metre column is two and a half thousand drops spread through five thousand square metres of air — thin enough that the eye reads each one separately instead of reading weather.

The two numbers that matter are this one and , because what is seen is drops per unit of air and not drops per second: quadrupling the rate while halving the column's area multiplies the density by eight.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.LifetimeSeconds
member.summary: How long a drop lives before it is recycled, in seconds.
member.remarks: Multiplied by the fall speed this is how far a drop travels, so it and together decide whether drops are still alive by the time they reach the eye. Too short and the column hangs above the player's head, visible only when looking up. Each drop is given somewhere between a little under half of this and all of it; most never see it, because a drop is retired the moment it reaches the ground. Even the shortest share has to outlast the slowest drop's fall from the top of the spawn slab to the ground.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SpawnRadiusMetres
member.summary: The radius of the column drops spawn into, centred on the eye, in metres.
member.remarks: The column travels with the camera, so this is not how far the storm reaches — it is how much of the view is populated. Below about twenty metres the edge of the column is inside the player's view and the rain visibly stops in mid-air at a fixed distance.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SpawnHeightMetres
member.summary: The vertical thickness of the spawn slab, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SpawnAboveCameraMetres
member.summary: How far above the eye the slab sits, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SpreadMetresPerSecondSquared
member.summary: How hard the air pushes a drop sideways, in metres per second SQUARED.

remarks.para: An acceleration and not a velocity, which is the whole of why the fall carries a range of angles rather than one. The force goes on being integrated for the drop's whole life, so a drop's lean GROWS with its age, and the air holds drops of every age at once. Handing it over as a one-off velocity instead — which this did — gives every drop the same tiny lean for its whole fall, and a storm of parallel lines.

What is tuned is the ANGLE and not the constant. A lean is the acceleration times how long the drop has been falling, and here a drop falls for about one and a half seconds: this column is ten to twenty metres deep and a drop is retired when it meets the ground. Reaching about seven degrees off vertical in that time takes tan(7°) × 11.5 / 1.5, which is where this comes from. Shorten the column or lengthen the life and this wants moving with it.
Each drop draws a direction as well as a magnitude. Drawing the two axes independently instead puts more drops on the diagonals than on the axes, which gives the whole field a grain.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.FallSpeedMetresPerSecond
member.summary: Terminal fall speed in metres per second, before .
member.remarks: A limit and not the speed a drop is given: drops are spawned nearly at rest and pulled down by until they reach it, which is what makes the streaks short at the top of the column and long by the time they pass the eye. Handing every drop its terminal speed at birth loses that entirely and gives a column of identical streaks descending as one rigid sheet.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.GravityMetresPerSecondSquared
member.summary: How hard drops accelerate downwards, in metres per second squared.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.FallSpeedScale
member.summary: Multiplier on the fall speed: 0 hangs the drops, 1 is the tuned speed.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindDirectionDegrees
member.summary: The compass direction the wind blows towards on average, in degrees.
member.remarks: The middle of the range the direction wanders over; see .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindSwingDegrees
member.summary: How far either side of that direction the wind wanders, in degrees.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindVariationSeconds
member.summary: How often the wind picks a new speed and direction to head towards, in seconds.
member.remarks: Not how long a gust lasts — the wind eases towards each new target over roughly this long and is given another before it arrives, so nothing about it ever settles. Short values make it restless in a way that reads as the camera swaying rather than as weather.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindMetresPerSecond
member.summary: Lateral wind speed in metres per second.
member.remarks: Rain that falls dead vertical reads as static no matter how fast it moves, because a vertical streak on a vertical path has no apparent motion across the frame. A little wind is what makes it look like weather rather than a screen effect.

The wind it settles around, not a fixed speed: the gust in is added to it and is signed. A storm with one wind speed is a storm whose rain leans at one fixed angle for as long as anyone watches, which reads as the whole screen being sheared rather than as air moving.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindGustMetresPerSecond
member.summary: How far either side of that the wind gusts, in metres per second.

remarks.para: Signed, and weighted towards the middle. Taken as a range between a floor and a ceiling, the wind only ever blew one way and spent most of its time near neither end of the range — the rain leaned right, and kept leaning right. Real air does not do that. This is added to with a sign, so the lean crosses back through vertical and occasionally goes the other way entirely, and it is drawn from a triangular distribution rather than a flat one, so the wind spends most of its time near the middle and only visits the extremes.

Read these as an angle, not a speed. What is on the screen is the lean, and the lean is the arctangent of this over the fall speed — so against a fall of eleven and a half metres a second, a wind of one is six degrees off vertical, which nobody can see and which reads as rain falling dead flat however carefully the wind is varied. Three and a half is about seventeen degrees, and the gust carries it between five and thirty. Any change to moves the whole range.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindUpdraftMetresPerSecond
member.summary: Vertical wind, in metres per second; positive lifts drops and slows the fall.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.GustAmount
member.summary: How strongly gusts modulate local density, from 0 (even) to 1 (sheets and gaps).
member.remarks: Gusts are a moving noise field sampled at the drop's position that scales its opacity, so the storm arrives in sheets rather than as a uniform screen of streaks. At 1 the gaps are total, which reads as the rain flickering on and off; the tuned value is well under half.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.GustMetresPerSecond
member.summary: How fast the gust field drifts, in metres per second.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.GustSizeMetres
member.summary: The size of one gust cell, in metres. Smaller is busier.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.DropWidthMetres
member.summary: The width of a drop's streak at unit distance, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.DropLengthMetres
member.summary: The unstretched length of a drop's streak, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.MotionStretch
member.summary: How far the streak stretches along its velocity, as a fraction of distance travelled.
member.remarks: A falling drop photographs as a streak because it moves during the exposure. Stretching along the drop's own velocity rather than straight down is what keeps wind-blown rain leaning the way it is actually travelling, instead of leaning while its streaks stay vertical.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WidthBoostPerMetre
member.summary: Extra streak width per metre of distance, so distant rain does not fall below a pixel.
member.remarks: The same cheat the impact particles use. A twelve-millimetre streak at sixty metres is a fraction of a pixel, which temporal antialiasing then removes entirely — the storm thins out with distance instead of building into a haze.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.FocusDistanceMetres
member.summary: Inside this distance a drop is drawn from the defocused sheet, in metres.

remarks.para: A lens focused on the scene cannot resolve a drop a metre from the front element, and that is drawn rather than culled: the streaks exist twice, once sharp and once out of focus, and a drop picks one or the other by depth.
It is a switch, not a blend. No drop is ever a mixture of the two sheets — every drop is wholly sharp or wholly soft. Cross-fading them instead looks like the rain is dissolving at a fixed distance.

Zero disables it, and zero is the default: every drop at every distance takes the sharp sheet. The defocused sheet ships and is addressed correctly; set this to the distance the lens is focused past and the near drops soften.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Colour
member.summary: The drop colour, as linear red, green and blue.

remarks.para: A reflectance and not a brightness: it is lit, so it says what fraction of the light around it a drop sends to the eye and nothing about how much light there is.

This is what made the rain white. Used as a brightness — a fixed level written into the vertex colour — it is a constant scene-referred value in a frame the auto-exposure then lifts to suit whatever the scene is. In a dark yard the exposure comes up, the scene stays dark and the rain goes to paper white, because the rain never got the memo that there is no light. Multiplied by the light there actually is, it tracks the scene: dark rain in a dark yard, and rain you can see in daylight.
A near-neutral grey with the faintest cool lean, sending back a little under two fifths of the light: water is clear, and most of what a drop shows is the scene refracted through it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Alpha
member.summary: Peak opacity of a drop at full .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.EmissiveIntensity
member.summary: Self-lit strength, added on top of the scene lighting.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Backlighting
member.summary: How strongly drops brighten from the light coming through them.

remarks.para: Water is not lit like a surface: a drop is a lens, and the light that makes rain legible is the light coming through it from behind. Without this a storm in front of a bright sky is a screen of grey lines that read as dirt on the lens.

A stand-in for the frame behind the drop. Ideally a drop glows with whatever is behind it — sky, a window, a muzzle flash. Nothing in this engine's forward pass can read the frame it is drawing into, so what stands in for that read is the sun's own colour weighted by how close the drop sits to it in the view. Outdoors, in daylight, the brightest thing behind a drop is the sun, and the stand-in and the real thing agree; a drop backlit by a lamp at night is the case it gets wrong, and it is the case to revisit when scene colour becomes available to this pass.
Applied only to drops beyond ; the near, defocused drops take none of it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.BacklightTint
member.summary: The colour the backlight glow is tinted by, as linear red, green and blue.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.AmbientIntensity
member.summary: How much of the surrounding light a drop shows through itself.

remarks.para: The ambient term: the light around the drop, desaturated and added to it, which is what stops rain reading as grey paint over a coloured scene. The same substitution as applies — the level's ambient stands in for the frame behind the drop.

Mind the scale. The level's ambient is a chromaticity: a unit-magnitude tint that says what colour the fill light is and nothing about how much of it there is. Added at full strength to a drop that was already a mid grey, every drop and every splash in the storm clamped to pure white — and with them went the glimmer, the backlighting and the gusts, because a channel pinned at 255 cannot show any of them. The rain came out as opaque white paint.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.AmbientSaturation
member.summary: How much colour survives in that ambient term, from 0 (grey) to 1 (untouched).

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.NearFadeMetres
member.summary: Inside this distance from the eye a drop is not drawn, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.GeometryFadeMetres
member.summary: Over how many metres a drop fades out as it approaches a solid surface.
member.remarks: Drops are flat sprites, so one intersecting a wall shows a hard diagonal cut where the quad crosses it. Fading against scene depth hides the seam. Set this too wide in a built-up level and everything within five metres of a surface — which outdoors is most of the ground — fades away, and the storm quietly disappears.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.ShelterHeightMetres
member.summary: How far above a drop cover is searched for, in metres; 0 disables the shelter test.
member.remarks: Kept modest on purpose. A generous search finds the surrounding hillside from inside a valley and shelters the whole level; the useful range is roof height, not sky height.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Splashes
member.summary: Whether the ground answers the rain with splashes.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashesPerSecond
member.summary: Splashes raised per second at full .

remarks.para: Splashes are their own weather, not a consequence of the drops. They were spawned where a falling drop crossed the ground, which is the physically obvious arrangement and is why none were ever visible: the drops fall through the whole column, so their landings were spread over the thousands of square metres the column covers, and the handful that landed near enough to be seen were each nine centimetres across. So splashes have their own spawn volume around the camera, because what the ground is doing is only worth drawing where the player can see it.
So this is a rate over , not a fraction of anything. It buys density exactly where it reads and nothing at all where it would not.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashReachMetres
member.summary: How far from the eye splashes are raised, in metres.
member.remarks: Small, on purpose. A splash is a decimetre of water: past a dozen metres it is under a pixel, so spawning them further out spends the whole budget on things that cannot be seen and leaves the ground at the player's feet bare.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashSmallFraction
member.summary: What share of splashes are the small flat kind rather than a standing crown.
member.remarks: There are two kinds. The large one is the crown — a flipbook of water thrown upwards and falling back, drawn standing on the ground and turned to the eye. The small one is a soft blob lying flat where a drop hit. Both are needed: crowns alone read as a field of little white trees, and blobs alone read as the ground being speckled rather than struck.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashRadiusMetres
member.summary: Half the width of a splash's quad, in metres, before its own per-splash variation.

remarks.para: A few centimetres, not tens. That is what a raindrop's crown actually measures; a fifth of a metre, which this was, is several times that.

It is the same mistake three times over. The splashes were too big; they were too BRIGHT, because a sprite covering twenty-five times the screen area emits twenty-five times the light however dim its colour; and their animation looked coarse, because a hundred-and-twenty-eight texel cell magnified that far has no detail left to be smooth with.

Each crown is drawn between about two thirds of this and all of it, which puts the visible crown at two and a half to four centimetres across. The small thrown droplets are cut from the same figure at a much smaller share.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashLifetimeSeconds
member.summary: How long a splash lives, in seconds.
member.remarks: This is also how long the crown's eight frames take, so it is the playback rate of the animation and not only a lifetime: too short and the flipbook strobes, too long and the water hangs in the air. Each crown takes between a little over half of this and all of it, which with the default plays the eight frames at roughly seventeen to thirty a second, about twenty on average.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashAlpha
member.summary: Peak opacity of a splash.

remarks.para: Half, against the drops' six tenths — which sounds like the wrong way round until you count what is actually on the screen. A splash is metres from the eye where a drop is tens, its sheet is a full-range mask with bright cores where a streak is mostly empty, and every impact draws a crown AND two droplets over the same few pixels. Additively, that stacks. At parity with the drops the ground came out lit by its own splashes.

Lit splashes, carrying no emissive at all, would leave a night yard's splashes as dark as everything else in it. Nothing in this forward pass lights a particle, so the brightness has to come off here instead.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashColour
member.summary: The splash colour before lighting, as linear red, green and blue.
member.remarks: Lit by the ambient term.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SplashLiftMetres
member.summary: How far a splash sits above the surface it forms on, in metres.
member.remarks: Not decoration: a splash lies flat, and drawn at exactly the ground height it is coplanar with the floor and loses the depth test to it. The quad then either z-fights or vanishes entirely, which looks like the splashes were never spawned. A couple of centimetres is enough to clear it and far too little to read as floating.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.Curtains
member.summary: Whether the distant drifting sheets are drawn.

remarks.para: Off by default. A full curtain would be a layered scrolling sheet, which has not been built, and what stands in for it here is a single soft cloud, which at any opacity strong enough to notice reads as a grey cloud parked in the middle distance rather than as rain too far off to resolve.

What they are for stands: individual drops stop resolving after twenty or thirty metres, so a storm made only of drops has a visible edge past which the air is clear. Turning these on fills that distance, at the cost of the above.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.CurtainCount
member.summary: How many sheets are alive at once.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.CurtainSizeMetres
member.summary: The size of one sheet, in metres.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.CurtainAlpha
member.summary: Peak opacity of a sheet.

remarks.para: Meant to be subtle, but 0.05 is below the point where an eight-bit vertex alpha survives at all once the distance fade has taken a bite out of it -- which is the difference between "restrained" and "not drawing". The band between those two is narrow, and 0.2 was over the top of it: with a real cloud mask rather than the generated one, a fifth of an opacity reads as a grey cloud hanging in the sky rather than as rain too far away to resolve.
The sheets are meant to be noticed as haze and never as objects. If one can be pointed at, it is too strong however good the mask on it is.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.CurtainMetresPerSecond
member.summary: How fast the sheets drift past, in metres per second.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.CurtainReachScale
member.summary: How far out the sheets are scattered, as a multiple of the drop column's radius.
member.remarks: One number for both the scattering and the distance fade. They were separate constants, and the fade's was the smaller of the two, so every sheet that landed inside the larger radius faded to nothing -- most of them.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindVelocity
member.summary: Returns the wind as a world-space velocity in metres per second.
member.remarks: Z is up in this world, so the compass angle turns in the XY plane and the updraft is the Z component. Computed here rather than at each call site so the convention lives in one place.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.WindVelocity(System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Returns a given wind as a world-space velocity in metres per second.
member.param: The lateral speed, in metres per second.
The compass direction it blows towards.
member.returns: The wind velocity.
member.remarks: Taken as arguments because the wind the storm is blowing at this instant is not a property of the settings — it wanders about by up to either way, and only the renderer knows where it has got to.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.PrecipitationSettings.SteadyStateDrops
member.summary: The number of drops alive in the steady state, which is what the buffers are sized for.
member.remarks: Spawn rate multiplied by lifetime. Worth having as one expression because it is the number that decides both the vertex budget and whether a tuning change is affordable: doubling the lifetime costs exactly as much as doubling the rate.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.QuadIndices
member.summary: The index buffer of a run of independent quads: quad n is vertices 4n to 4n + 3.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.QuadIndices.Build(System.Int32)
member.summary: Builds the two triangles of every quad, (0, 1, 2) and (0, 2, 3).
member.param: How many quads; at most 16384, the most a 16-bit index reaches.
member.returns: Six indices a quad.
member.exception: is negative or past what 16-bit indices reach.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for tracing: the hardware ray query, what it traces, the traced world and the distance field.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.HardwareRayTracing
member.summary: Whether tracing uses the hardware ray query rather than the software distance field.

remarks.para: The switch between the two GI modes, live: on, every trace that can reach the acceleration structure does — the screen gather, the radiance cache, the surface-cache relight and the sun's shadow — and off, the same shaders march the signed distance field and the sun falls back to the cascaded map. It only means anything on a backend that can trace at all; elsewhere the software path is the only path and the flag is ignored. Bound to F6 by default so the two can be compared in place.

Deliberately NOT archived, and that is a fix rather than an oversight. Every preset names it 1 — there is no tier that wants the software path, only a comparison that does — so the only way it is ever 0 is that somebody pressed the key. While it was archived, pressing that key wrote itself into settings.cfg: the next launch came up on the software path, the preset read as Custom because a managed value no longer matched, and the picture was quietly worse in a way nothing on screen explained. A key for flipping between two implementations must not be able to change what the game starts as. It is still named by the presets, so the settings screen still reports Custom while it is flipped and still puts it back when a preset is chosen.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.TracedSunShadows
member.summary: Whether the sun's shadow is traced, on a backend already tracing.
member.remarks:
The second half of the live switch. moves every trace in the frame between the hardware ray query and the software distance field at once; this one moves the sun's shadow alone, so the ray-traced shadow can be compared against the cascaded map while the indirect light, the reflections and the surface-cache relight all stay exactly as they were. That is the comparison worth being able to make in place: the two shadow systems draw the same geometry from the same sun and should agree about where a shadow falls, and only about how it looks at its edge.
It does nothing where is off, which already leaves the sun to the cascades, and nothing on a backend that cannot trace at all.
Not archived, for the same reason as : this exists to be flipped while looking at something, and a key that is flipped while looking at something must not decide what the game starts as tomorrow.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.TracedLampShadows
member.summary: Whether the lamps' shadow is traced against the world, on a backend already tracing.
member.remarks: The lights' own switch, beside the sun's. It traces a ray per lamp against the world so a lamp cannot light through a wall the camera cannot see -- the off-screen occluder the screen-space march can never find. Off, the lamps keep the screen-space march alone, which still stops the walls the view contains; so this is the difference between a lamp shadowed everywhere and one shadowed only where its wall is on screen. Needs and does nothing without it; toggle live to weigh its cost against the leak it closes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.TracedReflections
member.summary: Whether reflections are traced against the world, on a backend already tracing.

remarks.para: The reflections' own switch. With it on, a reflected ray the screen cannot answer is traced against the world and its hit resolved -- out of the lit frame where the camera can see the hit, and out of the surface cache's lit cards where it cannot. So a puddle or a pane shows what stands off-screen, or behind something nearer, or simply never drawn, none of which a screen-space march can reach.

It matters most on the surfaces that have no fallback. Standing water is given the sky by the shading whether or not a ray lands, so the trace fills in a wall there rather than filling in nothing; a metal or a glossy surface is given no reflection term at all, so a marched ray that missed left it mirroring the void. That is the case this exists for.

On, the trace is the whole of the reflection and the screen-space march does not run. Not a hybrid: a marched hit is the first surface the depth buffer happens to record along the ray, which is the right surface only when the camera drew it, so mixing the two gives a picture that is part exact and part plausible with the seam falling wherever the march happened to succeed. Off — or on an adapter that cannot trace, or while a mission's world and cards are still being built — the march is what answers instead, which is the approximation for the machines and the moments that cannot have the real thing. Toggle live to compare.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.DistanceFields
member.summary: Whether the level's signed distance fields are baked and resampled into clipmaps.

remarks.para: The structure everything in the realtime GI track traces through. A ray marched against triangles tests every triangle it might cross; a ray marched against a distance field asks how far the nearest surface is and steps exactly that far, which cannot overshoot.

Needs compute, so it is off wherever the context cannot honour it whatever this says. Off at every preset until the stages that consume it exist — a field nothing traces is a load-time cost with nothing to show for it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.DistanceFieldResolution
member.summary: How many voxels the longest axis of each model's distance field gets.
member.remarks: The cost of a bake is roughly this cubed per distinct model, and the memory exactly so — which is why it is a tier ladder rather than a constant, and why the cheapest tier keeps the floor. Thirty-two already gives this game's crates and huts voxels of a few centimetres, fine enough for a trace to land on the right side of a wall; what the higher tiers buy is thin geometry a coarse field rounds away. Paid at load and in video memory, never per frame.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.DistanceFieldValidate
member.summary: Whether the built clipmaps are checked against the exact field once, after a load.
member.remarks: Reads the clipmap back and compares every voxel against SceneDistanceField, which answers the same question exactly. Costs a synchronising readback and a few hundred thousand CPU evaluations, so it is a diagnostic rather than something to leave on — but a wrong distance field is invisible in a rendered frame, and this is the only thing that can see it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.TracedWorldRadius
member.summary: How far from the camera a placement is still put into the traced world.

remarks.para: Drawn by visibility, traced by distance. The acceleration structure used to be filled from the draw path, so it held exactly what the camera had at some point had in frame — and a window reflects what is BEHIND the camera, which is precisely what the frustum throws away. A pane could therefore only show a place the player had already stood and looked at, and showed more of the level the longer they played. These two settings replace the frustum with a distance-and-size rule: keep a placement unless it is both too far off and too small to matter.
Zero switches the whole mechanism off, leaving the structure to be fed by drawing alone. That is a diagnostic, not a setting: it restores the defect.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.TracedWorldAngle
member.summary: The projected size below which a distant placement stops being worth tracing.
member.remarks: The companion to , and what keeps that radius from being a hard wall. A placement is dropped only when it is BOTH beyond the radius and smaller than this angle, so a hillside or a hangar stays in the structure at any distance while a crate three hundred metres back does not. One degree keeps anything a reflection could plausibly resolve.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.RayTracingCVars.Presets
member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for reconstructing the frame: render scale, the temporal resolve and upscaler, and NVIDIA's DLSS, frame generation and Reflex.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.RenderScale
member.summary: How the picture is scaled relative to the window before being presented.
member.remarks: Below one this is supersampling in reverse — the scene is rendered smaller and upscaled, which is the cheapest way to buy back frame time. Above one it is supersampling proper. The temporal upscaler added in stage R5 is what makes values below one look acceptable.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.ThinGeometry
member.summary: How strongly the temporal pass holds on to geometry only one pixel wide.

remarks.para: A hardware rasteriser draws a triangle only where it covers a pixel's centre, so a fence wire narrower than a pixel is drawn or skipped depending on where the frame's jitter fell. That is what makes a distant fence crawl, and what makes it fade out entirely as the wire narrows — a wire covering a third of a pixel should be a third as bright, and instead it is absent two frames in three. This lets the temporal pass keep what earlier frames saw on those pixels rather than rejecting it, so the wire is averaged rather than gambled on.

A renderer that resolves sub-pixel coverage itself has no need of this, and we switch it on deliberately. A software visibility-buffer rasteriser resolves sub-pixel coverage properly, so it has no thin-geometry problem to detect. We have no such rasteriser, so the detection earns its keep here.

Not one, at any preset. A thin thing that is genuinely moving still has to be able to reject its own history, or it drags a smear behind it — and a wire is the shape that shows a smear most. Zero restores the untreated behaviour.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.TemporalHistorySamples
member.summary: The temporal history's per-texel sample ceiling, which sets how much of the past it keeps.

remarks.para: The history holds four texels per rendered pixel. A budget of sixteen samples per output pixel allows each texel four, which also zeroes the velocity weight clamp (the clamp's amplitude is 1 - 4 / ceiling). Measured here, four is the sharpest at rest but four times as flickery on distant ridges, and without the clamp a walk ghosts; thirty-two keeps the ridge stable, is marginally sharper in motion than sixteen, and leaves the clamp holding a moving pixel to an eighth of its history.
Not archived: the preset carries it, and a stale saved value here would silently undo a retune of the clamp it also governs.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.UpscaleHistory
member.summary: How many history texels the temporal upscaler keeps per rendered pixel, on each axis.

remarks.para: Twice the render resolution is what lets an upscale reconstruct detail finer than one frame holds: the jittered frames land between each other's pixels, and a history at the rendered size would average them back down. At native resolution and above there is no finer output to reconstruct, and the doubled history is four times the pixels written and read every frame for very little -- at 2560x1440 a 5120x2880 history.
0 chooses: one where the frame is rendered at or above the presented size, two where it is upscaled. 1 or 2 forces that scale.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.TemporalFeedback
member.summary: How much of the resolved pixel is this frame, or 1 for no accumulation.
member.remarks: The lower it is the more samples a pixel holds and the cleaner it converges, but the longer it takes to notice that the surface under it has changed. It is also what pays for the noise in every stochastic pass after this one, so it is a preset dial rather than a fixed constant.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.TemporalSharpening
member.summary: How much of the history's resampling blur is subtracted back out.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.Reconstruction
member.summary: What reconstructs the frame: the engine's own temporal resolve, DLSS, or DLSS ray reconstruction.
member.remarks: Not preset-managed: the NVIDIA kinds need the optional runtime and an adapter that runs them, and a preset that wrote one would be writing something half the machines it runs on cannot do. Where the chosen one cannot run the engine's resolve runs instead, and the log and the settings page say why. Only meaningful with temporal anti-aliasing on (r_taa below one) on the deferred path.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.DlssQualityMode
member.summary: How far below the output DLSS renders, when DLSS or ray reconstruction is the reconstruction.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.FrameGeneration
member.summary: How many frames reach the screen per rendered one, with DLSS frame generation.
member.remarks: Needs an RTX 40-series or newer, hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling, and Reflex, which it turns on. A multiplier the GPU cannot reach is clamped to what it reports.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.LowLatency
member.summary: NVIDIA Reflex: start each frame as late as the render allows, to cut input latency.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.FrameLimit
member.summary: A frame-rate cap the driver enforces through Reflex, or nought for none.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.FrameGenerationUiRecomposition
member.summary: Whether frame generation interpolates the picture and the interface separately.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.RayReconstructionRaw
member.summary: Whether ray reconstruction is fed the raw traced light, or the engine's own denoised light.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.RayReconstructionGuideView
member.summary: Which ray-reconstruction input to show in place of its output, for checking what it was fed.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionCVars.InterfaceLayer

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReconstructionKind
member.summary: What turns the jittered, render-resolution frame into the anti-aliased output-resolution one.
member.remarks: One choice, not three switches: these are mutually exclusive ways of resolving the same frame, and running one after another is never right. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for reflections: the screen-space march, traced reflections and glass.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.Reflections
member.summary: How many steps the screen-space march takes, or 0 not to march at all.
member.remarks: The MARCH's own step count, and nothing more. It used to speak for reflections as a whole because the march was the only way they were produced; a frame that traces (see ) never marches, so this no longer has anything to say about it. Zero therefore means "do not march" rather than "no reflections": on a machine that traces, the reflections stand and the screen-space path is simply switched off, which is the setting this name has always implied and never meant. Whether reflections happen at all is and .

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.ReflectionIntensity
member.summary: How strongly reflections are mixed in.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.ReflectionMaxRoughness
member.summary: The roughness past which a surface stops marching a screen ray and keeps the smooth fallback.
member.remarks: Held low deliberately. A screen-marched reflection is a SINGLE ray, so on anything but a near-mirror it reads the one surface that ray happens to hit -- for a parquet floor or a painted wall that is a dark, shadowed patch of the room, which the march then substitutes for the smooth probe fallback and the surface CRUSHES a stop or two darker than it should, besides shimmering as the ray wanders under motion. That single-ray march is what made interiors read dark and noisy. At 0.22 only genuinely glossy surfaces -- glass, a monitor, polished metal -- still march, where one ray IS the reflection; everything rougher keeps the probe field's smooth, bright, stable fallback. Without a denoised multi-ray reflection, not marching where one ray cannot help is the single-ray answer.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.TracedReflectionMaxRoughness
member.summary: The roughest surface a traced reflection ray is fired for.

remarks.para: The trace's own ceiling, and NOT . That one is a statement about the screen march's weakness — a marched ray reads whatever the depth buffer happens to record, so on anything but a near-mirror it substitutes one dark patch of the room for the smooth answer and the surface crushes a stop or two darker. It was set at 0.5 for that reason, and it is right for that reason. A ray has none of that failure: it returns the surface that is actually there, at whatever roughness the material claims.

So the two are separate numbers, and this one is set by what the material file actually says. Every metal materials.json names sits at 0.45, and glass at 0.08; ordinary walls and floors are at 0.6 and above. 0.6 therefore admits exactly what the level calls reflective and excludes what it does not, which is the only line worth drawing here.

There is still a ceiling at all because this is ONE ray, not a sampled lobe: past some roughness a single mirror ray is not a blurry reflection, it is a sharp reflection of the wrong thing. Raising it towards one is what a reflection denoiser would buy, and there is no reflection denoiser yet.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.TracedReflectionClamp
member.summary: The ceiling on a single traced reflection ray's radiance.

remarks.para: A reflection is ONE ray a pixel, so nothing averages away a ray that happens to land on something brilliant -- a lamp's own emissive card, a sun-lit white wall -- and what a single unbounded ray does to a mirror is a hard bright dot that moves with the camera. Capping the read is the standard firefly guard for a single-sample estimate.

Separate from r_screen_gi_max, which looks like the same number and is not: that one bounds a loop -- the gather reads the lit scene and the lit scene is then built from the gather -- and is set by where that loop stops running away. This bounds a single sample's variance and has no feedback in it at all, so tying the two would mean a change made for one reason silently landing on the other.

High enough to leave an ordinary reflected wall or sky untouched, which is the whole intent: this should clip the outliers and nothing else. Zero disables the trace's contribution outright, which is a diagnostic rather than a setting.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.ReflectionTexture
member.summary: How many texels square each texture is stored at for shading a traced hit.

remarks.para: A reflected ray that strikes something the camera cannot see — a body, most of all — is shaded from a reduced copy of that surface's own texture. This is how big those copies are, and it is the only thing standing between a reflected character and the source art.

The cost is quadratic and it is real. The array holds a thousand textures so that a level's pack, its interface and every character fit; at 128 that is 67 MB of video memory and at 256 it is 268 MB. There is no middle setting that is free. 128 is enough for a reflection glimpsed across a courtyard and visibly short of it for your own face in a window at arm's length, which is the shot people actually look at.
Read once, when the device is created: the array is allocated at start-up and this cannot resize it. Change it and restart.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionCVars.GlassReflection
member.summary: How much of what a window pane reflects reaches the picture.

remarks.para: A multiplier on the Fresnel share, and it exists because the honest number is unusably small. Glass seen square-on reflects four per cent, which is correct physics and almost invisible against a lit interior: the reflection is computed, it is in the frame, and nobody can see it. Every game that shows glass reflecting anything at a normal viewing angle is exaggerating, and this is the dial that says by how much.

It multiplies the Fresnel term rather than replacing it, so the ANGULAR behaviour is untouched: a pane still goes from barely-there head-on to a mirror at a glancing angle, which is what makes glazing read as glazing. What changes is only where on that curve the useful range sits. One is the physical answer; past about four a pane starts to read as polished metal rather than glass.
Use r_debug_view glass to see what is being weighted: it draws the panes' reflection raw, with this and the Fresnel share both taken off.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ReflectionSettings
member.summary: What surfaces reflect, and how far the frame is searched to find it.

remarks.para: The original has no reflections of any kind: its shiniest surfaces are a brighter texture. That is most obviously wrong on the things a player looks at while standing still — wet concrete, ice, the water in the level's floor plane, the metal of a weapon — because a surface that returns the same colour from every angle reads as painted rather than as polished.

Screen space is a real limitation, not an implementation detail. A reflection can only show what is already in the frame, so anything behind the camera, off the edges, or hidden behind something nearer simply is not there to be found. That failure has to be handled rather than hidden: a ray that finds nothing must fall back to a plausible answer and fade into it, because the alternative — a black hole where the reflection should be — is far more distracting than a reflection that is merely approximate.

Where the adapter can trace, none of that applies: the march does not run and a ray answers every reflective pixel, with the hit resolved against — see r_rt_reflections. What is described above is the fallback, for the machines and the moments that have no structure to trace. then governs only the march; the other two govern both, being statements about which surfaces reflect and how much, not about how the answer is found.

member.param: How many steps a reflected ray takes, or 0 for no screen-space search at all. With none, surfaces still take the fallback, so switching this off makes reflections coarse rather than absent.
How strongly the reflection is mixed in, where 1 is the physical amount.

The roughness past which a surface stops reflecting sharply enough to be worth marching for. A rough surface scatters its reflection over a wide cone, and a single ray through the middle of that cone is not an approximation of it — it is a mirror image with the wrong shape, which reads as a smear.

How thick, in metres, a surface in the depth buffer is assumed to be. A depth buffer records where surfaces start and never where they end, so a ray passing behind something has to be told how far behind counts as "through it" rather than "hit it". Too small and reflections tear where a ray slips behind a thin object; too large and they smear against everything they pass near.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.RenderBudget
member.summary: What each is allowed to cost, in milliseconds.

remarks.para: The figures the remaster track committed to at stage R3 and then wrote five more stages against without an instrument to check them: shadows 1.0, occlusion 1.0, lighting 2.0, reflections 1.5, fog 1.5, post 1.5. They are for ultra at 1080p, which is the configuration R9's acceptance criterion names — a preset that runs fewer of these stages, or a smaller window, is not what the numbers describe.

Together they come to 7.75 ms, which against a 16.67 ms frame leaves just under 9 ms for the G-buffer, the forward pass, the temporal resolve and the present. That is the sense in which this is a budget rather than a target: the parts have to add up to a frame.

The frame is 60 Hz, and was briefly 120. The stage figures above were retargeted to a 120 Hz frame and tightened to fit it — they summed to 5.25 ms of 8.33, which held. What did not survive is what came after: the screen probe gather arrived and took a 2.5 ms line, and 7.75 ms does not fit in 8.33. Nor could any honest number have: the gather measures about 3.9 ms at ultra, so fitting it under a 120 Hz frame alongside everything else would need it written down at a twelfth of what it costs. Ultra runs the gather, so ultra is a 60 Hz configuration and this says so rather than carrying a target the preset was never going to meet. The presets that light from the bakes have the same stage set minus the gather and are not what these figures describe.

The G-buffer fill, the forward pass and the temporal resolve carry no figure. They were never budgeted separately — they are the frame the effects are added to, not effects that can be turned off — so they are measured and reported without a line to beat.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.RenderResolutionPolicy
member.summary: Decides the render size, the output size, the jitter length and the mip bias together.

remarks.para: One decision because they are one fact. The jitter is a fraction of a render pixel, so a jitter worked out against one render size and a scene target built at another moves every sample by the wrong amount; the jitter has to cycle through more phases the further the render is below the output, so that each output pixel is still visited often enough; and the textures must pick their mips for the output, not the render, or the upscale shows them soft. Working each out in its own place is how they drift apart.

Under DLSS the numbers are NVIDIA's (DLSS Programming Guide §3.5 and §3.7.1.1): the render size is the one the runtime asks for — the render scale is set aside, there is no dynamic resolution — the phase count is eight times the area ratio, and the mip bias is the log of the ratio less one. Under ray reconstruction the phases never fall below thirty-two, which its integration guide asks of a noisy input.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.RenderStage
member.summary: The stages of a frame that are timed separately.

remarks.para: One entry per stage the remaster track set a budget for, in the order the frame runs them, plus the two that are not optional — the G-buffer fill and the forward pass — because a budget for the effects means nothing without the cost of the frame they are added to.

These are coarse on purpose. A timer query is a synchronisation point for the driver's pipelining, so one per draw call would change the thing it is measuring; one per stage answers the question the budget asks ("what does the fog cost") without perturbing it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SceneFog
member.summary: The original's distance fog: how fast the air closes, and what colour it closes to.
member.param: The colour a fully fogged surface takes, linear, from the level's FlatSky.
The extinction the exponential is evaluated with, per metre of view depth. Zero is no fog.

remarks.para: The original fogs per vertex and lets Direct3D do the blend. sub_512C30 computes the factor at 0x513462 and packs it into the vertex's specular alpha —

— where z is the view-space depth in game units, flt_BCABEC is the 0.001 that sub_493580 writes at start-up (0x4936E3), and flt_A7DA18 is the density sub_50FD20 (0x50FD20) publishes. With FOGTABLEMODE left at D3DFOG_NONE and every vertex already transformed, that alpha is the fog factor the hardware blends with: colour = f · surface + (1 - f) · fogColour.

The density is a level's own, and it comes from the GlobalLight task — not from FlatSky, whose Fog Amount is the cloud plane's fade. sub_527520 hands sub_50FD20 the showing GlobalLightKeyframe's fog colour and its density × 0.0005 (0x527B41), so with 4096 game units to the metre the whole chain collapses to : 0.002048 per metre per unit of declared density. See GlobalLightSettings for the bands and what the shipping levels ask for — anything from half a surface gone by 71 m to half of it still there at 2.9 km, each with its own colour.

The fog colour follows the blend, not the level (sub_5144E0): an opaque draw fogs to the level's colour, an additive one (ONE, ONE) to black (0x5145BB), and a modulating one (ZERO, SRCCOLOR) to white (0x514529) — each blend's own identity, so that a surface drawn as several passes fogs once rather than once per pass. is that rule, and is what a pass says instead of it.
The sky dome is not fogged at all: sub_52D060 sets FOGENABLE to zero along with its depth states before drawing it, which is what leaves the horizon a gradient rather than a flat wash.

member.summary: Gets the colour a draw of this blend fogs towards.

member.remarks: An additive pass must add nothing at full fog or the ground would be fogged once per material pass; black is what makes the passes sum to one fogged surface. sub_5144E0 sets exactly this, blend by blend, and it is why the terrain's several passes come out fogged like one. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SceneLighting
member.summary: The light the whole scene is lit by, for one frame.

remarks.para: A property of the frame rather than of any draw, so it travels as one value set once rather than as device state that could be left behind.

is in view space, pointing towards the sun, because the G-buffer's normals are. The shell rotates the level's world-space sun direction by the camera's orientation before setting it — the alternative, storing world normals, would cost the G-buffer precision for no gain when every consumer is a screen-space pass.

member.param: Where surfaces take their light from.
The view-space direction towards the sun. Expected to be unit length.
The sun's radiance. Larger than one is meaningful; the tone map handles it.
A flat stand-in for bounced light, used only by until the probe volume of stage R7 replaces it with something directional.
Whether the level's bakes already carry its direct light, so must not add a sun on top of them. See DeferredLighting.CompleteBake.

Scales the whole dynamically-computed irradiance, and is ignored under , which has to reproduce the original exactly.
It exists because this game's diffuse textures are not albedo. They were painted to be multiplied by a lightmap that averages well below one, so they already carry lighting; treating them as albedo and lighting them at unit irradiance counts that painted-in brightness a second time. The error is proportional to how bright the texture already was, which is why it shows up first on sand and snow and hardly at all on concrete.
How brightly the sky itself lights the world, where one is the sky's own physical brightness.

The sun colour and source intensity used to build an atmospheric sky, before . When absent, is used. Kept separate because calibrating the direct surface response must not also dim the sky and its irradiance harmonics.

The sky as a light source for the volumetric fog -- the level's own ambient, which the fog was calibrated against. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass
member.summary: Which part of a frame a draw belongs to.
member.remarks: The modern path shades in two stages — surfaces are recorded into a G-buffer, then lit in one pass over the screen — and a translucent surface cannot take part in that, because a G-buffer holds one surface per pixel. Naming the pass a draw belongs to is how the backend knows which of its two programs to use, without any renderer in the game having to know the pipeline exists.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass.Geometry
member.summary: Opaque and alpha-tested surfaces, recorded into the G-buffer to be lit afterwards.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass.Forward
member.summary: Surfaces drawn after lighting: glass, foliage that blends rather than cuts, muzzle flashes, decals, and the first-person arms and weapon.
member.remarks: The view model is here for a reason that is not transparency: it is drawn with its own narrower projection, so its depth does not belong in the same buffer the fog and the reflections read.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass.GlassLayer
member.summary: The front layer of the level's glazing: which pane is nearest at each pixel, and which way it faces, recorded before anything translucent is blended.

remarks.para: A pane's reflection is computed once per pixel, from one surface — so where two windows overlap, something has to decide WHICH. Writing each pane's normal into an image from the translucency pass does not decide it: blending is ordered by the rasteriser, but an image store is not ordered at all, between triangles or between draws, so whichever fragment landed last won and the answer changed from frame to frame. That is a reflection that fizzes with per-pixel noise.

So the question is asked in a pass with a DEPTH BUFFER OF ITS OWN, where the depth unit decides it — nearest wins, by construction, with no ordering to get right. It has to be a separate pass rather than depth writes in the translucency subpass, because the glazing there shares its depth buffer with the tracers, the muzzle flame and the smoke, and glass that wrote depth would occlude all three.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass.Shadow
member.summary: Depth-only rendering from a light's point of view.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScenePass.Card
member.summary: A model's surface captured into its page of the surface cache atlas.

remarks.para: Not part of drawing a frame at all. Each model is rendered a handful of times at load, through an orthographic camera per card, into a rectangle of an atlas — so that a ray hitting that model later can read what its surface looks like without the model being on screen, or in the frustum, or drawn at all.
It writes albedo, normal and material, and deliberately not motion: a card is a fixed view of a static model, so there is no previous frame for it to have moved from.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SceneTargetDescription
member.summary: What the offscreen scene is rendered into.

remarks.para: The original renders straight to the back buffer and keeps nothing, which is why it can have no shadows, no ambient occlusion, no reflections and no volumetrics: every one of those needs the depth buffer readable as a texture and the frame available after it has been drawn. This describes the target that makes them possible.
The size is the render size, which is not the window size when the render scale is not one. Presentation scales to the window at the end of .

The render height in pixels.
The width the frame is accumulated and presented at, or 0 for the render width. Larger than asks the temporal resolve to upsample rather than the final blit to stretch.
The matching height, or 0 for the render height.

Whether surfaces are recorded into a G-buffer and lit afterwards, rather than shaded as they are drawn. Required by everything from stage R3 on, because a shadow, an occlusion term or a reflection needs the surface's normal and roughness to still be there once the frame is complete.

Whether colour is stored with range beyond [0, 1]. When the target is an ordinary 8-bit buffer and the round trip is lossless, which is what the vanilla path uses so that going through the offscreen target changes nothing at all.
The optional deferred attachments required by the active preset.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SceneTargetDescription.IsUpsampling
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the frame is accumulated at a higher resolution than it is drawn.
member.remarks: The point of doing it this way round: a frame drawn at 70% and merely stretched is a frame with 70% of the detail, permanently. A frame drawn at 70% with the sample point moved each time and accumulated at full resolution is one where every output pixel is eventually sampled directly — the missing detail arrives over a handful of frames rather than never.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SceneTargetDescription.IsMultisampled
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the description asks for multisampling.
member.remarks: Never true while is. Multisampling a G-buffer means multisampling every one of its targets and resolving each — and resolving a normal by averaging it is not meaningful, because the average of two unit vectors is not a direction either surface has. Deferred renderers anti-alias temporally instead, which is what stage R5 brings; until then the render scale is the dial.
