member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for the screen probe gather and the world-space radiance cache it falls back on.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.ScreenGatherMaxIntensity
member.summary: How bright a single screen-traced ray may come back, before it feeds the next frame.
member.remarks:
The screen trace resolves a hit from the previous frame's lit scene, and this frame's indirect is built out of what it returns — which then lights the scene the next trace reads. Unbounded, that loop does not settle: past a certain gather strength each pass is brighter than the last, so the read is clamped.
In EXPOSED units, so the cap means the same brightness on screen by day and by night, and at ten on every preset. The modern presets carried 50.1 applied to raw scene radiance, which at night -- exposure sixteen and up -- let a ray through some eighty times brighter than ten exposed: the few of a probe's sixteen rays that landed on a lamp's fixture or its pool of light swung its estimate frame to frame, and that was the cloud drifting around every lamp at night.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.ScreenGather
member.summary: How strongly the screen probe gather's indirect light fills the deferred lighting.
member.remarks: Zero is off, which is vanilla alone: above zero, the gather traces the surface cache per screen probe into an atlas and the deferred lighting reads it as its diffuse fill over the far-field floor -- the stage where the traced global illumination reaches the screen. Not a name clash with (r_gi), which is the baked probe field; this is the live screen-space gather, and it needs the surface cache and the distance fields, so it does nothing without both. The magnitude compensates for how the gather reads the cache: the surface cache's final atlas holds each card's OUTGOING radiance -- the incident light already taken through the surface's albedo and the Lambertian one-over-pi -- and the deferred fill then takes the receiver's albedo again, so the raw gather lands roughly an order of magnitude below the ambient it stands in for. A strength around two and a half lifts it back, so a shadowed wall reads as lit concrete rather than black. It stays a knob while the look is tuned.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.RadianceCache
member.summary: Whether the world-space radiance cache updates and feeds the deferred fill's indirect.
member.remarks: The stable counterpart to the screen gather. A grid of world-anchored probes traces the surface cache every frame into the same L1-SH layout the baked probe field uses, so the deferred pass samples it unchanged -- but the radiance is live, not baked, so the sun and dynamic surfaces still feed it, and because a probe lives in a world cell rather than on the moving screen it does not shimmer under motion the way the gather does. It supersedes the baked field when on, and needs the surface cache (r_cards) and the distance field (r_sdf) to trace against. On at every preset above vanilla, each of which runs the surface cache and the distance field it needs. It is the shippable form of the real-time indirect the screen gather could not steady.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.RadianceCacheScale
member.summary: Calibration on the radiance cache's stored bounce, where 1 is the raw traced radiance.
member.remarks: The cache holds actual card radiance, and how strongly it is fed into the deferred fill is what turns a sunlit floor into a room lit by the light it bounces up its walls. Half was far too timid: it left a window room showing only the sun's own patches on the floor with no bounce climbing the walls, the single-bounce indirect starved to almost nothing. Lifted so the bounce actually carries the room -- validated on mission 1's office, where the sun through the window now fills the whole room, and on the outdoor spawn, which does not blow out. The sealed-room leak this would also amplify is cut at its source instead (see the sky-leak reject in the cache trace), not by keeping the whole bounce dim.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.ScreenGatherTrace
member.summary: Whether the screen probe gather traces on-screen geometry from the frame before the cache.
member.remarks: On by default, but only ever engaged while is up: each gather ray first marches the depth buffer and, on an on-screen hit, reads the previous frame's lit colour there -- on-screen bounce at full frame detail rather than the surface cache's coarse card -- falling through to the cache only when the ray leaves the screen or finds nothing. A knob to turn off for comparison; it does nothing when the gather itself is off.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.ScreenGatherCadence
member.summary: How many frames apart the screen probe gather re-traces. One is every frame.

remarks.para: The gather is the single most expensive pass in a real-time-GI frame -- it traces sixteen rays from each probe of a grid covering the screen, and at 1440p that is nearly a million rays. This runs it every N frames instead of every one, carrying the atlas forward in between.

What makes that sound is that a probe's value is a running average over 's own accumulation -- dozens of frames -- so a probe is already a slow-moving estimate and re-tracing it twice as often does not make it twice as right. What genuinely has to happen every frame is the FULL-RESOLUTION RESOLVE, which reprojects the result against each pixel's own world position: that is what pins the indirect to the world while the camera moves, and it keeps running at frame rate here. So the indirect still tracks the view every frame; only the rate at which new light is traced into it drops. The cost is how quickly newly revealed geometry fills in -- a frame or two longer.

Reducing the RAY COUNT instead was measured and is a worse trade: it makes every probe's estimate noisier, which the spatial filter then spreads, where this leaves each estimate exactly as good and only arrives less often.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.ScreenGatherFilter
member.summary: How far the screen probe gather's spatial denoise blur reaches, in probes. Zero is off.
member.remarks: The spatial half of the gather's denoise, paired with its temporal accumulation. The per-frame estimate is noisy and the temporal pass resets along depth edges, so the probes freshest near a wall shimmer; blending each probe with its neighbours, weighted so light does not cross an edge, smooths that. One probe each way is usually enough; higher is smoother but softer. Only ever runs while is up.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.GlobalIlluminationLeakReject
member.summary: The escape fraction below which a radiance-cache probe's sky is treated as a wall leak.
member.remarks: A cache probe traces the whole sphere; the fraction of its rays reaching open sky says whether the sky it sees is a real opening or a leak through a wall the coarse distance field cannot seal. Above this fraction the sky is kept in full, below a third of it dropped entirely, so a sealed room -- whose probes escape only on the few rays that slip through a wall -- falls dark rather than borrowing the day outside, while a window room, whose probes escape freely, keeps its sky. A window room is lit mostly by its sunlit floor bouncing regardless, so this can be firm without darkening it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ScreenGatherCVars.GiSource
member.summary: Diagnostic: which one source of the screen GI gather's light to keep.
member.remarks: The gather lights each probe from three places: screen-traced hits (the last frame's image), hits on the surface cache, and the sky where a ray escapes. With r_debug_view ssgi this shows one of them alone, so a GI artefact can be pinned on the source that carries it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SdfTextParams
member.summary: How a run of signed-distance-field text is shaded: the atlas's distance spread, and the optional outline and glow drawn from that one distance channel.

remarks.para: The fill colour is the per-vertex colour, so it can vary per glyph for a gradient or a per-glyph animation. Everything here is what the whole run shares. Distances are in the normalised space the atlas stores — the glyph edge is at 0.5, inside is greater — so and are fractions of that, independent of the size the text is drawn at.

is the number of atlas texels the distance field ramps over, taken from the atlas's SDF padding. The shader combines it with the on-screen size of a texel to keep the edge one screen pixel soft at any magnification, which is the whole point of the distance-field approach.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCascades
member.summary: Fits a cascaded shadow map to what the camera can see.

remarks.para: A directional light has no position, so a shadow map for one is a choice of box: which part of the world to spend the texels on. Everything difficult about cascades is in that choice, and two decisions here are what separate shadows that hold still from shadows that crawl.

The slice is bounded by a sphere, not by its corners. A box fitted to the frustum corners changes size as the camera rotates, so every texel lands somewhere new each frame and shadow edges boil. A sphere through the same corners has a radius that does not depend on the camera's rotation at all.

The centre is snapped to a texel grid fixed in the WORLD. Even with a fixed radius, a centre that moves smoothly slides the whole map by fractions of a texel and the staircase along every shadow edge swims. Quantising in light space means the map moves in whole texels, so the staircase stays put relative to the world — but only if the grid it lands on is anchored to the world. Everything else here is camera-relative, and quantising a camera-relative centre snaps to a grid that travels with the player: the box then holds the same position in front of them frame after frame while the world slides beneath it, which is the crawl the snapping exists to remove rather than a cure for it. The camera's own position is therefore carried into light space and added in before the floor.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCascades.CasterReach
member.summary: How far behind a slice, in metres, geometry is still drawn so that it can cast into it.
member.remarks: A caster does not have to be inside the slice to shadow it — a tower well outside the near cascade still throws a shadow across it. This is how far back the light's box is opened to catch them; too little and tall geometry stops casting, too much and depth precision is spent on empty sky.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCascades.LightRotationFor(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Builds the world-to-light rotation for a sun direction.
member.param: The world-space direction towards the sun.
member.returns: The rotation, rows being the light's right, up and forward axes.
member.remarks: The light looks along the direction its light travels, which is away from the sun. The reference up is chosen away from the forward axis so the cross product never collapses — with a sun overhead, which several missions have, a fixed world up would be parallel to forward and the basis would be degenerate.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCascades.Snap(System.Double,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Quantises one axis of the cascade centre onto a world-anchored texel grid.
member.param: Where the camera sits on this light axis, in world light space.
The cascade centre on the same axis, relative to the camera.
How much world space one shadow texel covers.
member.returns: The centre, still camera-relative, moved to the nearest grid line below it.
member.remarks: The addition and the floor happen in double precision because the sum is a world coordinate and this game's run to tens of thousands of metres; only the difference, which is smaller than the cascade, is narrowed. Doing the floor in single precision would quantise to the grid of representable floats near 40000 rather than to the texel grid, which at the near cascade's texel size is a coarser grid than the one being asked for.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for shadowing: the sun's shadow, contact shadows, ambient occlusion and the screen-space bounce.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.SunAngle
member.summary: How wide the sun's disc is, in degrees, which is what gives a shadow its penumbra.

remarks.para: The sun is not a point. It subtends a little over half a degree from here, and that is the entire reason a shadow is sharp where it meets its caster and soft a few metres away: near the contact a surface sees almost all of the disc or almost none of it, and further away the two answers overlap across several pixels. A point sun has no penumbra at any sample count, so this is not a quality dial — it is the physical fact the softness is derived from.

Every preset carries the same figure for that reason, and it is the real one: 0.5357 degrees, the sun's mean angular diameter seen from the earth. It only reaches the picture where the sun's shadow is traced rather than sampled from the cascades, which today means ultra with r_rt on; the cascaded path has no disc to sample.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ShadowAccumulate
member.summary: How many frames the traced sun shadow is averaged over before it is turned into light.

remarks.para: The trace fires one ray per pixel per frame, so its answer is a coin toss weighted by how much of the sun that pixel can see. The spatial reconstruction turns the worst of that into a penumbra, but a mask built from eight samples of a binary signal still visibly differs frame to frame — and this is what was seen as distant shadows redrawing themselves.

Leaving it to the temporal filter downstream does not work, and the reason is circular: shadow noise arrives there as a colour that changed, a changed colour reads as a history that no longer describes the surface, and rejecting the history is precisely refusing to do the averaging that would have removed the noise. So the mask is averaged here, on its own, where nothing has to be protected from being blurred — a shadow on static geometry carries no sub-pixel detail.
The number is a cap on a running mean rather than a fixed window, so a surface just come into view is not held back by frames it never had. One switches the averaging off.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.Shadows
member.summary: The side length in texels of each shadow cascade, or 0 for no shadows.
member.remarks: The cost is per cascade and quadratic: four cascades at 4096 is 268 MB of depth, which is more video memory than the entire rest of this game uses. Ultra buys its quality with a fourth cascade rather than with a larger one — more cascades put the texels where the player is looking, while a larger map spends them evenly over ground they cannot make out.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ShadowCascades
member.summary: How many cascades the shadow distance is split across.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ShadowDistance
member.summary: How far from the camera, in metres, shadows are drawn.
member.remarks: Further is not better past a point: the same texels get spread over more world, so distant shadows arrive at the cost of the ones under the player's feet.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ContactShadows
member.summary: How far a screen-space contact ray reaches, in metres. Zero disables it.
member.remarks: A shadow map has one texel per several centimetres at best, so it cannot resolve a weapon against the body carrying it or a crate against the floor it stands on. Contact is where its resolution runs out and where the eye looks first.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ShadowSoftness
member.summary: The shadow filter's radius in texels.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.AmbientOcclusion
member.summary: How many directions each pixel searches for its horizons, or 0 for no occlusion.
member.remarks: Follows the same convention as r_fog_quality: the quality dial doubles as the switch, because a separate on/off would let the two disagree and a preset would then have to set both.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.AmbientOcclusionRadius
member.summary: How far a surface may occlude another, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.AmbientOcclusionIntensity
member.summary: How strongly the occlusion is applied, where 1 is the physical amount.
member.remarks: Above about one and a half this stops being occlusion and starts removing the picture. The radius this backend uses is room-scale rather than contact-scale, so the term already overlaps what the indirect gather computes; multiplying that overlap by three darkened an office corner until the lockers standing in it dissolved into the noise floor, while the sunlit floor it could not reach stayed too bright — the two errors then hid each other in any average over the frame. Measured across five regions, three scored 8.2 levels of mean error against 5.6 at the physical amount, and only the physical amount kept the corner readable.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ScreenSpaceGi
member.summary: How many samples gather bounced colour, or 0 for no screen-space bounce.
member.remarks:
Off at every preset. This was the cheap screen-space stand-in for a bounce, and the world-space radiance cache now carries that bounce on every preset that has one -- which is all of them above vanilla. Running both stacked a second, screen-space estimate on top of the cache's: its occlusion term read darker than the cache's own, dragging interiors down a stop, while the per-pixel screen march added noise the cache does not have. Vanilla has no deferred pass to run it in.
Kept implemented rather than deleted, and reachable from the console, because it is the only bounce available to a device that cannot run the surface cache -- and because a stand-in that still works is what lets the real thing be measured against something.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.ScreenSpaceGiIntensity
member.summary: How strongly the bounced colour is added back.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowCVars.Presets

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowSettings
member.summary: How the sun's shadows are drawn.
member.param: How many shadow maps the view distance is split across.
The side length in texels of each cascade's map.
How far from the camera, in metres, shadows are drawn at all.

How the split distances are chosen between an even division and a logarithmic one. Zero divides the range evenly, which wastes almost all the near cascade's resolution on ground the player can see in detail; one is logarithmic, which is right for the near cascade and leaves the far one starved.

Depth offset applied when testing, in texels of the cascade being sampled, measured along the light. A shadow map's error is one of its texels projected onto the receiver, so that is the unit the bias belongs in — and the unit that makes one number right for every cascade, since a far cascade's texel covers more ground and wants proportionally more.
It was a constant fraction of the cascade's depth range, which makes about 250 metres deep whatever the cascade — so 0.0015 of it was some 0.4 metres of bias along the sun, and at a low sun that slid every shadow half a metre across the ground. That is peter-panning, and it was enough to read as the ray-traced and rasterised shadows disagreeing about where a shadow falls, because the ray traces from the surface itself and needs no bias at all.
How far, in metres, a screen-space ray is marched towards the sun to catch contact a shadow map cannot resolve. Zero disables it.
How thick an occluder found by that ray is assumed to be. Beyond this the ray is looking past a surface's edge at something unrelated, and treating that as an occluder draws long false shadows.
The shadow filter's radius in texels. Above 1.5 a wider kernel is used.

How far the sample is pushed along the surface's own normal before testing, in texels of the cascade being sampled. The error a shadow map makes grows with the angle between the surface and the light, and moving along the normal scales with exactly that, which removes the striping a depth bias alone cannot. In texels for the same reason as : a constant in metres is ten texels of the near cascade and a fraction of one in the far.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowSettings.TracedSun
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the sun's shadow may be traced against the scene's acceleration structure instead of read from the cascades, on a backend that can trace at all.
member.remarks: Off falls back to the cascaded map everywhere — the software path. The backend never reads the console itself, so the app decides here and every consumer (the deferred sun, the gathers that share the flag's spirit) follows the same answer.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShadowSettings.SunLit
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the sun is contributing any light at all this frame.
member.remarks: The day/night cycle fades the sun's colour to exactly zero once it sits a tenth below the horizon, and from then on every piece of sun-shadow work -- the cascade raster, the ray trace, its accumulation and its denoise -- produces a mask that is multiplied by nought. The app clears this at that point so the whole pipeline can stand down; through twilight, where a dim sun still lights, it stays set and everything runs. Defaults to lit so a caller that never thinks about the cycle keeps today's behaviour.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ShelterMapTransform
member.summary: Where the level's roofs are, as one texel per square of ground: how to turn a world position into a texel of the shelter map, and a packed texel back into the height of the surface standing over it.

remarks.para: Standing water has to know whether the sky can reach a surface — a warehouse floor does not pool with water while its own roof keeps the rain off it — and that question is asked per pixel, in the lighting shader, which knows nothing about the level. It used to be answered by handing the shader a handful of building bounding boxes and looping over them. That was wrong twice over: a building standing at an angle to the world axes fills barely a third of its own box, so the box dried the apron in front of it, and any structure the level had not labelled a building sheltered nothing at all, so its floor rained indoors.

So the answer arrives as a picture instead: a top-down raster of the height of the solid world, built once when the mission loads. A pixel converts its world XY to a texel, fetches the height stored there, and is sheltered when that height stands over it — one fetch and a comparison, in place of a loop, and right everywhere rather than right near a labelled box.

World metres, not camera-relative. Everything else the wetness carries is rebased on the camera because the levels sit tens of kilometres from the world origin. This is not, because the map is a fixed property of the level and rebasing it would mean re-uploading a transform every frame for no gain: a world coordinate of tens of kilometres still resolves to a millimetre in a float, which is four hundred times finer than one texel.

member.param: The world X, in metres, of the low corner of texel zero.
The world Y, in metres, of the low corner of texel zero.
How much ground one texel covers, in metres.
How many texels the map holds along world X.
How many texels the map holds along world Y.
The world height, in metres, the packed value counts up from.
How many metres one step of the packed value stands for.
How far over a surface the roof must stand before the surface counts as sheltered. The ground is in the map like everything else, so without this every square of ground would shelter itself.

How far over a surface a roof may be and still be its roof. A level's footprint can hold two areas at wildly different altitudes, and one top-down raster cannot tell a ceiling from a mountainside a kilometre above it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars
member.summary: The renderer's console variables for the sky: its light, the atmosphere, and the night sky and moon.
member.remarks: One of the renderer's variable containers; says how they are reached.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.SkyLight
member.summary: How bright the sky is as a source of indirect light, where 1 is the level's own ambient.
member.remarks: The GI reads the sky as the colour a ray that escapes the geometry returns -- the skylight that fills every outdoor surface and reaches in through a window. The level's Dirlight carries only a dim ambient triple (its "Back Color", around a quarter), authored as a subtle fill on top of the flat ambient rather than as the sky's whole radiance; read literally as the sky it leaves the open exterior reading like dusk. This scales it up to a daytime value. It touches only what looks at the sky, so a sealed room is unaffected while the courtyard and the window-lit wall lift -- and it only ever reaches a preset that runs the gather or the probe field, so vanilla and the baked path are untouched.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.AtmosphereSunScale
member.summary: Scales the sun that generates the atmospheric sky, independently of direct light.
member.remarks: The atmosphere produces both the visible sky and the diffuse SH that lights surfaces. It used to read , which meant calibrating direct sunlight silently scaled the sky by the same amount and could never change their balance. Keeping the old preset values here preserves the measured sky while is corrected independently.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.NightSkyScale
member.summary: How much of the moon's light the atmosphere scatters into the night sky.

remarks.para: A moonlit sky is the daytime sky's own blue, lit by a source some four hundred thousand times dimmer. Handed the moon at face value the march drew what the eye reads as a dim DAY, so it was knocked down to two percent. That left the sky and the harmonics projected from it black, and with them every shadow the moon did not reach: nothing lit a night but the moon's direct light and the lamps.

What made the moonlit blue read as day was the missing night vision, not the blue. With the resolve's night shift taking the colour out of the dim sky, a third of the moon lets the sky light the world again and still reads as night.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.NightAirglow
member.summary: The night sky's own glow at the zenith, in the atmosphere's units.
member.remarks:
Airglow: the upper atmosphere's faint emission, which is most of a clear moonless sky's light. It is what keeps a night without a moon from being black, and it brightens towards the horizon, where the eye looks through more of the glowing layer. Nought turns it off.
On for every preset, faintly. Once the exposure meters the whole frame, the night is metered off the sky and the ground together, and without the glow a clear night had almost nothing in it to meter: a black frame with stars. The glow is the moonless night's own light, so it is what that frame should be showing -- at 0.0005, a dark night; 0.004 reads as a bright one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.Stars
member.summary: Whether the night sky draws its stars, the galaxy and the moon's disc.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.Moonlight
member.summary: How strongly the moon lights the world, against the cycle's own moon; 0.1 by default.
member.remarks: Scales the moon's light -- what throws moon shadows and lights the ground -- and with it the moonlit sky, which is scattered from the same moon, as a dimmer moon makes a darker sky. The disc keeps its own dial (), and the airglow that lights a moonless night is not the moon's at all.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.MoonBrightness
member.summary: How bright the moon's disc and halo are drawn in a night sky; one is the default.
member.remarks: The disc only: the moonlight on the world is the directional light and is not touched by this.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SkyCVars.Presets

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Sky.AtmosphereTransmittance
member.summary: How much of the sun's light gets through the air to the ground, by how high the sun stands.

remarks.para: The same atmosphere the sky is marched through (Common/SkyAtmosphere.slang: the planet, the Rayleigh and Mie layers and the ozone band, constant for constant), integrated once along the path to the sun. This is what colours the sun at sunset: the blue is scattered out of the long, low path first, then the green, and what reaches the ground is orange, then red, and much dimmer -- while the light scattered out of it is what makes the sky blue overhead. Tinting the sun light by this transmittance keeps the direct light and the sky it sits in in agreement.

It replaces a hand-made warm tint that was multiplied into the sun AND fed to the sky, which the sky then reddened a second time by its own scattering: at sunset every direction of the sky came out a uniform orange-brown and every wall facing the sun a saturated red.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheBinding
member.summary: Everything a backend pass needs to turn a traced hit into the light that surface sends: the cards the level was captured onto, the grid that finds one, and the atlas holding what each card ended up lit to.

remarks.para: The surface cache is the engine's, built and lit above the renderer seam, and the passes that read it have so far been the engine's own compute shaders — which bind it by unit through and friends. A backend-owned pass cannot do that: it owns its descriptor set outright and has to be handed the resources by name. This is that handover, and nothing more — the backend never builds, lights or invalidates any of it.

Why a backend pass wants it at all. A reflected ray that leaves the screen has no answer in the frame, and the only record of what stands off-screen is the cache. The lookup itself lives in the shader library, as Common/SurfaceCache.slang, and is shared source precisely so that the gather and the reflection land on the same card.

member.param: The page records: one run of vectors per card, as the lookup reads them.
The lookup grid's buckets, each a start and a count into .
The page indices the buckets point into.
The card atlas's albedo, whose alpha says which texels were written at all.
The card atlas's depth, which decides between cards a point lies inside.
The lighting atlas: the outgoing radiance each card settled at.
How wide the lighting atlas is, in texels.
How tall the lighting atlas is, in texels.
How many buckets the grid has. A power of two; the hash masks with it.
The grid's low corner, in the cache's own space.
How much world one grid cell covers, in metres.

Where the camera stands relative to the cache's origin. The cache measures everything from its own centre so that a level tens of kilometres from the world origin still resolves in a float; a pass working in camera-relative world has to add this to get into the space the lookup reads.
How much of the cache's radiance a traced ray keeps — the same artistic control the gather applies, so a reflection of a wall and the indirect light off that wall agree about how bright it is.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiBounce
member.summary: How much of the surface cache's bounced radiance a traced gather ray keeps.

remarks.para: One is the physical answer: the cache holds real outgoing radiance and a ray that hits a card should keep all of it. This scales the cache's answer down without touching the sky, which is resolved separately. Applies to the screen gather and the radiance cache alike.

It was 0.15, then 0.35, and both were tuned against a broken target. The target image showed the office floor at 0.2 out of 255 — black — because the cache that produced it had no coverage over this level's geometry, so its rays hit surfaces with nothing cached and came back with nothing. 0.15 existed to reproduce that darkness; 0.35 was half a step back from it, arrived at by a whole-frame sweep that could not see what the deficit was doing to the exposure.

It is back at the physical one, and the measurement that put it there is the fill, not the frame. Sampled over 1056 office-floor points at fixed exposure with no tone map, the tenth percentile is the sky-and-bounce fill and the ninetieth is the same surface with the sun on it. At 0.35 the bounce carried under half the light a physically-normalised bounce delivers; at one the fill lands about twenty per cent generous while the sunlit end stays within one per cent, which is the closest a single scalar gets, and it is on the right side: the deficit was what pinned the auto-exposure against its ceiling.

What it costs is the office ceiling, which comes out bright. That region is a strip light this port lights as an emissive fixture, so most of the excess is the fixture's own emission rather than bounce this value is delivering; the room's floor, wall, window and sun pool all improve, and so does the exterior.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiFarRefresh
member.summary: How many slices the whole surface cache is refreshed in, one a frame; 0 turns it off.
member.remarks: The cache near the camera is refreshed every frame within ; this sweep keeps the REST of it current -- a far surface follows the sun, the lamps and the world filling in within slices / frame rate seconds, instead of keeping its load-time light until the player walks up to it. Fewer slices is a faster sweep and a dearer frame.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiCacheRadius
member.summary: How far from the camera the surface cache keeps refreshing itself, in metres.

remarks.para: The cache covers the whole level, and every frame the relight and the bounce advanced a cursor through it — so a fixed share of every frame went on cards kilometres away, in parts of a map the player will never stand in. These levels are enormous and a player sees a corner of one; on mission 1 that was over two milliseconds a frame spent almost entirely outside the room.

It was not merely unseen work, it was work that could not produce an answer. The relight traces its shadows against the distance-field clipmaps, which follow the camera and reach a few hundred metres; past that there is no field, so a far card re-derived exactly the value it already held.

Beyond this radius a card keeps the lighting the load-time seed gave it — the seed still covers the whole level, so nothing goes dark. What a far card stops doing is tracking change: a lamp switched across the map will not relight the wall beside it until the player comes within this distance. Nought restores the old behaviour of refreshing the entire level every cursor round.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiAmortize
member.summary: How many frames the surface-cache relight spreads its tiles across.
member.remarks: The real-time GI relight is world-space -- its cost is the same at any output resolution, so it is the biggest single item in the budget on a high-resolution frame. It traces one slice of the cache a frame and walks the cursor over this many frames; a static level under a fixed sun re-traces a tile to the answer it already holds, so a wider spread is nearly free in a converged still and only slows how fast a newly revealed surface fills its multi-bounce light. Raise it to trade that fill-in latency for per-frame GPU time (roughly the whole GI stage divides by this), lower it for the snappiest response.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiMinSlice
member.summary: The fewest surface-cache tiles one steady-state relight or bounce slice dispatches.
member.remarks: A floor on the slice, because the tracing hides its ray latency only in a large dispatch. Too high a floor packs a whole round of work into a few frames and idles the rest, which is a spike every round.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiConverge
member.summary: How far the surface cache is converged at load, before the level's first frame is shown.

remarks.para: The bounce is a progressive radiosity solve: each pass folds one more bounce into the last one's result, so the cache climbs towards its multi-bounce equilibrium over the frames after a load rather than arriving at it. Run in front of the player that is the "lighting up" -- a level that opens flat and visibly fills with light over the first second or two, which reads as the game loading badly rather than as a renderer converging.

This runs that climb during the load instead, where the frame is already being held: the whole cache is relit once WITH shadows and this many bounces are folded in, so the first frame the player sees is the converged one. The direct term matters as much as the bounces -- in the steady state it is spread over frames, so without this a level opens with its cards unshadowed and darkens as the slices arrive.

It could not be done before the distance fields were cached: converging needs something to trace shadows against, and the field used to arrive seconds after the level did. Zero restores the old ramp, which is also what a device with no cached field falls back to.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GiTemporalFrames
member.summary: How many frames the surface-cache relight's temporal accumulation converges over.

remarks.para: The cap on the relight's accumulation weight: the blend's alpha bottoms out at one over this, so a tile keeps adapting to a moving sun rather than freezing, while integrating far more hemisphere directions than the sixteen a single trace covers.

This is the knob for the slow travelling ripple over interior surfaces -- the "heat haze", visible with the camera standing perfectly still. Each time the relight's cursor reaches a tile it blends a freshly traced estimate in at this alpha, and that estimate does not agree with the stored one: a tile gathers from its neighbours' FINAL lighting, and under each neighbour was last updated at a different point in the cursor's sweep, so every tile integrates a slightly different snapshot of the room. The disagreement is systematic rather than random -- raising the bounce gather's ray count from sixteen to thirty-six moved the shimmer 1.5%, while halving the amortisation (twice the retrace rate) doubled it -- so the only lever that reaches it is how much of one retrace is admitted. Thirty-two measured a 2.1x reduction against the old eight.

The cost is adaptation latency. With at 24 a tile is retraced every twenty-four frames, so the accumulation's time constant runs about 3.5 seconds at eight and about thirteen at thirty-two. That is only the multi-bounce term settling behind a sun the day/night keys are actively scrubbing; the direct sun, its shadows and the screen gather's own trace are immediate. Lower it if a scrubbed sun matters more than a still interior.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.SurfaceCache
member.summary: Whether every model's surface is captured into the card atlas.

remarks.para: The structure that lets light bounce off geometry the camera cannot see: a ray hitting a model reads its captured surface rather than needing the model drawn. On at every preset that gathers, which is all of them above vanilla; off at vanilla, where an atlas nothing samples would be load time and video memory spent on nothing.

No longer restart-scope. It was, along with , and — and that made switching a preset a trap rather than a setting, because r_lighting dynamic applies at once and DISCARDS the bakes while the thing meant to replace them could not arrive until the next launch. The frame went flat and nothing said why. The capture is now made on demand and the lighting model waits for it; see DesktopGame.RealtimeGi.cs. Turning it on mid-level costs one long frame, because the capture is a render pass over every distinct model and cannot be anything else.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.SurfaceCacheDensity
member.summary: How many texels of card a world unit of surface is given.
member.remarks: The dial that decides both the atlas size and how much detail a bounce carries. Higher resolves a doorway rather than averaging over a wall, and costs the square of itself — paid at load and in video memory rather than per frame, which is what makes it a sensible thing to ladder by tier. It is also the first thing a fresh install pays for, enhanced being the preset applied when no settings file exists, so the cheapest tier is deliberately close to the floor.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.SurfaceCacheDump
member.summary: Where to write the captured atlas as images, or empty to write none.
member.remarks: A capture can only be judged by looking at it. Wrong winding shows as models captured inside-out, a wrong card rotation as mirrored pages, a missing scissor as pages bleeding into each other — and every one of those produces an atlas full of entirely plausible surfaces.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.SurfaceCacheProbe
member.summary: What the lighting pass writes into its atlas: light, or a chosen diagnostic.
member.remarks:
A shadow trace that fails leaves nothing to look at — a black atlas is equally consistent with a wrong world position, an unbound sampler, a uniform that never arrived and a field that is genuinely closed over. Each probe writes one of those intermediates where the light would have gone, so the dump can tell them apart: 1 writes what the trace sees at its start point, 2 the reconstructed world position within the outermost clipmap, 3 the world normal, 4 how the trace ended, 5 whether the card index sends a texel back to itself.
Keep the maximum in step with the shader. This clamps, silently and by design, so a probe added to the shader but not added here runs as whichever probe the clamp lands on -- which presents as the new probe reporting nothing whatsoever, and is indistinguishable from the thing it was measuring being broken.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.GlobalIlluminationBoost
member.summary: The diffuse colour boost the surface cache reflects light through.
member.remarks: The single lever for how bright the bounced light is. Each time light reflects off a card, the surface's albedo is raised by pow(luminance, boost) before it passes light along, so a lower value lifts a dark, low-albedo surface's reflectance towards one and lets a sunless interior carry far more indirect -- which the raw retail albedos (~0.4) otherwise swallow after a bounce or two. One is off (physical albedo). It never reaches one (the surface would return everything it received and the feedback would diverge); the shader clamps it below. This is what to reach for when interiors read dark, ahead of exposure or more bounces.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceCacheCVars.Presets
member.summary: The registry the renderer's own settings describe themselves to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial
member.summary: How a surface responds to light, beyond the colour its texture gives it.

remarks.para: The original's data has nothing of this kind: a surface is a diffuse texture and a lightmap, and how shiny it is was the lighting artist's problem, not the renderer's. So these values are authored for the port, matched onto textures by name in materials.json — snow is a rough dielectric, a gantry is metal, a window is smooth and barely diffuse.
That makes them a deliberate divergence rather than a reconstruction, and they only ever apply on the modern path: under the vanilla preset nothing reads them.

member.param:
How wide the surface scatters a reflection: 0 is a mirror, 1 is chalk. Drives both the specular highlight and, from stage R8, how sharp a screen-space reflection is allowed to be.
The default is 0.6 and it was 0.8, which turned out to be the quiet reason the whole material pipeline read as inert. Nothing in the renderer moves a surface's roughness DOWN from here -- the derived map multiplies around it, the floor-gloss term only touches up-facing surfaces -- so this is the floor for every wall in the game, and at 0.8 that floor was already inside the range where a GGX lobe is a hemisphere and one surface answers light exactly like the next.
Whether the surface reflects its own colour rather than the light's. Physically this is nearly always 0 or 1; values between exist only for surfaces whose texture mixes both.

How much light the surface gives off on its own, as a multiple of its albedo. Lamps and screens. One is the surface's own colour unlit — the sky dome, a tracer, a muzzle flash. A lamp wants more than one: a fluorescent tube painted at three quarters grey is not a light until it is scaled past what a lit surface could ever reach, which is what makes the bloom find it and the eye read it as the source rather than as a pale panel. See for how far that goes.

Whether this surface is a solid occluder of light. False for the thin and cut-out surfaces neither a depth buffer nor an opaque ray can describe honestly: a depth buffer records where a surface starts and never where it ends, so the horizon search treats anything thin as reaching to infinity and darkens whatever stands behind it; an opaque triangle in a ray-tracing structure blocks a shadow or gather ray whole, with no per-texel alpha test to let the light through a pane of glass or between the wires of a fence. So the flag gates both the ambient occlusion and the traceable world. Glass, wire fences, foliage and soldiers are the ones that matter.

Whether the temporal resolve must not blend history onto this surface this frame. For the draws where the engine knows the previous frame shows something unrelated — a body's first appearance, anything the simulation teleports — where reprojection would confidently fetch the wrong pixels. Per draw and per frame: set it for the one frame the discontinuity happens, then stop, or the surface never converges.

Whether the surface is seen THROUGH rather than merely cut out, and so cannot be drawn into the G-buffer at all.
Deferred shading has one surface per pixel and no way to blend, so the geometry pass resolves every partial alpha into a decision: keep the texel or discard it. For foliage and wire that is the right answer, because a cut-out really is a hole. For a pane it is not — a window at alpha 0.28 is flat, so it has no alpha gradient for the dithered coverage path to work from and takes the hard alpha < 0.5 cut instead, which throws away every texel of it. The glazing is not transparent in that picture; it is absent, and with it go the depth, the normal and the roughness that a reflection would have needed.
So a surface marked here is held out of the geometry pass and drawn in the forward translucency subpass instead, where it keeps its own alpha and is blended over the lit scene. That is the only place in the frame where a pane can both let the room behind it through and carry a reflection of its own.
It does NOT follow from a low roughness, and the two must not be conflated. Polished marble and a chrome fitting are as smooth as glazing and entirely opaque; what makes glass glass is being seen through. Nor does it follow from being false, which foliage and wire also set.

Whether the surface has no specular response at all: no highlight from the sun or a lamp, no ambient sheen, no reflection, and no standing water.
For cloth and skin, which is to say for bodies. A soldier drawn as the default dielectric took the whole of the modern path's gloss machinery -- the derived roughness map multiplying 0.6 down towards a mirror, the floor-gloss term smoothing every helmet and shoulder because they face up, the traced reflection that anything under its roughness ceiling receives, and a puddle on the top of every head in the rain -- and read as plastic. Roughness alone cannot say this: every one of those terms moves roughness, and the puddle ignores it.
Retail has no specular on its models to reproduce. This is the ground's treatment -- specular nought, roughness one -- extended to the surfaces that should never shine, plus the wetness and reflection passes being told to leave them alone.

Whether the surface is a falling raindrop, drawn as the lens it is rather than as a light.
A drop is clear water: what the eye sees in it is the scene behind, bent across the streak and a little concentrated along its rims, with a glint only where a lamp or the sun stands behind it. Drawn as an added light instead, every drop was a white line. A draw marked here goes to the rain pipeline, which refracts a copy of the lit scene through the streak; a backend without it draws the drop's glint alone.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.ExcludedFromOcclusion
member.summary: The emissive channel's value for a surface excluded from ambient occlusion.

remarks.para: The G-buffer has no channel to spare — every one of its four targets already carries the surface's own alpha, because GL blends each attachment by that attachment's alpha. So the exclusion rides in the emissive channel, which in practice only ever holds nought or one: a surface either glows or it does not. A third value at a quarter is unambiguous against both, and leaves the emissive > 0.5 test every other pass already uses working untouched.
It is a compromise and worth replacing with a proper flags channel if the G-buffer ever gains one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.MaximumEmissive
member.summary: The brightest a surface may declare itself, as a multiple of its albedo.
member.remarks: Set by what the channel can carry rather than by taste: the packing below spends the band above a half on the strength in steps of a sixteenth, and eight bits leave a hundred and twenty-seven of them. Nothing in the game asks for more — a tube at eight times its albedo is already the brightest thing in any interior — and a value past it is clamped rather than wrapped.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.EmissiveStepsPerUnit
member.summary: How many packed steps one unit of spans.
member.remarks: Sixteen, so that a strength of exactly one — the sky dome, a tracer, every emissive draw that existed before lamps did — lands on exactly one code and comes back exactly one. A round step is what keeps this packing from putting a fraction of a percent onto the sky, which is inside the tolerance capture comparisons are read at.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.PackedEmissive
member.summary: Gets the value written into the G-buffer's emissive channel.

remarks.para: Emission wins where a surface asks for both: a glowing surface is already ignored by the occlusion pass, so there is nothing to say.

The channel carries the STRENGTH and not merely the flag. It is one byte, and the three things it has to say do not overlap: nought is an ordinary surface, a quarter is the occlusion exclusion above, and every code past a half is emissive with the multiple recovered from how far past. A byte at 128 + 16x is that multiple x, so one is 144 and comes back exact; the smallest emissive code is 129, a sixteenth, which reads as a glow rather than as nothing. Every emissive > 0.5 test in the passes downstream is untouched by this.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.PackEmissive(System.Single)
member.summary: Packs an emissive strength into the G-buffer's channel.
member.param: The multiple of albedo the surface emits; clamped into range.
member.returns: The channel value, always above a half so the flag tests downstream still see it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.Default
member.summary: Gets the material a surface with no rule matching it gets.

remarks.para: Rough and non-metallic: the reading that makes an unclassified surface behave like painted concrete, which is what most of the game is. A shiny default would put highlights on every wall in the game the first time the sun moved.

Spelled out rather than written new(): for a struct that means the zero instance, not the primary constructor's defaults, so it would have produced a mirror-smooth surface with roughness nought — the opposite of what is wanted.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.Sky
member.summary: Gets the material the sky dome is drawn with.

remarks.para: Light rather than a lit surface, which the emissive strength of one says, and NOT a solid occluder, which is the part that matters to the ray-traced world: built into the acceleration structure the dome is a closed shell around the level, and every ray fired at the sun from anywhere inside it hits — the traced mask came back shadowed for every sun-facing pixel in the frame, indoors and out, which reads as a level with no sunlight rather than as a bug in the sky.

Spelled out as a material rather than left as a bare emissive override because emission alone can no longer mean it. A lamp is emissive too, and a lamp is ordinary solid geometry that belongs in the traced world: it has to shadow the sun like the ceiling it hangs from. Saying "emits, and is not an occluder" names the sky and nothing else.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.Body
member.summary: Gets the material a soldier's body is drawn with.

remarks.para: Matte, because cloth and skin do not shine; see .

And out of the ambient occlusion. A soldier is thin, close and moving, which is the worst case for a search that has to guess how deep a surface is from its front face alone -- it darkened the ground behind every guard in a halo of speckle that followed him about.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.SurfaceMaterial.IsDefault
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether this material is the default one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.TacticalDisplaySettings
member.summary: Turns the resolved frame into the picture on the map computer's tube: a phosphor display transform plus the power-on behaviour that goes with one.

remarks.para: This is a display transform, not an overlay. The world under it has to stay readable — the map is the whole reason the screen exists — so the grade is derived from the resolved luminance and the terrain, the roads and the roofs all survive it. A translucent green rectangle laid over the frame would be much simpler and would turn the useful picture into a blank field, which is exactly the mistake the retail path's own comment records.

It is separate from rather than a generalisation of it. That flag is the retail handheld's calibrated look and the vanilla preset's regression gate; this is the remaster's, and it animates. Keeping them apart means turning the tactical interface on cannot change what -vanilla puts on screen, which is the property the whole remaster track is checked against. The two are never on together.

Everything here is continuous because the transition is the point. The screen does not appear: the camera climbs, the grade fades in under it, a refresh band sweeps down the tube and the interface arrives behind it. A boolean cannot express any of that.

member.param: How much of the phosphor transform is applied, 0 for the ordinary picture to 1 for the tube. Also scales the tube's own geometry — the curvature, the scanlines and the shadow mask — so the screen bends into existence rather than snapping on.

The power-on energy, 0 to 1: the horizontal tearing, the block noise and the brightness surge a display makes in the moment it is driven. Independent of because the disturbance peaks while the grade is still arriving.
How strongly the refresh band shows, 0 for none. The bright line that runs down a tube being driven for the first time, and the thing that makes the arrival read as a screen rather than as a fade.
Where that band is, 0 at the top of the frame to 1 at the bottom.

A continuously rising time in seconds, for the flicker, the drifting scanlines and the animated noise. Wall-clock rather than a frame counter: the tube's own behaviour must not run faster on a faster machine.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalAaSettings
member.summary: How this frame is blended into the ones before it.

remarks.para: The scene is sampled at a different sub-pixel offset each frame (see ) and every frame is mixed into an accumulated history, so a pixel ends up holding an average over many samples of its own area. That is supersampling paid for in time instead of in bandwidth, and it is the only anti-aliasing here that does anything about the edges a deferred renderer cannot multisample cheaply — the lighting discontinuities, the specular glints, the fog's dither.

The whole difficulty is that the history is only valid where the previous frame drew the same surface. Where it did not — behind something that moved, or outside the previous frame's view — the history is another surface entirely, and blending it in is a smear that follows the camera around. The backend therefore reprojects each pixel into the previous frame and constrains what it finds there to the range of colours around the pixel now; a history outside that range is a disocclusion rather than a sample, and is discarded.

member.param: Whether to accumulate at all. When false the frame is passed straight through.

The share of the resolved pixel taken from the current frame, from 0 to 1. Low values converge to a cleaner image and hold more samples, at the cost of responding to change more slowly; the usual range is 0.05 to 0.15. One disables the accumulation without disabling the jitter, which is the useful setting for seeing what the jitter alone is doing.
This frame's horizontal sub-pixel offset, in pixels.
This frame's vertical sub-pixel offset, in pixels.

How much of the history's own blur is subtracted back out, from 0 to 1. Resampling the history with bilinear filtering every frame is a low-pass filter applied over and over, and a scene that is merely panning slowly can go visibly soft; sharpening the resampled result counteracts exactly that. Too much of it rings around high-contrast edges. The backend scales this by before applying it, because the sharpening lands on the history and the history feeds back into itself — so without the scaling the same number would mean a gentle touch at a high feedback and a tenfold overshoot at a low one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalJitter
member.summary: The sub-pixel offsets the camera is nudged by, one per frame.

remarks.para: A rasteriser takes one sample per pixel, at its centre, and everything temporal anti-aliasing does follows from moving that sample somewhere else each frame. Over a few frames the pixel has been sampled all over its own area, and averaging those samples is supersampling paid for in time rather than in bandwidth — which is why this is also what makes the noisy passes affordable: fog, ambient occlusion and screen-space GI can each take a fraction of the samples they would need to be clean in one frame, and let the accumulation finish the job.

The offsets come from a Halton sequence rather than from random numbers or a regular grid. Random offsets clump, leaving parts of the pixel unsampled for several frames and the rest oversampled; a grid is uniform but revisits the same few positions, so its pattern beats against the geometry. A low-discrepancy sequence is the thing that is neither: every prefix of it covers the pixel evenly, so the average is unbiased however few frames the history has survived.

Base 2 and base 3, the conventional pair, and sixteen of them. A longer sequence samples the pixel more finely but takes proportionally longer to converge after the history is thrown away — which happens on every camera cut and every fast turn, so it is not a rare case worth pessimising.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalJitter.Length
member.summary: The number of offsets before the pattern repeats.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalJitter.At(System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets the offset for a frame, in pixels, each component within ±0.5.
member.param: The frame counter. Any value, including a negative one, is accepted.
member.returns: The offset from the pixel centre.
member.remarks: Centred on zero rather than running 0 to 1, so that a jitter of index zero is the unjittered camera and a sequence cut short at any point has averaged to somewhere near the pixel centre rather than to a corner of it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalJitter.At(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets the offset for a frame from a sequence of a given length.
member.param: The frame counter. Any value, including a negative one, is accepted.
How many offsets the sequence cycles through; see .
member.returns: The offset from the pixel centre, each component within ±0.5.
member.remarks: The same Halton pair, only longer. Rendering further below the output spreads each render pixel over more output pixels, and the sequence has to visit more points of it before each of those has been sampled as often as an unscaled one would be.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.TemporalJitter.Halton(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Computes the radical inverse of an index in a base.
member.param: The one-based index into the sequence.
The base, which should be prime.
member.returns: A value in [0, 1).
member.remarks: The index's digits in the given base, mirrored about the point: 5 in base 2 is 101, and 0.101 in base 2 is 0.625. Mirroring is what makes the sequence low-discrepancy, because incrementing the index changes the most significant digit of the result and therefore lands the next sample in the largest remaining gap.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Temporal.TemporalFrameState
member.summary: What every temporal pass needs to know about this frame and the one before it.

remarks.para: A temporal filter answers one question over and over: where was this pixel last frame? Answering it takes both frames' view rotations, both projections, how far the camera moved, and both jitters — and every pass in the chain takes the same set, which is why it is one record rather than a dozen parameters repeated.

The camera offset is a delta rather than two positions on purpose. A world position far from the origin has no single-precision room left for a frame's worth of movement; the difference has it all, which is why it is taken while the positions are still double.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Temporal.TemporalResolveSettings
member.summary: What the temporal resolve is asked to do, as distinct from where the camera is.
member.param: Whether history is accumulated at all; off, every frame starts fresh.
How many frames a texel's history may average over. The higher it is the steadier a still picture, and the longer a wrong answer survives once the camera moves.
How much of the resolve's sharpening filter is applied, nought to one.
The exposure the resolve will apply, which the rejection is judged in: two colours that differ by less than a stop after exposure are the same colour to an eye and should not reject.
How much of the shading rejection is believed: the floor on how much of this frame the guide takes.
How far a thin feature is allowed to relax its rejection, nought to one. A wire or a railing is narrower than the filter's own kernel, so judged strictly it rejects every frame and never accumulates.

How many history texels there are per rendered pixel on each axis. Two, and the reason is measured: sizing the history from the presented output instead is finer still under an upscale, and with a kernel that only reaches half an input pixel most of those texels see no sample on a given frame.
Which intermediate the resolve shows instead of the picture, or nought.
member.remarks: The values live in , not in this constructor. A record struct's parameter defaults apply only to a call that leaves an argument out, and new T() is not such a call: it is the struct's own zeroing constructor, which runs none of them. Written as parameter defaults they would be silently skipped by the shortest way anyone writes — and a history scale of nought sizes the history at nothing, which the resolve then reads back as a texture nobody wrote.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureLodBias
member.summary: How far a texture's mip selection is pushed towards the sharper levels.

remarks.para: A frame rendered below the output size picks its mips for the smaller image, and the upscale then shows them too soft; a temporal resolve with any feedback averages detail away on top. Both are paid back by biasing every mipmapped texture's selection by the log of the render scale, and a little more under temporal feedback -- which is what temporal upscalers commonly ask of the engines that feed them.

It reaches further than sharpness. A cut-out's coverage is its alpha tested against a threshold, and a thin one -- a chain-link fence, a wire -- loses its strands the moment a softer level averages them under the threshold: in the picture and, drawn from the light, in the shadow it casts.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureLodBias.FromSettings
member.summary: The bias the current settings ask for, to be applied to every mipmapped texture's sampler.
member.returns: The bias, in mip levels; negative is sharper.
member.remarks: Clamped to one at the top of the scale so supersampling never biases coarser -- it already samples below its own mip rate, which is the whole point of it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ToneMapOperator
member.summary: How high-dynamic-range light is mapped onto what a display can show.
member.remarks: The scene is shaded in linear light with no upper bound — a muzzle flash, the sun through fog, a specular highlight on wet metal all exceed white — and something has to decide what "white" means before it reaches the screen. That decision is the single biggest lever on how the game reads, so it is a setting rather than a constant.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ToneMapOperator.None
member.summary: Clamp to [0, 1] and present. Not a tone map at all.
member.remarks: The identity, and the only value under which the offscreen path can be pixel-identical to the original's direct-to-backbuffer output. That is what makes it the regression gate's setting rather than a look anyone would choose.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ToneMapOperator.Neutral
member.summary: A gentle filmic shoulder that leaves midtones where the original put them.
member.remarks: The default. Chosen so that turning the modern pipeline on does not by itself restage every level: it rolls off what would have clipped and otherwise stays out of the way.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ToneMapOperator.Aces
member.summary: The ACES filmic curve, in Narkowicz's fitted form.
member.remarks: Contrastier, with the saturated highlight roll-off people read as "cinematic".

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.ToneMapOperator.Agx
member.summary: The AgX curve.
member.remarks: Desaturates as it approaches white rather than hue-shifting into it, which keeps a bright sky or a fog bank from turning cyan. The most forgiving of the three with very bright volumetrics.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.TracedWorldTransform
member.summary: The absolute world transform a traced world places a draw at, recovered from its model-view.
member.remarks: The game hands every draw a model-view, camera-relative by construction; a traced world holds its placements in absolute world space, because a structure built this frame is traced again the next from a camera somewhere else. Undoing the view needs the frame's own rotation and position, which is why only a draw made with the frame's camera -- the G-buffer and the first-person rig, not a cascade or a card -- can be placed at all. Written once so both renderers place the same draw at the same bits.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.ViewPlanes
member.summary: The camera's clip planes, as the original's Direct3D setup publishes them.

remarks.para: sub_493580 (0x493580) initialises the renderer's plane globals once, in game units — 4096 to the metre:

item.description: 409.6 units — , the world layer's near plane. Scripts can move it through SetNearClippingPlane (0x497D00); nothing retail does.
204.8 units — half of it, the first-person layer's near plane; see ViewModelProjection.

409,600,000 units — . It is the far end of the object frustum test in sub_49FEB0 and of the terrain draw walk's own reject at 0x5131A9, and the same figure feeds the depth encoding sub_512C30 builds at 0x512C3A.

remarks.para: A hundred kilometres is not a rounding of four. The far plane stood at 4000 m from the first fly-through until it was measured — twenty-five times short — and everything past it was clipped: the mountain ranges that surround missions 5, 9 and 11 ended in a straight line at the horizon, and a view from any height showed the ground beyond four kilometres simply absent. The terrain descent had been emitting those chunks all along and the renderer had been drawing them; the projection threw them away. Restoring the retail distance costs about 5% of the frame's GPU time on mission 5 at ultra and no depth precision at all: the port renders reverse-Z into a 32-bit float depth buffer, where the mapping is near / z to within a millionth and the near plane, not the far one, sets the resolution.

member.summary: The world layer's near plane in metres — 409.6 game units.

member.summary: The far plane in metres — 409,600,000 game units.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumeFormat
member.summary: What one voxel of a volume texture holds.
member.remarks: A short list on purpose. Every volume this renderer builds is one of three things — a distance field, a radiance cache, or an occupancy mask — and each wants a different trade between range and bandwidth. Offering the whole of GL's format table here would let a caller pick something no pass can read.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumeFormat.R8
member.summary: One byte per voxel. What a signed distance field is stored in.
member.remarks: A sphere trace needs to know how far it may step, not the distance to the millimetre — an error of a fraction of a voxel costs a step, never correctness. Four times the precision would cost four times the bandwidth on the hottest read in the renderer.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumeFormat.Rgba8
member.summary: Four bytes per voxel, for a volume carrying a colour and a weight.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumeFormat.Rgba16F
member.summary: Four half-floats per voxel, for radiance that runs past one.
member.remarks: The format anything holding light wants. A bounced colour is not bounded by one, and clamping it to a byte is what turns a bright interior into a flat grey one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters
member.summary: The volumetric fog's grid and the parameter block its two dispatches read, the same for every backend.

remarks.para: The grid is a frustum in disguise -- screen tiles across and down, depth slices deep -- so a lookup from the shading pass is a single fetch at the pixel's own screen position and depth. The FogScatter module lights it, FogIntegrate accumulates it front to back, and the shading samples the result.

Written once here so that the renderers cannot drift apart: the parameter block's layout is the shaders' FogParams, and the slice distribution is what the shading must agree on to find the slice the integration wrote.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.TilePixels
member.summary: How many screen pixels one froxel spans, across and down.
member.remarks: Sixteen. Every lamp is tested against every cell, so the cost grows with the cell count, and sixteen keeps that count low for a medium whose whole nature is low frequency.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.MinSlices
member.summary: The fewest depth slices the quality dial can ask for.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.MaxSlices
member.summary: The most depth slices the quality dial can ask for.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.HistoryWeight
member.summary: How much of the previous frame's answer a froxel keeps.
member.remarks: Nine tenths: the new sample contributes a tenth, so the eight jitter offsets are averaged over roughly a cycle while a change in the lighting still settles within a few tenths of a second.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.TeleportMetres
member.summary: How far the camera may travel in one frame before the accumulated volume is thrown away, in metres.
member.remarks: A walk or a sprint moves a fraction of this and the reprojection handles it. A jump this large is a teleport -- a level change, a spawn, a camera cut -- and reprojecting through it drags the fog of one place over another for the ten or so frames the blend takes to forget it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.ShadowBias
member.summary: A depth bias on the shadow lookup, in the map's own normalised depth.
member.remarks: Small, and constant across cascades: a point of air does not shadow itself, and the only thing this has to clear is the depth quantisation of the map.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.Floats
member.summary: The number of floats in the parameter block both dispatches read.
member.remarks: Two rotations and four cascades of matrix, seventeen vectors of scalars, then the volumes, the lamps and the flashlight.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.FlashlightOffset
member.summary: Where in the block the flashlight starts, in floats.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.ExtensionFloats
member.summary: The vectors appended after the flashlight: phase, dust, records, the field's misc, origins and ranges.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.SunAngularRadiusSine
member.summary: The sine of the sun's angular radius, which a traced froxel aims across.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.DustReachMetres
member.summary: How far from the eye the outdoor dust thins out over, in metres.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.DepthDistributionScale
member.summary: How quickly the depth slices grow with distance.
member.remarks: The slice index runs as this many times the base-two logarithm of an affine function of depth, so a larger value spaces the slices more evenly and a smaller one crowds them towards the eye. Thirty-two keeps the near slices a fraction of a metre thick while the far ones still reach the fog's distance.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.NearOffsetMetres
member.summary: How far beyond the near plane the first slice starts, in metres.
member.remarks: The air between the lens and the near plane plus this is too thin to matter, and starting the grid a little out keeps the first, thinnest slices from being spent on it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.Grid(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: The grid for a render size and a quality.
member.param: The render width in pixels.
The render height in pixels.
How many depth slices the quality dial asks for.
member.returns: The froxel counts across, down and deep.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogParameters.SliceDistribution(System.Single,System.Single,System.Int32)
member.summary: The exponential slice distribution, pinned so that slice 0 lies at the effective near depth and the last slice's far face at the fog's reach.
member.remarks: Depth runs as z(s) = n + (f - n) (2^(s/S) - 1) / (2^(N/S) - 1), which the shaders evaluate in the form s = S log2(B z + O). Solved in double precision: the offset is a small difference of large terms when the slices are many.
member.param: The near plane, in metres.
How far the fog reaches, in metres.
How many slices the grid is deep.
member.returns: B, O and S, with one over the slice count.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.VolumetricFogSettings
member.summary: The participating medium the scene is seen through.

remarks.para: The original's fog is a single exponential in view depth, packed into a vertex alpha byte — a distance haze and nothing more. It cannot pool in a valley, it does not know the sun is there, and nothing can cast a shaft through it, because it has no notion of where anything is. This describes a medium instead: something with a density that varies through the world and that scatters the sun's light towards the eye.
The faithful exp2(-z·k) path is a separate, later piece of work and is what -vanilla restores; nothing here tries to be it.

member.param: Extinction per metre at the base height. How quickly the medium swallows what is behind it.
The height in metres over which density falls to a third. This is what makes fog pool: without it a medium is uniform and reads as a flat wash rather than as air.
The world height, in metres, at which applies.
How much of what the medium takes out of a beam it scatters rather than absorbs, per channel. Near white for water droplets; lower and tinted for smoke and dust.

The Henyey–Greenstein parameter, from −1 to 1. Positive scatters forward, which is why a fog bank glows when you look towards the sun and stays flat when you look away — and is most of what makes volumetric fog read as light rather than as a grey filter. Around 0.7 for atmospheric haze.
How far, in metres, the medium is marched. Beyond it the cheaper analytic haze takes over, because marching to a 4 km far plane would spend the whole budget on air nobody can resolve.
How many samples each ray takes. The single biggest cost, and the quality dial.

How much of the phase function is spread back towards isotropic, from 0 to 1, standing in for the multiple scattering a single-scattering march does not simulate. Without it the medium is blinding towards the sun and invisible away from it.

The share of , from 0 to 1, that does not thin with height. A purely height-banded medium vanishes the moment the camera climbs out of it — which is right for a valley seen from a ridge, and wrong for the ridge itself, because real air hazes the distance at altitude too. This is that floor: the level's own atmosphere keeps its depth wherever the player stands, while the banded remainder still pools in the low ground.
A multiplier on the sun's contribution to in-scattering.
A multiplier on the sky's contribution.
The density, per metre, of the fine dust out of doors near the eye: it scatters the sun and the lamps and nothing else, and is what a shaft of light or a floodlight's cone is seen in.
The same dust's density indoors, where the medium itself is nought.
