member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.WeatherCVars.WeatherForce
member.summary: Whether weather falls in levels the retail data never gave any.
member.remarks: Only three of the retail missions author a RainEffect task, so without this the weather can only ever be looked at in those three -- which is not enough to tune it, and not enough to find the places it goes wrong. Forcing it ignores the level's own answer and uses everywhere; the level's authored fall band is replaced by the renderer's own defaults, since a level with no rain task has no band to read.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.WeatherCVars.Storm
member.summary: Whether the remastered storm replaces the original's rain band.

remarks.para: Off under vanilla, because the original's rain is a fixed band of thin vertical streaks and that is what vanilla means here. Everywhere above it the storm is a real particle system: drops blown by a gusting wind, leaning the way they travel, sheltered by roofs and answered by splashes on the ground.
The two never draw together. Rain that is drawn twice does not read as heavier rain, it reads as rain with a second, wrong-looking layer behind it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.WeatherCVars.Wetness
member.summary: Whether the storm wets the ground it falls on.

remarks.para: Separate from because it is a different renderer doing different work: the storm is particles in the forward pass, and this is every surface in the frame being shaded as wet — darker, glossier, and holding standing water wherever the ground is level and low. That is deferred work, so it needs the deferred path and it costs what a handful of extra instructions per shaded pixel costs.

It is what the rain is for, visually. Drops falling past a bone-dry road read as an effect laid over the level; the same drops over ground that darkens, pools and throws the sky back up at the camera read as weather the level is in.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.WetnessSettings
member.summary: How wet the world is: what the rain has done to the ground, as opposed to the rain itself.

remarks.para: Why this is not part of the storm. Falling drops are particles and belong to whoever draws particles. Standing water is a property of every surface in the frame — it darkens albedo, collapses roughness, flattens the normal and puts the sky in the floor — and none of that can be done by drawing anything on top. It has to happen where the surface is shaded, so it arrives at the device as its own state and is applied in the deferred lighting pass to whatever the G-buffer holds.

Applied at shading, not in the G-buffer. The obvious place is the G-buffer fragment shader, which is where a surface's material is decided. It cannot go there: that shader has no world position and no room in its push constants to be given one, and a puddle is a function of world XY before it is a function of anything else. The lighting pass already reconstructs world position from depth for the probe lookup, so it gets the puddles for free. The cost of that choice is that passes reading the G-buffer normal — the gather, the temporal filter — do not see the ripples; what they see is the dry surface, which is stable, and it is the specular response that sells wet ground anyway.
Everything is in metres and seconds, matching rather than the world's own units, and converted once where it is used.

member.param: How wet the world is, 0 dry to 1 soaked. Scales every other effect here, so a single number turns the whole thing off and a storm can bring it up as it settles in.
What share of level ground stands under water, 0 to 1. Not a multiplier on the wetness: a road can be soaked and hold no puddles at all, and one that is merely damp can still have every hollow full.
How far across one hollow in the ground is. The puddle mask is a height field at this scale, and water fills what is below the level sets.

How hard the rain strikes standing water, 0 to 1. This is the rain's own intensity rather than a look control: it decides how many of the staggered ripple layers are running, so a drizzle rings a few slow circles and a downpour boils.
The spacing of the ripple lattice: how far apart drops strike.

How much the wind textures the water, 0 to 1. Separate from the rain's ripples because it outlasts them — a puddle goes on being ruffled after the shower has passed, and water that is glass-flat the instant the rain stops reads as a mirror lying in the road.
Elapsed seconds, which the ripples and the wind are animated from. Supplied rather than read from a clock inside the shader so that a captured frame is reproducible.

member.summary: A dry world: what a level with no weather submits, and what every backend starts at.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.WetnessSettings.Storm
member.summary: A street in steady rain: what the storm brings the ground up to at full intensity.

remarks.para: Soaked but not drowned. The wetness stops short of one so that the damp darkening and the puddle mask keep some headroom, and a little under half of the level ground stands under water, which is enough for the yard to read as flooded in patches without turning into a lake.

The ripple lattice is half a metre, which puts a few strikes in every puddle a stride across and keeps each ring big enough to see from standing height. The wind's ruffle is kept low: it is the texture a puddle keeps between strikes, not a wave pattern of its own.

member.returns: The scaled settings.
member.remarks: The coverage and the ripples scale, the puddle and ripple sizes do not: a lighter shower makes smaller puddles and quieter water, it does not make the hollows in the road move further apart.
